title: possible OAuth2 regression: expires_in seems to get ignored
body:
After deploying a new version of the prom/prometheus images last week we see prometheus requesting a new OAuth token for every scrape, before that it would correctly honor the expires_in timeout provided in the response. 

Our token response looks like this: 
```json
{
  "access_token": "SECRET_TOKEN_HERE",
  "token_type": "bearer",
  "expires_in": 3600
}
```

scrape config:
```yaml
    -   job_name: app_metrics
        metrics_path: /api/metrics
        scheme: https
        oauth2:
            client_id: prometheus
            client_secret_file: /run/secrets/monitoring_user_password
            token_url: 'https://nginx/api/auth/token'
            tls_config:
                insecure_skip_verify: true
        scrape_interval: 1m
        tls_config:
            # we need to skip tls verification here because we do not have a valid cert for the "nginx" hostname
            # we cannot set a proper hostname via environment variables because prometheus does not support them here
            # and we do not want to build a config at container runtime/startup
            # and we cannot use http because the nginx config does not support that atm
            # its ""safe"", because  (a) we only fetch metrics and (b) all communication is local
            insecure_skip_verify: true
        static_configs:
            -   targets: [ 'nginx' ]
```

Before 1st of July we generated one token per host per hour for prometheus, after deploying a new container version that went up 60 per host per hour, which is one per scrape: 

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7e69568a-ad7a-440a-b815-589b487db427)

Since we did not change the API, and the change matches the release time of v2.53.5 (aka "prom/prometheus:latest" on docker hub), [which also updated the go oauth2 package](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/commit/b0b3676f351e9ab5875b24aaf4a582eaa22b7615#diff-75ac49421e167637c6c5bb17a75652f6bdd91b11a61fd441c5fa9b8140469e85R52-R64) I think the new prometheus version changed something. 

What I am trying to find out here is this: Are we doing something wrong that _somehow_ worked with a previous version of prometheus, but does not work anymore, or is there a new bug in prometheus that incorreclty handles token expiry?

title: WAL checkpoint can drop series references still needed for samples kept in checkpoint
body:
### Context

`wlog.Checkpoint` takes several parameters which govern the checkpointing process:
- `mint` is the timestamp at which the WAL is being truncated
- `first` is the id number of the first non-checkpoint WAL segment
-  `last` is the id number of the last WAL segment that will be included in the checkpoint
   - [this is set to 2/3 of current last WAL segment](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/tsdb/head.go#L1327-L1334)
- `keep` is a function that takes a series ref and `last` and returns whether the series record is still necessary after WAL segment `last` is deleted

The checkpoint process then scans through the old checkpoint and WAL segments `[first, last]` and:
- for each series encountered, writes it into the new checkpoint if `keep` returns `true`, and drops it otherwise
- for each other type of record encountered, writes the samples/histograms/etc. into the new checkpoint if their timestamp is `> mint`, and drops it otherwise

Lastly it deletes WAL segments `[first, last]` from disk.

### Issue

WAL segments are not time aligned, so `mint` will almost always fall in the middle of the timerange contained within some WAL segment. (In fact, WAL segments are not guaranteed to be non-overlapping, so it's possible for `mint` to fall in the middle of multiple WAL segment timeranges).

The problem occurs if a series is marked as not necessary after a WAL segment `X` (`keep` for the series returns `false`), but some samples for that series appear in segment `X` with timestamps `> mint`. The checkpoint will throw away the series reference, but copy over the samples `> mint`. The next time the WAL is replayed those samples will be missing a series reference and will be dropped.

### Example

Details from an occurance in a production system:
- series `foo` that has samples in the WAL through segment `3108`, the last one at `ts = 08:00:00.087Z`
- the WAL segments contains records with the following time ranges:
   ```
   ...
   segment 3106 has samples from 07:48:00Z to 07:56:09Z
   segment 3107 has samples from 07:51:00Z to 07:59:25Z
   segment 3108 has samples from 07:55:00Z to 08:00:04Z
   ...
   ```
- the checkpoint runs with:
   - `mint = 08:00:00Z`
   - `last = 3110`

The result is that the series record for `foo` is dropped but the sample at `ts = 08:00:00.087Z` is written into the checkpoint.

I've written a unit test that demonstrates this [here](https://github.com/pr00se/prometheus/commit/9cfcba4c16cfe6cf9a97cf70548173e87af93f3b). You can see the failure [here](https://github.com/pr00se/prometheus/actions/runs/16181960623/job/45680325531).

---

In practice, https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/12286 actually prevents this from happening for series that are deleted from the head during routine garbage collection. However, since https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/16060 duplicate series encountered during WAL replay are similarly marked as "deleted" with their expiries set much closer to the actual WAL segment their final samples exist in, making this issue more likely to occur.

title: prometheus-agent: Attach source IP
body:
### Proposal

I have a dynamic set of nodes which forward metrics to a central server using prometheus-agent. The nodes show up by hostname. The config looks like this:

```
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: node
    # Scrape node-exporter from this node
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['localhost:9100']

    relabel_configs:
      - target_label: instance
        replacement: "mynode-183:9100"

remote_write:
  - url: "http://10.40.20.20:9090/api/v1/write"
    queue_config:
      batch_send_deadline: 5s
      max_samples_per_send: 500
      max_shards: 10
```

Where `mynode-183` is the hostname of the node, injected into the config by a script that runs on startup.

To detect misconfiguration (duplicate hostnames), I now want to see on the central server, which metric comes from which IP (in addition to the hostname). Easy enough, I'll just add:
```
      - source_labels: [__address__]
        target_label: exported_address
        replacement: "INJECT_IP_ADDR"
```

plus a script which gets the IP and injects it into the config..and hopes that it remains static until reboot..

I think that prometheus should provide more support in tracking where metrics are being pushed from.

title: Templated Alerting Rules cause refirings (state lost)
body:
### What did you do?

When an `AlertingRule` is defined using labels that contain a Go template (e.g: `instance_ext=instance_{{ $labels.instance }}`, storing the state works correctly (label is templated), but retrieving the state is broken as it queries for the un-evaluated template.  
  
This leads to refirings when the ruler is restarted as the previous alert state isn't considered anymore.

### What did you expect to see?

The state is restored correctly, by querying for the right labels

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

The store is queried with `"instance_{{ $labels.instance }}"` - which is wrong.

This happens _always_ when at least one template is defined in the alert - which breaks its state.
This bug was introduced in 1dd0bff (#13980) (v2.53.0 / 0.53.0). This propagated to Thanos with version `v0.36.0-rc.0` (last known good version is `v0.35.1`).


By reverting the commit - I was able to confirm that the state is restored correctly when templated labels are used.

title: tsdb: use Matcher.Prefix() when traversing on-disk block postings offset table
body: ### Background When finding matching posting lists for a matcher both the head and the block index readers traverse the whole set of label values. https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/b07b5521395e9a6ed008895a7b3ca1d785a1467e/tsdb/index/index.go#L1796-L1811 ### Problem Sometimes a matcher is a prefix matcher, so it matches a continuous set of values. The label values in the postings offset table in the block are sorted. Traversing all other values in the block is unnecessary and can be expensive This is a profile form a Mimir ingester ### Proposal In the block index reader 1. Add prefix to the `IndexReader.PostingsForLabelMatching`: `PostingsForLabelMatching(ctx context.Context, name string, prefix string, match func(string) bool)` 2. Use binary search to offset to a posting list which has the prefix. 3. Stop traversing the posting lists when we meet the first value which doesn't have the offset anymore.

title: scrape endpoint: Support dynamic output for browser agents
body:
### Proposal

Users often use a web browser to test their endpoints, to confirm that their metrics are working.  Content Negotiation with the scrape endpoint is done solely through the Accept and Content Type headers, which cannot reasonable be configured when using a web browser. When the endpoint receives no specific Accept headers, it returns the oldest/simplest scrape output it supports, Prometheus 0.0.1 text format.

This fallback behavior can cause confusion, for instance when a user is expecting UTF-8 characters but the browser only shows underscore-escaped metrics.

I suggest we do some basic user agent sniffing to detect browsers and use that to trigger some changes to the scrape output:

- Comments at the top of the output giving some status, such as the format of the output (Content Type values).
- Default to UTF-8 display (this will not change the output for users with legacy metric/label names).
- Support URL parameters to change the desired output -- escaping selections, optional exemplar display, etc
- Optionally: a drop-down selector to provide the user an easy way to set those URL parameters.

One small edge case is we would have to decide if URL parameters override content negotiation headers if they are also provided.

title: Support for instant queries with string literal or range vector results in PromQL test scripting language
body:
### Proposal

During testing of the Mimir Query Engine there were a number of valid instant queries which could not be defined and tested within the PromQL test scripting language.

It is currently not possible to use the script language to define a string literal instance query. ie

 `eval instant at 50m "Foo"`

It is also not currently possible to use the script language to define an instant query which returns a range vector. ie 

`eval instant at 1m some_metric[1m]`

An example of how these test scripts could look if supported are as follows;

```
eval instant at 50m ("Foo")
	"Foo"

eval instant at 50m "Foo"
	"Foo"

eval instant at 50m ("")
	""

eval instant at 50m ""
	""
```

With the following example I have introduced a new expect directive to allow for the specification of the expected range timestamps. 

```
load 10s
  some_metric{env="a"} 1+1x5
  some_metric{env="b"} 2+2x5

# Return a range vector - note that we use the range vector to define our expected timestamps in the result vectors
eval instant at 1m some_metric[1m]
  expect range vector from 10s to 1m step 10s
  some_metric{env="a"} 2 3 4 5 6
  some_metric{env="b"} 4 6 8 10 12
```

title: MemPostings is a performance bottleneck for some scenarios
body:
### What did you do?

As noted a while ago on #13642 MemPostings, which implements the index for in-memory series, can be a performance bottleneck because it's simply a very large Go map with a single mutex.
This single mutex serialises all writes to that map and so there's a limit to the speed at which we can insert new series into the map.
Since the index is used for all reads (queries) and writes (scrapes) the performance here is pretty important. This is further complicated by the requirement that the list of series IDs must be always returned as sorted, so it's sorted on write.
It is usually is fast enough, mostly because by nature of metrics the vast majority of operations are read, not write, but there are cases where it is super slow - this is mostly when we need to quickly append a huge number of series to the index. This is when:
- We replay the WAL on startup - we need to write IDs of all series in the WAL
- A new scrape job is added with tons of series, or existing job adds tons of new series - we need to append IDs of new series
- We start with no WAL - after first scrape of each target we will need to append IDs of all scraped series


The most common scenario is probably replaying the WAL and this is why WAL replay disables sorting on append, instead it sorts everything once replay is done. While WAL is replayed nobody can query the index so that' fine. WAL replay also hides a lot of issues with performance of the index - if it's slow replay takes longer but there's no impact on queries or scrapes (because they cannot happen at this point).

But for less common scenarios that result in a big batch of writes the performance is pretty poor. The easiest way to reproduce it is to take a Prometheus instance that scrape a large pool of targets and scrapes ~30M time series, stop it, remove all WAL files and start it. You will see that it takes 30-60M for such instance to full write all series from initial scrapes and stabilise append rate. During that time any alerting rules might fire with false positives because the data in the index is incomplete until all series are written.

#13642 tried to improve this via sharding, but it was pointed out that sharding would break atomicity of writes of a labels set, since different labels would end up on different shard, so there could be races when we query data back.

Would be great if MemPostings performance was improved but given the requirements of:
- Returned data must be sorted 
- Atomicity of writes must be preserved

it's hard to solve this easily. Especially that there might be other requirements.
For example: we could buffer writes via a channel and a background goroutine that does the actual write, but would that be ok?

### What did you expect to see?

_No response_

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

Prometheus started with no WAL files is very slow for the first N minutes

title: Handle OOMs gracefully by rejecting scrapes adding new series
body:
### Proposal

With sudden growth of series, sometimes it is inevitable to hit OOMs in Prometheus. But instead of halting the scrapes altogether, we can instead reject scrapes that try to add new series to the TSDB (partial scrapes is not okay, so we must reject entire scrape). This can have an associated metric to alert on, and by doing so, Prometheus will run in a degraded state until the memory issue is fixed and won't halt operation altogether.

The proposal is we add a flag to Prometheus telling us the threshold when to start rejecting scrapes (tooling can derive this number from the memory allocated, eg. 90% of memory requested, leaving 10% buffer for the new samples until some action is taken). `runtime` package will allow us to see how much memory is Prometheus consuming from the perspective of OS.

title: index.ExpandPostings: double slice size instead of using append
body:
Using `append` leads to more frequent resizing and copying of the slice


https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/6693a913b24cca33b98a2d98f1f954d8415a4583/tsdb/index/postings.go#L537-L543


If we manually double the size of the slice ourselves, this should help with heap fragmentation and reduce the CPU overhead of copying. 

There are no benchmarks for `index.ExpandPostings`, so a benchmark would be helpful to see the impact of the change on differently-sized `Postings` implementations

title: LFX Mentorship: Wireframes for "Exploration" use-cases
body:
# What the Mentorship will explore?

During the [March-May/2025 cohort of LFX mentorships](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/15909), we performed UX Research to explore users' problems when sending and using OpenTelemetry Resource Attributes to Prometheus.

The research was successful, and we've identified many areas for improvement. One amongst them is what we're planning to investigate even further during the September-November 2025 cohort of LFX.

While interviewing OpenTelemetry and Prometheus Stakeholders, we've noticed how they were originally designed with different use cases in mind:
* Prometheus: Monitoring, where you know precisely the signals your infrastructure is exposing, and you keep the amount of volume under control. When looking for data, you know exactly what you want, write your PromQL query, get your result, and are happy.

* OpenTelemetry: Exploration, where you ingest all kinds of available telemetry and slice and dice it with different "lenses". You may want to look at your data from a "This is a Kubernetes Cluster" point of view, or "This is a fleet of Virtual Machines" point of view, or "This is a set of services performing HTTP requests " point of view. You look for relationships in your telemetry, suggesting a UI oriented approach rather than writing queries yourself.

## What we look for in candidates

We're looking for UI/Product Designers or UX Researchers with strong design skills.

Prometheus is developed by a community, and it depends on people who are genuinely interested in joining that community!  We'd love to see a candidate who has similar interests and wants to find a way to be helpful among many developers.

## Expected outcome from this mentorship

Two or more sets of wireframes that present the user journey for the exploration use case.

## Study material for candidates

We suggest understanding Prometheus and OpenTelemetry, how they differ, and how they work together.
We understand Designers don't have much contact with them and we don't expect any experts in this area, but knowing the basics will definitely help :)

Going through the [interviews](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLK87GQAYMTgM9Q5vjz7gIp8hW0o53FubD) and [blog post](https://opentelemetry.io/blog/2025/ux-research-prometheus-otel) from the previous mentorship can also help!

title: Add native syntax support for repeating time series in unit tests
body:
### Proposal

Prometheus currently lacks native syntax for expressing repeated time series patterns in unit tests. This limitation becomes especially problematic when testing rules that involve counting large numbers of series, such as:
```
count (kube_pod_container_status_waiting !=0 ) > 500
```
To simulate such scenarios, users must manually copy and paste hundreds or thousands of distinct series into the input_series block of the unit test, which is error-prone, inefficient, and difficult to maintain.

**Proposal**
Introduce a concise syntax for generating repeated or templated time series within unit tests, e.g. 
```
input_series:
  - series: 'kube_pod_container_status_waiting{environment="prod", pod="pod_${counter}"}'
    values: '1+0x10'
    repeat: 1000
```

title: WAL Replay not using more memory than before the restart
body:
This is to track some ideas from https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/6934

The current algorithm tries to replay WAL as fast as possible after restart, which can use more memory than the Prometheus use.

This could be problematic for cases where Prometheus is under pressure (tons of metrics and low memory limit) and some operation like an expensive query or API call is OOM-ing it. The recovery is impossible due to startup using even more memory, so manual removal of WAL is needed. 

For any other OOMs around too many series scraped, where no specific query or API caused the OOM, but it's just high use due to too many series scraped, this feature (improving startup use) is not going to help alone, but might unlock other options like compact/truncate on start to move big load to TSDB blocks for further debugging and work.

Please use this issue if you have thoughts around replay memory consumption alone. To discuss the OOM detection ideas and the general OOM handling or safeguards, let's use the https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/13939 issue. For the general unexpected OOMs, where clearly Prometheus uses unexpected amount of memory, given the scraped/ingested load you put through it, please open separate issue.

## Acceptance Criteria

* A mode (or by default, if fast enough) where Prometheus startup does not use more memory then the "normal" use.  

## Ideas

* Add a mode where Prometheus is slowing down and replaying in segments that guarantee stable resource usage.
* Truncate before replay (https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/13939)
* General garbage optimizations if possible.

title: [nhcb] Add PromQL compatibility layer for querying nhcb as classic histogram
body:
Essentially implementing logic similar to [PROM-31 reading via PromQL option 3](https://github.com/prometheus/proposals/blob/main/proposals/0031-classic-histograms-stored-as-native-histograms.md#reading-via-promql-2) but as a standalone Prometheus PromQL feature flag.

## Motivation

NHCB was created to allow custom bucket use cases while providing some benefits of the exponential native histogram like improved TSDB and WAL efficiency, transactionality for exporting/importing and consistent new PromQL syntax.

Unfortunately that PromQL syntax change feels like the main friction for users and it's hard to have Prometheus with nhcb benefits for storage and remote write without rewriting user queries.

For this reason `promq-nhcb-as-classic` feature flag is proposed that will cause all nhcb to look as normal classic histogram on the PromQL side. This is relatively easy logic that can sit in the middleware between TSDB and PromQL (storage interface), similar to https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/16841 work.

With such a flag, Prometheus operators will be able to switch to nhcb without users noticing, literally means replacing classic histograms with native ones under the hood, while making sure queries still work. 

Just to state the obvious: It's not possible to present exponential native histograms as classic histograms, because that would defeat the benefits of the resolution conversion and it would be unreadable (too many buckets).

## Risks

* One argument is that this work is futile, given the user has to eventually switch the syntax to the new histograms anyway; in fact we might demotivate people from doing so. The counter argument is that I don't see  users switching to nhcb alone without that, because some the friction of changing PromQL is just too high and too scary. Furthermore the motivation for the new syntax should be the ability to NOT manually specify buckets and auto resolution change of exponential buckets, which nhcb's won't give.
* Query performance impact. For the main use case being Prometheus operators switching to nhcb without users noticing, I don't see any huge query overhead for the simple algorithm below on a single Prometheus box -- it's quite rare to ingest metric_bucket{} and metric{} (e.g. a gauge) in the same time. One interesting case is the migration option of exposing both native and classic histogram - but in this case no one will use the `promql-nhcb-as-classic` and `convert_classic_histograms_to_nhcb` options and if they do, they do the performance would be on par with querying nhcb using native PromQL syntax.
* Further ecosystem adoption impact (Thanos, Mimir, Cortex) -- those does not need to implement this flag, although transactionality and efficiency might encourage them - there's no requirement though.

## Potential algorithm

* Direct series selection of metric_bucket{} would have to look up metric_bucket{} and metric{}; ignore metric{} samples that are not nhcb and return the float buckets decoded directly or from the custom histogram.
* Direct series selection of metric_count{} similar to buckets, look up both metric{} and metric_count{}. Ignore metric{} samples that are not nhcb. 
* Direct series selection of metric_sum{} similar to buckets, look up both metric{} and metric_sum{}. Ignore metric{} samples that are not nhcb. 

Querying metric{} should work on nhcb as well as it is now.

This can happen behind the select interface. In future a hint could be passed to allow further systems (e.g. TSDB blocks to know which type to return).

cc @krajorama @beorn7 WDYT? I remember we discussed this at some point and we rejected this as too much work for the benefit, but within Prometheus only scope alon, given hard requirements on Remote Write transactionality for some receivers (Otel and Google), and relatively easy algorithm and implementation, perhaps it's challenable?  (:

title: Native Summaries
body:
### Proposal

This requires a bigger proposal, MVP and motivation, but I wanted to officially start early discussions and potential work here.

The idea is to introduce the native summaries -- the replacement for "[classic summaries](https://prometheus.io/docs/specs/om/open_metrics_spec/#summary-1)" we have now that is build from multiple counter series. Native summaries would be contained as a single series that's more efficient and transactional. 

PromQL could be adapted in similar fashion to native histogram PromQL syntax for consistency (also reusing the https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/functions/#histogram_count-and-histogram_sum functions). However due to lower, mostly historic use of summaries in the ecosystem (see Considerations), perhaps it would be easier and sufficient to only emulate classic view while storing native summaries under the hood (similar to https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/16948 idea).

## Motivation

Native histograms were created for many reasons, but one of them was storage efficiency and transactionality. With native histogram representation, you don't have potentially 30 series for one histogram, but one which makes for incredible benefits around indexing and storage, despite more beefier sample size (float vs struct).

As per transactionality, having one series and not 30 also gives guarantee that all parts of the Prometheus (and ecosystem) will see each part of histogram (buckets, sum, count) exactly at once. This is especially important for distributed systems with remote write and sharding, as well as querying vs scraping drift etc (when no isolation is possible e.g. on Thanos).

The same efficiency and transactionality problem exists for classic summaries as well, solved by adding the native summaries.

## Considerations

* Summaries are still used widely, although less than other types. However we tend to NOT recommend them in practice, especially with the new improved native histograms. However they do still exists and are not deprecated (and there is not plan for that as of now).
* Native histograms brought sparseness and exponential bucketing; there is no such dimension in native summaries planned -- which makes them easier to implement.

WDYT @krajorama @beorn7 @bboreham @roidelapluie @RichiH

title: Functions for range and subquery range_start_ts(), range_end_ts(), range_span_seconds(), range_step_seconds()
body:
### Proposal

To make it easier to write range queries without relying so heavily on client-side substitution of time range and duration values, it would be extremely helpful to have functions that evaluate to the range query (or subquery)'s start-timestamp, end-timestamp, and most importantly step duration in seconds.

## The problem

Presently, if I have a client executing a range query in 30s steps over a 10m time span, then executing it in 1h steps over a 24h time span, I have no way to make the PromQL itself adapt to this. This is most important for the step duration.

E.g. if I want a range query showing the periods in which containers are unready, I can write:

```promql
# find containers that were unready over any part of the range
group by (uid, container) (
  min_over_time(kube_pod_container_status_ready[10m] @ end()) == 0
)
# Only report range query results for containers that were unready at any point
# in the overall range
* on (uid, container)
  group_right()
  min by (uid, container, pod, namespace) (
      # only examine container readiness states for samples strictly in the time
      # period of this range step.
      avg_over_time(kube_pod_container_status_ready[30s])
  )
```

... but I have to hard-code the range duration (`10m`) and step (`30s`) in the query itself, or rely on client-side query substitution. And as there's no standard for such substitution this makes the queries harder to author in a manner that's portable between rules, dashboards, etc.

## Proposed solution

I want to instead be able to use the currently-nonexistent function-like expressions `range_step_seconds()` and `range_span_seconds()` to make the query adapt to the execution context. 

### Spec

The following expressions would be evaluated to float values in units of seconds (time spans or unix epoch timestamps as appropriate):

* `range_step_seconds()` - evaluates to the step size in seconds for the range query *or subquery* currently executing
* `range_span_seconds()` - evaluates to the total time-span covered by the current range query *or subquery*
* `range_start_ts()` - evaluates to the start timestamp for the current range query *or subquery* ; not the same as `@ start()` because it can be used outside modifier context, and it works within subqueries in instant queries
* `range_end_ts()` -  evaluates to the end timestamp for the current range query *or subquery*; same comments as start

*`range_step_start_ts()` -  evaluates to the start timestamp for the current range query or subquery's step, the timestamp at which `metric{}[range_step_seconds()]` begins
* `range_step_end_ts()` -  evaluates to the end timestamp for the current range query or subquery's step, the timestamp at which `metric{}[range_step_seconds()]` ends
* `range_step_count()` - convenience for `range_span_seconds() / range_step_seconds()`

`range_end_ts()` is distinct from `timestamp(last_over_time(up{}[range_span_seconds()]))` in that it (a) is cheaper and (b) returns the exact timestamp of the end-of-range, not the timestamp of the sample timestamp closest to the end of the range. And `range_start_ts()` is even more important due to PromQL's lack of `first_over_time(...)`.

`range_step_start_ts()` and `range_step_end_ts()` should be usable in `@` modifiers and anywhere a float-literal is accepted.

`range_step_seconds()` and `range_span_seconds()` should be usable:

* in range selectors e.g. `foo[range_span_seconds()]`, `foo[range_step_seconds()]`
* in subquery range specifiers e.g. `(expr)[1h:range_step_seconds()]`, `(expr)[range_span_seconds():5s]`, `(expr)[1h:range_step_seconds()]`, `(expr)[range_span_seconds():range_step_seconds()]` 
* where float literals are accepted e.g. `foo / range_span_seconds()`
* in `offset` modifiers e.g. `offset range_span_seconds()`

`range_start_ts()`, `range_end_ts()`, `range_step_end_ts()` and `range_step_end_ts()` should be usable:

* in `@` modifiers
* anywhere a float literal is legal

### Details and examples

It would

title: Add first_over_time() and ts_of_first_over_time()
body:
### Proposal

PromQL presently lacks `first_over_time()` and `ts_of_first_over_time()` functions to pair with the current `last_over_time()` and new `ts_of_last_over_time()` functions.

This makes a variety of operations considerably more difficult, such as

* computing the duration over which a metric existed
* finding the timestamp a metric first appeared
* finding the first value of a metric within a step in a range query; currently it's necessary to use `last_over_time()` with `offset`, and that's only been made possible by [the new `step()` feature](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/16777)

I mostly feel the lack of `first_over_time()` when I'm trying to do meta-queries that are exploring and characterising metrics themselves.

For example, to find when a metric first appeared I need an inefficient and lower-resolution subquery based approach like:

```
min by (job) (min_over_time(timestamp(up{job=~"some-job"})[1d:5s]))
```

where the most recent timestamp can be trivially and considerably more efficiently found with:

```
max by (job) (ts_of_last_over_time(up{job=~"some-job"}[1d])
```

[VM recognised the need for this](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/8966#issuecomment-866734884) and added `tfirst_over_time(m[d])` etc. 

## Related

* https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/16722
* https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/16962

title: Support start(), end() and new step() function in subqueries
body:
### Proposal

It would be helpful to be able to use `@ end()`, `@ start()` and [the new `step()` pseudo-function](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/16777) in subqueries.

Presently `@ end()` and `@ start()` are eagerly expanded to the instant timestamp in an instant query. If the instant query contains a range subquery, this behaviour is surprising. This makes it difficult or impossible to construct queries like "for all metrics that satisfy condition X in any part of the period of interest, count the total number of time-slices in which they satisfied a condition".

One complexity of supporting this is how it should behave in nested subqueries - how does the author say "evaluate this in the context of the inner-most subquery" or "the outer-most subquery" etc. Do they need to take optional parameters for nesting levels? Or support labelling subqueries, and take a parameter for the label identifier?

Initially, even just evaluating them in the context of the outermost subquery in an instant query would be helpful.

## Related

* https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/16965

## References

* https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/15838
* https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/16962
* https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/16777

title: Support start(), end() and new step() in duration expressions, and where float literals are permitted
body:
### Proposal

It would be very helpful to be able to use the timestamp from `@ start()` and `@ end()` as a scalar anywhere that a float literal is permitted, such as:

* in scalar arithmetic expressions  for things like computing values per-second of the wall-clock range covered by the query ( `rate()` and `deriv()` compute it over the range-vector's time range, which may differ from the time-range of the query as a whole);
* in arithmetic in range and subquery selectors including the `min()` and `max()` introduced along with the [experimental new `step()` function](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/16777), to compute ranges like `foo[(end()-start())+step():step()]` to produce a subquery that targets values wholly within the outer range query's span, without the first step capturing values older than the start of the range query's span

It's possible to somewhat work around the current limitation with expressions  like `timestamp(last_over_time(up{}[5m]) @ end())` - but the timestamp reported will be the timestamp of the last sample in the range, which may be several seconds before the true end-of-range depending on the sample interval. It's also more difficult for the start timestamp [due to the lack of  a `first_over_time(...)` function](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/16963).

There's precedent for this in [the new `step()` pseudo-function](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/16777), which is accepted in range expressions though not yet in place of a literal:

```
$ promexec 'step()'
query error: bad_data: invalid parameter "query": 1:5: parse error: unknown node type: *parser.DurationExpr
command terminated with exit code 1
```

## Related

title: Add step_end(), step_start() for use in duration expressions and offsets to enable running aggregations (window expressions) like cumulative running sums
body:
### Proposal

It's difficult or impossible to write a running cumulative sum in PromQL at the moment, because:

* `end()` and `start()` are not supported in duration expressions like `step()` is, and there's no equivalent for the current step's bounds like `step_end()` and `step_start()`, so duration arithmetic like `sum_over_time(foo[(start() - step_end()])` is not possible; and
* There's no way to directly obtain an "index" or "step number" for the current range step being evaluated, so it cannot be multiplied by `step()` to compute a left-bound for a duration like `foo{}[(step()*step_index())]`.

## Proposal A

Add `step_start()` and `step_end()` pseudo-functions that can be used in duration expressions along with the current `step()`. Also permit `end()` and `start() ` to be used in duration expressions.

This makes it possible to express a left-bounded running sum as e.g.:

```
sum_over_time(
  foo{}[ (start() - step_end() ])
)
```

... by computing a range duration relative to the range start timestamp and the end-of-step timestamp. This implicitly executes `@ step_end()`.

For a right-accumulating running sum (counting down to the end), this would work:

```
sum_over_time(
  foo{}[ end() - step_start() ] @ end()
)
```

This would work in the duration and step parts of subquery duration expressions too.

If someone needs the 'index' of the current step, it could be derived with `step_start()/(end()-start()/step())`. It probably isn't useful enough to bother supporting directly.

## Proposal B

An alternative option would be support for _absolute time_ range selectors, which take epoch timestamp bounds instead of a duration, and would accept the same kind of expressions as a duration expression, including pseudo-functions `end()`, `start()`, `step()` and new  `step_end()` and `step_start()` .

These would take the form `selector{}[start_ts ..  end_ts]`.

E.g. to compute a left-accumulating running sum, one might write:

```
sum_over_time(
  foo{}[ start() .. step_end() ])
)
```

and for a right-accumulating sum (counting down to the end):

```
sum_over_time(
  foo{}[ step_start() .. end() ] @ end()
)
```

For subqueries nested in range queries, a step duration could be specified as normal e.g. `foo{}[start()..step_end():step()*2]`. In this case, if the absolute range's min and max timestamps are not evenly divisible by the step this will result in a range query with a shorter final step interval (and possibly a warning).

It'd also possibly make sense to support a slice expression form for subqueries, like `foo{}[start()..step_end()::10]` where the duration is left implied, and the desired number of evenly divided intervals is specified.

This syntax could be mildly convenient to make it easier for applications to cover exact ranges in queries without the need to covert the start-bound into a duration relative to the end-bound. But mostly it'd be useful for use with duration expressions.

## Related

* https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/16963
* https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/16964
* https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/16965
* https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/16962
*

title: promtest: load directive with mixed float/histogram series will silently discard all histogram samples before the first float sample
body:
### What did you do?

When writing a new test case to extend the tests for `count_over_time` and `last_over_time`, I added a mixed histogram/float series where some float samples arrive _after_ some histogram samples.

**TL/DR: [See this test case](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/17025#issuecomment-3166051620)**

Consider this promtest, which I will assume is to be placed at path `promql/promqltest/testdata/mix_histogram_over_time.test`:

```
load 10s
    data_histogram{type="mix_histfirst"} {{schema:0 sum:1 count:2}} {{schema:0 sum:2 count:3}} 0 1

eval instant at 1m count_over_time(data_histogram[2m])
    expect no_info
    expect no_warn
    {type="mix_histfirst"} 4

clear
```

and run as 

```sh
go test -v -run 'TestEvaluations/testdata/mix_histogram_over_time.test' ./promql
```

### What did you expect to see?

I expected the histogram samples to be retained irrespective of their order relative to float samples in the same series, so `count_over_time` would return 4 for the above series as the test case asserts.


### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

Surprisingly, the histogram samples in the series were completely ignored. `count_over_time` returns 2 for the series, as it counts only the float samples.

Not only that, but no warning or info message was reported by `promtest` (because the warning was at ingestion time in the `load` directive, not at runtime on the `eval` directive) so the failure occurred silently.

Running `go test -v -run 'TestEvaluations/testdata/mix_histogram_over_time.test' ./promql` will yield

```
=== RUN   TestEvaluations
=== RUN   TestEvaluations/testdata/mix_histogram_over_time.test
=== RUN   TestEvaluations/testdata/mix_histogram_over_time.test/line_5/count_over_time(data_histogram[2m])
    test.go:1321: 
        	Error Trace:	/home/craig/projects/EDB/UPM/upm-stack/prometheus/promql/promqltest/test.go:1321
        	Error:      	Received unexpected error:
        	            	error in eval count_over_time(data_histogram[2m]) (line 5): expected 4 for {type="mix_histfirst"} but got 2
        	Test:       	TestEvaluations/testdata/mix_histogram_over_time.test/line_5/count_over_time(data_histogram[2m])
--- FAIL: TestEvaluations (0.03s)
    --- FAIL: TestEvaluations/testdata/mix_histogram_over_time.test (0.03s)
        --- FAIL: TestEvaluations/testdata/mix_histogram_over_time.test/line_5/count_over_time(data_histogram[2m]) (0.00s)
FAIL
FAIL	github.com/prometheus/prometheus/promql	0.045s
FAIL
```

despite there clearly being 4 samples in the series.

If the order of the series is changed to

```
	data_histogram{type="mix_histfirst"} 0 1 {{schema:0 sum:1 count:2}} {{schema:0 sum:2 count:3}}
```

then the test will pass.

### Details

In promtest, histogram samples are silently dropped in a `load` directive containing mixed float and histogram samples. The dropped samples are _not_ detected by `expect no_info` or `expect no_warn`, resulting in confusing test run results.

This might also affect scrapes of real world endpoints if prometheus permits a client to emit multiple samples in one scrape so long as those series have client-defined timestamps; I haven't verified that. It seems like a very niche case though.

#### Analysis

Prometheus's appender discards histogram samples for series where there is a newer float sample than the histogram sample _in the same append transaction_ because it appends all histogram samples after all float samples, causing histogram samples older than the oldest float sample to be discarded as out-of-order.

https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/8f6a71e188aee13223e49ecfcc5333ab2167ffa7/tsdb/head_append.go?plain=1#L1497-L1499

This is usually harmless, because it wouldn't make sense to mix histogram and float samples in a single scrape.

But it _does_ affect the test suite, since `github.com/prometheus/prometheus/promql/promqltest.(*loadCmd).append()` appends all samples for a series in one transaction:

https://github.com/prom

title: Proposal: Add OR operator with parenthesis support for label matchers in PromQL
body:
## Motivation

Currently, PromQL has limitations when users need to express complex label matching conditions. While regex patterns can handle simple cases of matching multiple values for a single label (e.g., `{status=~"200|204|301"}`), they fall short for more complex scenarios involving different labels or combinations of conditions.

### Example

Let's say there is a need to query metrics from multiple services that are identified by different labels:
```
http_requests_total{env="production", cluster="west-1", cell="west-1-1", service="api-v1"} 
or http_requests_total{env="production", cluster="west-1", cell="west-1-1", app="api-v2"}
```
The current PromQL syntax requires writing multiple selectors and joining them using or, which is not very convenient and can lead to verbose queries.

Instead, it could be written more concisely with an OR operator:
```
http_requests_total{env="production", cluster="west-1", cell="west-1-1", (service="api-v1" or app="api-v2")}
```
The query translates to postings list math seamlessly, too.

## Industry Precedent

It could be argued that problems like these can be resolved by using a combination of relabeling/recording rules.
However, metric collection can be widely complex in large systems with many teams and services. Additionally, recording rules put an unnecessary load on the system.

Other competing TSDB solutions have support for similar syntax in their metrics languages:

### [VictoriaMetrics' MetricsQL](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/keyconcepts/#filtering-by-multiple-or-filters)
```
http_requests_total{env="production", cluster="west-1", cell="west-1-1", service="api-v1" or env="production", cluster="west-1", cell="west-1-1", app="api-v2"}
```
### [Datadog Query Language](https://docs.datadoghq.com/metrics/advanced-filtering/#boolean-filtered-query-examples)
```
http_requests_total{env:production AND cluster:west-1 AND west-1-1 AND (service:api-v1 or app=api-v2)}
```

## Proposed Syntax

If parentheses are present, groups are delimited by or. Each group maintains its functionality within. 
```
metrics{version="1", service="api" or version="2", app="api"}
```

Parentheses bound the matchers group:
```
metrics{(service="api" or app="api"), (version_v1="v1.0.0" or version_v2="1.0")}
```

There can be multiple levels of parentheses, so more complex matchers could be expressed:
```
sum(rate({
    env="production", 
    (
        (__name__="http_server_requests_total", status="200") 
        or 
        ({__name__="grpc_server_requests_total", status_code="OK"})
    )
)[5m]}
```

## Real-world use cases

### 1. Legacy System Migration
During modernization efforts, old and new systems often use different labeling conventions:
```
transaction_count{
  (component="billing-legacy", env="prod") or
  (service="billing-v2", environment="production") or
  (app="billing-modernized", stage="prod")
}
```
### 2. Querying metrics scraped with different labels
```
http_requests_total{env="production", (service="api-v1" or app="api-v2")}
```
### 3. Combining metrics with different label schema
```
sum(rate({
    env="production", 
    (
        (__name__="http_server_requests_total", status="200") 
        or 
        ({__name__="grpc_server_requests_total", status_code="OK"})
    )
)[5m]}
```

title: Non-cardinal labels
body:
### Proposal

GitHub issue #9139 explains under header "Proposal: non-cardinal labels" why labels which do not increase cardinality are a good idea.

This is my point of view: Because Alerts in Prometheus are not flexible enough (or maybe I've missed something), I have resorted to adding labels to some metrics in order to influence the associated alert. For example:
```
- job_name: 'blackbox-http'
  scrape_interval: 2m
  metrics_path: /probe
  params:
    module: [http_2xx]  # Look for an HTTP 200 response.
  static_configs:

    - targets:
      - http://192.168.1.10/
      labels:
        instance: 'my-normal-server'

    - targets:
      - http://192.168.1.11/
      labels:
        instance: 'my-unreliable-server'
        alert_for: 30m

```
Then, I have different alerts depending on the "alert_for" label value. They are almost identical, the only difference is the "for:" duration:

```
  - alert: BlackboxProbeFailed
    # This is the default rule for all jobs which have no 'alert_for'.
    expr: probe_success{alert_for=""} == 0
    for: 0s
    labels:
      severity: critical
    annotations:
      summary: Blackbox probe failed (instance {{ $labels.instance }})
      description: "Probe failed\n  VALUE = {{ $value }}\n  LABELS = {{ $labels }}"

  - alert: BlackboxProbeFailed30m
    expr: probe_success{alert_for="30m"} == 0
    for: 30m
    labels:
      severity: critical
    annotations:
      summary: Blackbox probe failed (instance {{ $labels.instance }})
      description: "Probe failed\n  VALUE = {{ $value }}\n  LABELS = {{ $labels }}"
```

This example is a simplification, I have whole groups of targets with different 'alert_for' values.

This label kludge does work, but, if I change the "alert_for" label value for a target or a group of them, the time series change, so I lose the continuous history.

I added label 'alert_for' just for alert management purposes, so it shouldn't really affect the cardinality.

title: Start scraping immediately on startup without waiting for WAL replay to finish
body: ## For potential LFX mentees This is now part of LFX mentorship program (2026 Mar-May) https://github.com/cncf/mentoring/tree/main/programs/lfx-mentorship/2026/01-Mar-May#start-scraping-immediately-on-startup-without-waiting-for-wal-replay-to-finish _Note: The content below can be updated anytime. It is recommended to keep an eye on it. But nothing should change drastically._ If you are interested in applying for this project, please read below. _Read the eligibility rules before you apply https://docs.linuxfoundation.org/lfx/mentorship/mentees#eligibility-rules-for-mentees_ **Knowledge building** * Catch up on any discussion that has happened on this issue so far. * Familiarize a bit with how WAL works at a high level because this is where the trickiest problems exist for this issue (shameless plug: maybe refer [this](https://ganeshvernekar.com/blog/prometheus-tsdb-wal-and-checkpoint) blog post for WAL in Prometheus, and perhaps also part 1 and part 3 posts) * Familiarize yourself with the series refs for the in-memory series ([this one](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/ade3f08eca384af91661f889c038707f21fd48d3/tsdb/head.go#L2386)) and how it links with the WAL (it is okay if you don't understand it completely). **Think about** * How you would solve these following problems * When you start scraping series immediately after Prometheus starts up, they will get some new series refs in the memory that are different from the WAL records. When you are replaying the WAL in parallel, how will you stitch those new series refs with the series refs in the WAL? A series is uniquely identified by its labels. * Currently WAL will not have duplicate series references because currently the head block always gives an auto-increment refs based on the last series ref. And it is non-trivial to deal with duplicate refs. But if we start scraping immediately after startup, we won't know what was the last ID. How do you solve this? There are multiple options here. We can store the last ref somewhere on disk, or come with a clever mechanism to handle duplicate refs in the WAL without huge performance bottleneck. What do you think will work the best? **Nice to mention in your cover letter** * How familiar are you with Go. * Briefly describe how would you approach the overall project. You do not need to explain the code level details or know the entire solution at this time. This is intentionally an open ended question. * Estimated timeline of your deliverables during the 3 month period (include at least 2 weeks to understand the code and the problem). * (optional) If you have any ideas for the above problems, feel free to describe that. It is okay to pick one of the ideas from the discussions here, BUT, explain it in your own words and do not paraphrase. **Few deliverables expected from you (during the program)** * Most of the communication will happen in writing. So, a written design doc detailing out the solution to this project and the series ref problems mentioned above. * A working PR with comprehensive test coverage. --- ### Proposal **Problem** See the parent issue that describes the problem in detail: https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/18073 The aim of this issue is to fix the gap in the raw scraped data when Prometheus is restarting. **Proposal** When Prometheus is replaying WAL, don't pause scraping. Start the scrapes immediately and stitch together the scraped data with WAL replay data. Comparing the diagram with the parent issue, once we start scraping immediately after startup, this is how the state will look. The gap will be filled for the raw data, but we will still have gaps for the rule data (yellow). Depending on how fast the pod restarts, we will lose a few scrapes between restarts per pod (orange). Any gap under 5 mins is already filled by the query engine

title: Re-group samples together in WAL in a background compaction
body:
### Proposal

**Purpose**

Currently, each sample requires a series lookup during WAL replay. This situation can be improved if we have multiple samples for the same series grouped together. Having fewer lookups and slightly efficient disk format can help in WAL replay speeds.

**Proposal**

WAL directory is made up of multiple files of sizes 128MiB. Every time a file is full and a new file is created, we can run a background job that "compacts" this newly full WAL file and groups all the samples of a series together. Each WAL record can have a batch of series with all their associated samples in that record (i.e. the samples that appear only in that WAL file).

WAL Replay: If the original WAL file was named `00007383`, the compacted file can be `00007383.compacted`. So during a replay, if there exists a compacted file for a file number, the replay can simply choose to replay this.

We cannot get rid of the existing WAL files because of the remote write.

title: Offset should not be allowed before a range vector selector
body:
### What did you do?

I’d like to clarify whether defining the `'[' <range> ':' [<resolution>] ']'` after offset is considered expected and valid PromQL syntax.

What I checked

I reviewed PromQL [basics](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/basics/#offset-modifier) and [subquery](https://prometheus.io/blog/2019/01/28/subquery-support/#subqueries) docs, and [promqltest testdata](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/tree/main/promql/promqltest/testdata). All examples I found show range defined **before** offset, not after. I couldn’t find a documented case of the opposite order. It is hard to reason validity without [a formal specification](https://promlabs.com/blog/2020/08/06/comparing-promql-correctness-across-vendors/#what-is-correct-in-the-absence-of-a-specification).

Is the syntax with range/resolution after offset (expr offset X[range]) expected and valid?
If so, how should it behave compared to the canonical expr[range] offset X form?




### What did you expect to see?

I would expect queries that specify the range after the offset to be invalid.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?


From my observations:

- `demo_counter_total[2m:10s] offset 5m` – works
- `demo_counter_total[2m] offset 5m` – works
- `demo_counter_total offset 5m[2m]` produces an error: "invalid parameter "query": 5:29: parse error: no offset modifiers allowed before range"
- `demo_counter_total offset 5m[2m:10s]` – works

With functions:

- `rate(demo_counter_total[2m:10s] offset 5m)` – works
- `rate(demo_counter_total[2m] offset 5m)` – works
- `rate(demo_counter_total offset 5m[2m])` produces an error: "invalid parameter "query": 5:29: parse error: no offset modifiers allowed before range"

title: prometheus_target_reload_length_seconds metric slows down all scrapes
body:
### What did you do?

I've restarted one of Prometheus server I manage.

### What did you expect to see?

prometheus_tsdb_head_active_appenders metric to stay roughly flat.
We have an alert for that metric because high number (>10k) of pending appenders it usually indicative of performance issues with Prometheus.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

prometheus_tsdb_head_active_appenders jump up high and stayed high for a long time, which is unusual.
I took a goroutine dump and notice that there's a high number of scrapes locked on the same lock:

```
10: sync.Mutex.Lock [Created by scrape.(*scrapePool).sync in goroutine 63973 @ scrape.go:612]
    sync       sema.go:95                  runtime_SemacquireMutex(0, 0, 0)
    sync       mutex.go:149                (*Mutex).lockSlow(#120862)
    sync       mutex.go:70                 (*Mutex).Lock(...)
    sync       mutex.go:46                 (*Mutex).Lock(...)
    prometheus summary.go:310              (*summary).Observe(#120861, *)
    scrape     scrape.go:1404              (*scrapeLoop).scrapeAndReport(*, {#418, #271, #271}, {*, #271, #271}, 0)
    scrape     scrape.go:1375              (*scrapeLoop).run(*, 0)
10: sync.Mutex.Lock [Created by scrape.(*scrapePool).sync in goroutine 64166 @ scrape.go:612]
    sync       sema.go:95                  runtime_SemacquireMutex(0, 0, 0)
    sync       mutex.go:149                (*Mutex).lockSlow(#120862)
    sync       mutex.go:70                 (*Mutex).Lock(...)
    sync       mutex.go:46                 (*Mutex).Lock(...)
    prometheus summary.go:310              (*summary).Observe(#120861, *)
    scrape     scrape.go:1404              (*scrapeLoop).scrapeAndReport(*, {#418, #271, #271}, {*, #271, #271}, 0)
    scrape     scrape.go:1375              (*scrapeLoop).run(*, 0)
```

The scrapeAndReport points at this lines:

https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/v3.5.0/scrape/scrape.go#L1402-L1404

and the reason for that is that the metric that each scrape tries to increment is a summary:

https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/v3.5.0/scrape/metrics.go#L93-L100

so it's a bit more expensive than all other scrape loop metrics (which are all simple counters).

So the end result is that this summary metric is expensive to update but ALL scrapes will try to increment it and wait for that single lock there.

Given that this metric might be "nice to have" but IMHO isn't really that useful I suggest to remove.

It's not entirely obvious why prometheus_tsdb_head_active_appenders spiked but it's possible that we got unlucky that due to randomness a lot of scrapes got scheduled very close to each other and they compete with each other for this lock more than usual.

title: Clarification on avg() Behavior in Range Queries with Sparse Gauge Data
body:
Hello Prometheus Community,

I'm seeking to clarify how PromQL evaluates aggregation functions like avg() in a range query (for graphing), especially when the query's step is smaller than the metric's actual scrape interval.

My Use Case:
I am running the following query in a graph panel:

Query: avg(system_cpu_time{project_name="robotshop-dev"})

Time Range: 24 hours

Resolution / Step: 1 minute (60s)

The actual scrape interval for the system_cpu_time metric is longer than 1 minute, or there are intermittent gaps, meaning there isn't a raw sample at every single 1-minute mark.

Observed Behavior:
The query renders a continuous, unbroken line graph, with a data point plotted for every 1-minute step. This implies that PromQL is producing a value even for timestamps where no raw sample was actually scraped (e.g., at 10:01:00).

My Questions:

My assumption is that for each evaluation step (e.g., at 10:01:00), PromQL looks for the most recent sample within the default lookback delta (5m). If it finds a sample (e.g., one scraped at 10:00:30), it uses that sample's value in the avg() calculation for the 10:01:00 step. Is this understanding correct?

Is this "last known value" propagation the standard, intended mechanism for handling gauges in range queries to ensure graph continuity?

Confirming this mechanism would be very helpful for us to confidently interpret our graph results. Thank you.

title: Request: Update metrics.proto Definition for Consistency with Prometheus Java Client 1.x.x+ API Changes
body:
Hi Team,

I noticed that the proto definition at [metrics.proto](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/prompb/io/prometheus/client/metrics.proto) still references the MetricFamily data structure, which originated from the legacy client API. With recent updates to the core Prometheus Java client (version 1.x.x+), the definition and packaging for MetricFamily has changed, and the corresponding data models have moved to new modules and packages.

In the current prometheus-metrics-model (example: 1.0.0-alpha-3), there is no longer a direct MetricFamily class. Instead, the new model in the io.prometheus.metrics.model.snapshots package represents metric families using:

- MetricSnapshot
- MetricSnapshots
- MetricMetadata
- Labels

Reference - [java-doc](https://www.javadoc.io/static/io.prometheus/prometheus-metrics-model/1.0.0-alpha-3/index-all.html)

Would it be possible to review and update the proto file accordingly to ensure compatibility with the new data model and client libraries? Keeping this definition current helps downstream integrations and avoids confusion for users migrating from the older APIs.

Thank you for your attention.

title: Add proxy_url to targets as meta label
body:
### Problem
I'm working in a network topology of several local private networks which are connected to a global network via a host pc. For service discovery of my targets (the one in the privat networks as well as the host pcs) I use http SD. However, using the [PushProx](https://github.com/prometheus-community/PushProx), I have to statically configure the proxy_url per job: 

```yaml
- job_name: "example_job"
    proxy_url: http://host_pc:8080
    http_sd_configs:
      - url: "https://example_SD/local_targets"
```  
This doesnt allow me to dynamically configure the proxies depending on the current state of my network topology. 

### Proposal
If the proxy url would be (also) passed as a meta label, I could add this url to my http SD and relabel it to cinfigure the proxy, something like this: 

```yaml
- job_name: "example_job"
    http_sd_configs:
      - url: "https://example_SD/local_targets"
      relabel_configs:
        - source_labels: [hostpc]
          target_label: __proxy_url
          replacement: 'http://${1}:8080'
```  
My current approach is to write this dynamic part of the yaml with a script but this is of course a bit unconventional and not ideal.

title: tsdb.DefaultStripeSize is way too big at 16384
body:
This is more of an issue for multi-tenant derivatives, but I think it's also wrong inside Prometheus.

The number is defined here:
https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/ba808d1736b851ff5b8eccc055b949fd4a34b0c2/tsdb/head.go#L1896

It is used to size a central data structure for TSDB - the lookup maps for series, and the locks that protect them.
https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/ba808d1736b851ff5b8eccc055b949fd4a34b0c2/tsdb/head.go#L1922-L1933

With the default number of stripes, 16384, each of `locks`, `series` and `hashes` allocates around 1MB, which may not seem much in the Prometheus context, but given the [attention paid](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/ba808d1736b851ff5b8eccc055b949fd4a34b0c2/tsdb/head.go#L1915-L1916) to avoiding cache line sharing, worth reflecting that 1MB is about the size of a typical L2 cache.

The justification given for striping the data structure is to avoid lock contention. By "birthday problem" reasoning, 16384 gives us 128 parallel operations with less than 50% chance of collision. This is at the absolute top end of what anyone would be running Prometheus at, so way too high for a default.

I would suggest changing it to 256.

Update: I was under the impression that #6644 "made stripe size configurable" added a flag, but it was just internal configurability.  So probably we need to add that flag to let people change it back.

title: Scrape configuration to limit label churn / added series
body:
## Problem: Cannot limit per-instance or per-job label _churn_ over time

Prometheus presently supports limiting the number of distinct series that may be scraped for an instance in a single scrape, with the `sample_limit` scrape setting. This effectively limits the permitted `scrape_samples_post_metric_relabeling` for an instance (with some [caveats](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/16427) around scrape cache size, label rewrite cache size, and staleness marker handling).

But there is no meaningful way to limit the number of series a workload may create _over time_. A rogue workload that emits series with rapidly changing labels can add a huge number of series to the TSDB. This has a similar impact on TSDB index sizes and Prometheus query memory use to a workload that emits an excessively wide data set in a single scrape.

Excess label churn can be _monitored_ using `sum_over_time(scrape_series_added{...}[$duration])`, possibly with a threshold computed from `scrape_samples_post_metric_relabeling` to ignore some amount of absolute  label churn that represents low percentage churn in jobs with very high overall series counts. But there's not currently any way to make a Prometheus instance _actively robust_ such that it automatically defends against excessive churn.

## Proposal: Enforce scrape-time limit on `scrape_series_added`

Ideally Prometheus would have a way to limit the label or series churn a workload can introduce to the TSDB.

### Option 1: Threshold on `scrape_series_added` with a first-scrape exception

Ideally Prometheus would have a way to limit the `scrape_series_added` of a workload.

```
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: "somejob"
    # ...
    sample_limit: 100
    series_added_limit: 5      # discard new series once scrape_series_added > 5 for this scrape
                               # and report in a new scrape_series_discarded{limit="series_added"}

```

A simplistic limit would be useless since new instances would be adding only new series, so they'd immediately hit the limit. So enforcement of the limit could be skipped if there are no recent samples for this `up{job, instance}` in the TSDB, probably defining "recent" as within 2 configured scrape-intervals for this job.

### Option 2: Limit the sum of scrape_series_added over a time window

Instead of a first-scrape exception, the churn limit could be expressed as a limit on new series added over a time window.

In this case the limit would be applied for new series introduced by the instance over some configured duration, dropping new series added once the threshold defined by `sum_over_time(scrape_series_added{job="$job",instance="$instance"}[$duration])` ) over the specified duration is reached.


```
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: "somejob"
    # ...
    sample_limit: 100
    # Discard new series if the rolling sum of
    # scrape_series_added{job,instance}[$duration] would
    # exceed the configured limit.
    series_added_over_time_limit: 200
    series_added_over_time_limit_duration: 1h
```

With this approach the `series_added_over_time_limit` would have to be >= the `sample_limit` or scrapes of new jobs would fail. So to be useful, the duration over which the churn limit is to be computed must be fairly long, since a problem "rogue" job may only be rapidly churning a small subset of its series.

## Limitations

This proposal would help with label churn over time, but would not limit all sources of excessive memory use. Notably:

> [[...] metrics dropped via metric_relabel_rules are still cached](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/12443)

and of course there's no memory quota on queries so queries can use potentially unbounded memory.

Being able to limit label churn would still be a significant step toward making Prometheus more robust without as much hands-on tuning and management.

## Possible implementation issues for discussion

### Requires appender to query the TSDB

The first approach would require the appende

title: Add a Ceiling Function that Mirrors Excels Ceiling Function
body:
### Proposal

I'd love to have a ceiling function in PromQL that mirrors the `ceiling` function of Excel compared to the current `ceil()` function Prometheus provides.

The difference is that Excel's function always rounds to the nearest multiple of significance. An example where you I've found this behavior useful is for building a dashboard that provides devs with sensible recommendations for their memory requests in k8s.

In Excel, I can do `ceiling(input, significance)` and even if the input was 1.2, and the significance was 10, the output would be 10. In PromQL `ceil(input)`  would simply round up to the nearest int and the output would be 2.0.

**Refs:**

- https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/ceiling-function-0a5cd7c8-0720-4f0a-bd2c-c943e510899f
- https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/2.55/querying/functions/#ceil

title: Add a latest(...) aggregation function to keep the matching sample with the most recent timestamp [abandoned, with test case and ugly workaround]
body:
### Proposal

For handling enumerated state sets and numerous other cases where series labels may change to convey a _value_ rather than to identify a new series, PromQL should have a function or operator that can filter series by value then discard all but the input sample with the most recent timestamp. To be useful this operation must retain all labels on the retained series, like `topk(...)` etc.

This operation should behave like `last_over_time(..)` over a _set of_ series where some labels are ignored for the purposes of determining the identity of a series.

Essentially the instant-aggregation flavour of `last_over_time`, much as `sum` is for `sum_over_time` and so on, except that it'd have series label retention like `topk` rather than discarding non-aggregated labels like `sum`.

## Problem

There's no reliable method to select the series with the most recent timestamp from a related set of series with some common identifying labels, plus some auxillary label(s) carrying string-values like states. This is typical for the state-set enumeration pattern. Automatic staleness markers cannot be relied upon because they are not reliably added under some circumstances:

* when the workload being scraped is subject to a rollout redeploy so its `instance` changes and the state of interest changes close to the same time;
* when Prometheus itself crashes/restarts concurrently with a change in the state of a monitored resource;
* when series are pushed for OTLP ingestion from an emitter that does not generate stale-markers for recently-transitioned-away-from states; etc

The widely accepted workaround used with Prometheus is to emit a set of all possible states for every scrape, with a value of 1 identifying the currently active state, and 0 emitted for all others.

But this is wasteful of tsdb index and sample storage space, especially for wide state-sets where many states are possible but most workloads are in a single state for most of their lifetimes. If there are 1000 resources with 20 possible states, every scrape cycle will ingest 20,000 series of which 19,000 carry no useful information at all, and are a complete waste.

### Example

Given tsdb containing this time-series

```
some_enumerated_state{workload_id="a", state="starting"} 1 60
some_enumerated_state{workload_id="b", state="running"} 1 60

some_enumerated_state{workload_id="a", state="running"} 1 120
some_enumerated_state{workload_id="b", state="running"} 1 120

some_enumerated_state{workload_id="a", state="running"} 1 180
some_enumerated_state{workload_id="b", state="exited"} 1 180

some_enumerated_state{workload_id="a", state="running"} 1 240

some_enumerated_state{workload_id="a", state="exited"} 1 300
```

it is presently difficult to reliably determine that at `t=310` the most recent `state` value for `some_enumerated_state{workload_id="a"}` is `exited`, especially if the consuming app/query
cannot know for certain whether the series will have 0-valued placeholders for inactive states.

**last_over_time(...) hardcodes scrape interval, fragile**

One might attempt to use something like:

    last_over_time(some_enumerated_state{workload_id="a"}[30s])

... with a range duration somewhere between 1x and 2x the scrape interval of the series. But this will only work when the series scrape interval is very regular, identical for all resources of interest, and it is never subject to missed scrapes. It also requires the query to hardcode the scrape interval for its input. At best it is clumsy, fragile and hard to maintain. It's also difficult to derive a range interval that will reliably select exactly one sample, without ever missing a sample or ever selecting 2 samples (which on state change might result in an apparent superposition of 2 concurrently active states).

**`vector binop scalar` discards timestamp**

A simple query at t=310 for:

```
some_enumerated_state{} == 1
```

title: HTTP Service Discovery should support retries
body:
### Proposal

HTTP service discovery should support simple HTTP retries. Additionally, any service discovery mechanism using `http_config` should support retries with standard settings like retry interval, exponential backoff, and configurable retry attempts. 

While a low refresh interval helps recover from SD failures, having optional retries comes at small complexity cost to the Prometheus config while accounting for a wide range of SD architectures. It is critical Prometheus has the right targets list and there are good arguments as to why Prometheus scrapes themselves shouldn't have retries. However actual target fetching should have better recovery options from transient failures besides waiting for a refresh interval.

Some SD backends could have high fetching costs that mean a long refresh interval is used. When combined with Prometheus' behavior to not persist target lists between restarts, one missed SD refresh cycle after a reboot can be disastrous. 

Retries should be instrumented with some extra counter metrics and logs too.

body:
I will be opening a series of PRs to optimize PromQL "join" (binary vector operations, AND, OR, UNLESS) performance. Opening this issue to make tracking of this work easier. For each optimization PR, I will be adding a comment here, with cumulative performance improvement (relative to master), while each individual PR will contain incremental benchmark results (relative to previous PR).
PromQL join performance heavily depends on the length of label sets, and in practice we see label sets that are at least hundreds of bytes long. Therefore I am using a new benchmark that contains more labels (https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/17130) for evaluating join performance.

title: use hashring in remote write to solve High cardinality problem
body:
### Proposal

#### problem
High cardinality is a very annoying problem in Prometheus. 
If there are too many time series, Prometheus will consume a lot of memory and eventually crash.

prometheus could deploy as agent mode, only remote write to thanos.
for now, there could only one thanos receiver。

#### solution
Prometheus writes to a thanos receiver cluster, which can automatically scale horizontally through HPA when memory pressure is too high.

During remote writes, Prometheus uses a hash ring to evenly distribute time series across the Thanos receiver cluster.

For example, if the total number of timeseries is 100 million, each Thanos receiver will only receive 10 million timeseries.

Previously, if 100 million timeseries required a single 100GB Prometheus machine, this can now be reduced to ten 10GB Thanos receivers, making it easier to allocate.

### What did you do?

Following is an excerpt from https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/histograms/#errors-of-quantile-estimation section

> Continuing the histogram example from above, imagine your usual request durations are almost all very close to 220ms, or in other words, if you could plot the "true" histogram, you would see a very sharp spike at 220ms. In the Prometheus histogram metric as configured above, almost all observations, and therefore also the 95th percentile, will fall into the bucket labeled {le="0.3"}, i.e. the bucket from 200ms to 300ms. The histogram implementation guarantees that the true 95th percentile is somewhere between 200ms and 300ms. **To return a single value (rather than an interval), it applies linear interpolation, which yields 295ms in this case.** The calculated quantile gives you the impression that you are close to breaching the SLO, but in reality, the 95th percentile is a tiny bit above 220ms, a quite comfortable distance to your SLO.


> To return a single value (rather than an interval), it applies linear interpolation, which yields 295ms in this case.

Whereas, the linear interpolation expression in BucketQuantile method of the code takes bucket count into account:
```
bucketStart + (bucketEnd-bucketStart)*(rank/count)
```

This makes the example misleading. The linear interpolation will only return 295ms if the bucket has 100 observations.

title: Idea: max rate of out-of-order samples in a single series
body:
### Proposal

The out-of-order feature in Prometheus is aimed at the case where most samples are in-order but a few arrive out-of-order. However I see about one case a week where someone has contrived to send thousands of OOO samples and hence TSDB has lots of small chunks to manage, pushing up CPU and memory usage.

I believe these are mostly the result of misconfiguration, such as 'labeldrop' rules which make separate series collide.  Unfortunately, when the data traverses a long pathway to get to TSDB it can be hard to track down the problem.

I propose that there be a maximum rate of OOO samples in any one series, for example 10 in a minute. This can be implemented by storing the time when the last OOO chunk was created in `memSeriesOOOFields` and checking each time a new chunk is cut (by default an OOO chunk holds 32 samples).

Creating an error will highlight the problem and avoid the additional expense.
