title: PROM-52: formalize composability with the 'additive' property; add tests to prove the property
body:
## Summary

PROM-52 ([`0052-extended-range-selectors-semantics`](https://github.com/prometheus/proposals/blob/main/proposals/0052-extended-range-selectors-semantics.md), implemented in [prometheus/prometheus#16457](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/16457), released in 3.7 behind `promql-extended-range-selectors`) introduces `anchored` and `smoothed`. By combining a left-open / right-closed range `(start, end]` with a separate baseline *anchor*--the latest sample with timestamp `≤ start`, fetched from outside the range within `lookback_delta`--`anchored + increase/rate/delta` has an important `additive` mathematical property that the proposal illustrates informally but doesn't state or test (yet):

> For any series `m` and any three timestamps `T₀ < T₁ < T₂`, let:
>
> - `r₁` = the length of `(T₀, T₁]`, subject to `r₁ ≤ lookback_delta`
> - `r₂` = the length of `(T₁, T₂]`
>
> The three anchored windows below cover these intervals. (Recall the PromQL rule: `m[duration] anchored @ T` covers `(T − duration, T]`--the `@` instant is always the *right* edge, and the range extends backward from it.)
>
> | Window | Covers |
> |---|---|
> | `m[r₁]      anchored  @ T₁` | `(T₀, T₁]` |
> | `m[r₂]      anchored  @ T₂` | `(T₁, T₂]` |
> | `m[r₁ + r₂] anchored  @ T₂` | `(T₀, T₂]` |
>
> Invariant:
>
> ```promql
> increase(m[r₁]      anchored)  @ T₁
>   +
> increase(m[r₂]      anchored)  @ T₂
>   =
> increase(m[r₁ + r₂] anchored)  @ T₂
> ```

This invariant is what makes anchored `increase` composable: splitting a wider range into adjacent sub-ranges and summing the results gives the same answer as asking for the wider range directly--and it does this for any possible sub-ranges. In contrast, with plain `increase`, the PROM-52 proposal notes on line 119 that *"two consecutive range selectors therefore fail to capture the increase"*.

## What we get with the `additive` property

The `additive` property is the formal expression of the "composability" goal the proposal mentions on line 147 ("offer greater composability and flexibility") and line 222 ("Improved composability across range boundaries"), but neither of those phrasings is pinned down. The `additive` property:

1. Gives users a precise, testable reason to prefer `anchored` for any workflow that splits or stitches time ranges (recording rules that roll up, alerts on windowed counter increases, dashboards that zoom between panel ranges, etc.).
2. Locks the invariant into the engine's contract via tests so future refactors can't drift.
3. Resolves a subtle ambiguity at the shared boundary `T₁`: a sample whose timestamp equals `T₁` is a *member* of the earlier range (right-closed) but is *not* a member of the later range `(T₁, T₂]` (left-open). The same sample is nonetheless reached by `anchor(T₁)` for the later range; the anchor lookup ("latest sample with `t ≤ T₁`") reaches backward from, and including, the range's left boundary, even though the boundary itself is not in the range. That dual role--"last in the earlier range" *and* "anchor of the later range," rather than double-membership--is crucial to achieving the `additive` property.

The proposal's partial-dataset example (lines 231–237) (*"The first window slightly underestimates while the second window slightly overestimates the actual increase"*) is this invariant in action. The per-window numbers aren't coincidentally canceling; they're composing.

## Related prior art

This property is the design goal of the Invoca `yrate` family (referenced in the PROM-52 "Other docs or links" as [Prometheus y-rate](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1CF5jhyxSD437c2aU2wHcvg88i8CjSPO3kMHsEaDRe2w/edit)). Invoca has run `yrate` in production for ~3 years with this invariant as a documented contract. In this time we have found composability via `additivity` to be indispensable: dashboards zoom from fine to coarse granularity without numerical surprises, recording rules roll up cleanly, and alerts fire reliably on windowed counter increases

title: WAL-free remote write
body: ### Proposal I'd like to propose a new mode of operation for the Prometheus server, taking the concept of the agent mode even further: bypass the WAL completely and call remote write directly from the scraping code as an Appender implementation. The graph below shows the memory usage of a Prometheus server scraping about 200k time series from a single endpoint. In full server mode, it's peaking at ~900 MB. Then the configuration is switched to agent mode which takes ~660 MB, which is a nice improvement. The third segment is bypassing the WAL completely: the memory usage goes down to ~510 MB, which is about half the full WAL mode usage. WAL-free mode has obvious reliability downsides when the Prometheus server is up but the remote write endpoint is not (metrics would be lost), but there are scenarios this is acceptable (e.g. in our use case, both components are deployed in a single container and any downtime is common between them). This could also potentially be a workaround for https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/10431 which still apparently eludes reliable reproduction. What are your thoughts on this feature? Would you be interested in having this? What would the next steps be?

title: feat: native OCI (Oracle Cloud Infrastructure) compute service discovery
body:
## Summary

Add native service discovery for Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) compute instances, following the same pattern as existing cloud SD integrations (Hetzner, Vultr, IONOS, etc.).

## Prior art

[#10226](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/10226) was opened in 2022 by an Oracle employee and closed without a PR landing. The closure note recommended HTTP SD as the preferred path. I have been running [oci-prometheus-sd-proxy](https://github.com/amaanx86/oci-prometheus-sd-proxy) - an HTTP SD implementation for OCI - in production and it works well. However, native SD is still the better long-term experience for users: no extra service to deploy, no token management overhead, and consistent `__meta_oci_*` labels alongside other cloud providers in the same Prometheus config.

## Why now / why me

- I run OCI compute at scale and can validate the implementation against a real fleet, not mocked fixtures.
- Oracle offers an always-free tier with 4 Arm cores + 24 GB RAM - I am happy to wire up a dedicated OCI account for CI-level integration tests so the maintainers do not need OCI access themselves.
- I will take full ownership of the implementation, tests, docs, and ongoing maintenance. If OCI APIs change, I will send follow-up PRs.
- OCI is the only major hyperscaler without native Prometheus SD. AWS (EC2), GCP (GCE), Azure, and OpenStack are all covered.

## Binary size concern

The previous attempt reportedly added ~12 MB to the binary. I plan to address this upfront:

- Audit which OCI SDK packages are actually needed (Compute + VirtualNetwork + Identity only - no broad SDK import).
- Vendor only those packages and their transitive deps, similar to how other cloud SDs scope their imports.
- Measure the size delta before opening a PR and document it explicitly.

If the delta remains too large, I will propose a build-tag approach (`--tags=oci`) consistent with how some integrations are conditionally compiled, and raise that trade-off with maintainers before the PR is ready.

## Proposed labels

Consistent with existing cloud SD labels, the integration would expose:

```
__meta_oci_instance_id
__meta_oci_instance_name
__meta_oci_instance_state
__meta_oci_instance_shape
__meta_oci_availability_domain
__meta_oci_fault_domain
__meta_oci_region
__meta_oci_tenancy_id
__meta_oci_compartment_id
__meta_oci_private_ip
__meta_oci_public_ip
__meta_oci_tag_<key>             (freeform tags)
__meta_oci_defined_tag_<ns>_<key> (defined tags)
```

## Auth support

- API key (user OCID + RSA key) - works anywhere
- Instance principal - works when Prometheus runs on OCI compute (no credentials needed, uses IMDS)

## Maintenance commitment

I am committing to:
- Responding to issues and PRs touching `discovery/oci` within a reasonable time
- Keeping the OCI SDK dependency up to date
- Providing a real OCI environment for integration test validation

Happy to start a draft PR once there is a signal that this is welcome. If binary size is a blocker, I will open a focused discussion on that before writing the full implementation.

/cc @roidelapluie @bboreham

title: Provide refresh interval config for GOMEMLIMIT to support dynamic memory limits
body:
### Proposal

The Automatically set `GOMEMLIMIT` to match Linux container or system memory limit functionality currently initializes `GOMEMLIMIT` only once at startup by invoking `memlimit.SetGoMemLimitWithOpts` with `memlimit.WithRatio` as the sole option. Consequently, if the container’s cgroup memory limit changes during runtime, for example, when a Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) updates resource limits, the Go runtime’s `GOMEMLIMIT` remains unchanged and continues to reflect the value determined at startup.

The underlying `automemlimit` library already supports periodically refreshing the memory limit via `WithRefreshInterval`, which could be used to ensure `GOMEMLIMIT` stays synchronized with runtime cgroup memory limit changes.

title: promql/parser: parentheses around a plain duration literal are lost on round-trip
body:
Note: I've generated this issue with Claude Opus 4.7 after using it to verify the issue.

While reviewing #18768 I noticed that `(N)` inside a duration-expression position (offset, range bracket) is dropped on `Expr.String()` round-trip when N reduces to a single `*NumberLiteral`. Wrapping a multi-term `*DurationExpr` survives because `*DurationExpr` has a `Wrapped` field; `*NumberLiteral` has no such field.

### Reproduction

With `ExperimentalDurationExpr: true`:

#### Cases that lose parentheses

| Input                  | `Expr.String()`  |
|------------------------|------------------|
| `foo offset (5)`       | `foo offset 5s`  |
| `foo offset +(5)`      | `foo offset 5s`  |
| `foo offset -(5)`      | `foo offset -5s` |
| `foo offset (5m)`      | `foo offset 5m`  |
| `foo[(5s)]`            | `foo[5s]`        |

#### Cases that round-trip correctly (for reference)

| Input                    | `Expr.String()`          |
|--------------------------|--------------------------|
| `(5)`                    | `(5)`                    |
| `-(5)`                   | `-(5)`                   |
| `+(5)`                   | `+(5)`                   |
| `(5) + 1`                | `(5) + 1`                |
| `foo offset (5m + 1m)`   | `foo offset (5m + 1m)`   |
| `foo offset -(5m + 1m)`  | `foo offset -(5m + 1m)`  |
| `foo[(5s + 1s)]`         | `foo[(5s + 1s)]`         |

Pure-scalar contexts use `*ParenExpr`, which prints its own parens. Duration-expression contexts with a `*DurationExpr` payload preserve parens via the `Wrapped` field. The mismatch is only when the payload is a single `*NumberLiteral`.

### Notes

This pre-dates #18768. That PR fixes a panic on `foo offset -(5)` but inherits this round-trip limitation, which is why I'm filing it separately.

title: promql: "found duplicate series for the match group" error message is non-deterministic
body:
## Summary

The PromQL `found duplicate series for the match group ... [X, Y] ...` error emitted by `VectorBinop` in `promql/engine.go` formats two label-set strings in non-deterministic order. Two identical queries running on the same data can produce byte-different error messages across runs because the two strings come from Go map iteration order upstream.

## Reproducer

```
load 5m
  dup_metric{label="alpha"} 1
  dup_metric{label="beta"}  2
  scalar_metric{}           3
```

Running ` scalar_metric > on() dup_metric` produces this error, but the order of the pair inside ` [ , ]` flips across runs:

```
execution: found duplicate series for the match group {} on the right hand-side of the operation: [{__name__="dup_metric", label="alpha"}, {__name__="dup_metric", label="beta"}];many-to-many matching not allowed: matching labels must be unique on one side
```

vs

```
execution: found duplicate series for the match group {} on the right hand-side of the operation: [{__name__="dup_metric", label="beta"}, {__name__="dup_metric", label="alpha"}];many-to-many matching not allowed: matching labels must be unique on one side
```

## Root cause

The error site at \`promql/engine.go:3108-3109\` splices \`rs.Metric.String()\` and \`duplSample.Metric.String()\` into \`[%s, %s]\`. The order in which the two arrive at this loop is influenced by upstream Go map iteration: the RHS Vector ultimately comes from a Matrix built by iterating \`seriess map[uint64]seriesAndTimestamp\` in \`rangeEval\` (engine.go around line 1571) and \`rangeEvalAgg\` (around line 1700). Go randomizes map iteration order per-process since Go 1.0, so two processes evaluating the same query land on different orderings.

The final Matrix returned to clients is sorted by \`sortMatrixResult\` (engine.go:893-900), so user-visible query results are deterministic; the error-formatting path is the only place this non-determinism leaks out.

## Downstream impact

This is the root cause of a flake observed in Cortex (~6 hits/month in CI), where the fuzz test compares two engines' error outputs byte-for-byte: cortexproject/cortex#7546. A tactical downstream workaround exists in cortexproject/cortex#7550 (tolerant error comparator), but the cleaner fix is to make the upstream error deterministic.

## Proposed fix

Sort the two label strings at the error site before formatting. PR follows.

title: Idea: simplify FastRegexMatcher by removing prefix/suffix/contains
body:
### Proposal

This idea comes from a discussion in #18540. 

As I understand it, the checks for `prefix`, `suffix` and `contains` are used as a pre-check which can say that a string will not match the regex (which is assumed to be the common case).  If that check passes, the entire expression is then checked.

However we also have `literalPrefixSensitiveStringMatcher`, which holds the prefix and a matcher for the remainder of the string. It seems to me that we don't need both mechanisms.  Similarly `literalSuffixStringMatcher` and `containsStringMatcher`.

As @chencs notes, this requires generalising `stringMatcherFromRegexpInternal` to use `newLiteralPrefixStringMatcher`  in more cases, perhaps reusing the code from `optimizeConcatRegex`.

title: Enhancement: Replace SHA-1 with SHA-256 for Rule Group pagination tokens
body: # Description Currently, in `web/api/v1/api.go`, the `getRuleGroupNextToken()` function utilizes the deprecated `crypto/sha1` algorithm to generate unique opaque strings for Rules API pagination tokens. ``` func getRuleGroupNextToken(file, group string) string { h := sha1.New() h.Write([]byte(file + ";" + group)) return hex.EncodeToString(h.Sum(nil)) } ``` While this is a non-cryptographic use case (pagination tokens), SHA-1 is widely considered deprecated. Many enterprise environments, security compliance frameworks (e.g., FIPS), and automated security scanners now flag any usage of SHA-1, leading to friction during security audits. # Solution We would like to propose replacing crypto/sha1 with crypto/sha256 in the getRuleGroupNextToken function. This would align Prometheus with modern security standards and eliminate "false positive" flags from security scanners. The change would be localized strictly to: File: `web/api/v1/api.go` Function: `getRuleGroupNextToken()` # Describe alternatives you've considered None. SHA-256 is the standard replacement for such hashing needs. # Cryptographic Discovery Report

title: Proposal: Configuration Assistant for validating and applying prometheus.yml changes
body:
## Proposal

This issue proposes a Configuration Assistant for the Prometheus UI.

The goal is to explore whether the UI can provide a safer workflow around editing and applying `prometheus.yml` changes.

## Problem

Prometheus configuration is powerful, but editing `prometheus.yml` manually can be difficult for newer users. Users need to understand YAML syntax, indentation, Prometheus-specific configuration structure, and reload behavior.

Common problems include:

* YAML indentation mistakes
* invalid scrape intervals
* missing required fields
* reload failures after editing configuration
* limited feedback before applying a change

Today, users usually edit `prometheus.yml` outside of the UI and then reload Prometheus. This is flexible, but it can be error-prone for users who are still learning Prometheus configuration.

## Proposed direction

A Configuration Assistant could help users:

* edit or paste Prometheus YAML configuration
* run validation before reload
* preview scrape jobs, targets, scrape intervals, and metrics paths
* apply the configuration
* trigger reload
* show success or error feedback

This would not replace the YAML workflow. Instead, it would provide a UI-assisted workflow around the existing configuration model.

## MVP prototype

I opened a prototype PR here:

<PASTE YOUR PR LINK HERE>

The prototype includes:

* a new Configuration Assistant page in the Prometheus UI
* lightweight local validation
* scrape job preview
* a lifecycle-gated backend endpoint for applying configuration changes
* validation using Prometheus's existing configuration loader
* backup of the previous configuration before overwrite
* restore of the previous configuration if reload fails

The apply endpoint is gated behind `--web.enable-lifecycle`, because writing the configuration file and triggering reload is a sensitive operation.

## Open questions

There are several design questions that would need discussion:

* Should Prometheus UI support writing to `--config.file` at all?
* Should this remain external tooling instead of being part of Prometheus core?
* Should the assistant only validate and preview configuration, without applying changes?
* What security model would be appropriate?
* Should this be limited to local / development deployments?
* How should advanced Prometheus configuration be represented or previewed?

## Notes

The current prototype is intentionally small and should be treated as an MVP for discussion rather than a complete product design.

title: FastRegexMatcher: false-positive match for .*<lit>(group)<lit>.* with a capturing group
body:
### What did you do?

`FastRegexMatcher` produces a result that disagrees with Go's stdlib RE2 for
patterns of the shape `.*<lit1>(capturing group)<lit2>.*`.

Minimal reproduction:

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"regexp"

	"github.com/prometheus/prometheus/model/labels"
)

func main() {
	const pattern = `.*\|(foo)\|.*`
	const input = "|foo-bar|"

	m, _ := labels.NewFastRegexMatcher(pattern)
	fmt.Println("FastRegexMatcher:", m.MatchString(input)) // => true  (WRONG)

	fmt.Println("stdlib RE2:      ", regexp.MustCompile(`^(?:`+pattern+`)$`).MatchString(input)) // => false (correct)

	// Control: non-capturing group is correct.
	mc, _ := labels.NewFastRegexMatcher(`.*\|(?:foo)\|.*`)
	fmt.Println("non-capturing:   ", mc.MatchString(input)) // => false (correct)
}
```

At the PromQL/label level this surfaces as a selector like
`{label=~".*\|(foo)\|.*"}` incorrectly matching a series whose label value is
`|foo-bar|`.

### What did you expect to see?

`false` — matching Go's stdlib RE2 and the equivalent non-capturing pattern. The
literal between the delimiters is `|foo|`, which does **not** occur in
`|foo-bar|` (after `foo` comes `-`, not `|`).

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

`FastRegexMatcher` returns a **false positive** (`true`) when the captured
literal is a *prefix* of a longer token in the input. Making the group
non-capturing (`(?:...)`) restores correct behavior.

**This is not specific to the `|` delimiter.** The same bug appears with any
delimiter when the captured literal is a prefix of a longer input token, e.g.
pattern `.*-(ab)-.*` falsely matches `x-abc-y`.

### System information

Darwin 25.5.0 arm64

3.12.0

title: Add query_log_min_duration configuration to filter query logs by execution time
body:
### Proposal

Introduce a new configuration parameter under the global configuration settings, `query_log_min_duration` (of type `model.Duration`), to specify a minimum execution duration threshold. 

When `query_log_min_duration` is configured, only queries that take longer than the specified duration to evaluate will be logged to the file specified in `query_log_file`. If it is not configured (or set to `0s`), all queries will be logged as they are today, maintaining backward compatibility.

Example configuration in `prometheus.yml`:

```yaml
global:
  query_log_file: /var/log/prometheus/query.log
  query_log_min_duration: 2s  # Only log queries that take 2 seconds or longer to evaluate
```
---

### Use case. Why is this important?

In high-traffic production environments, query logging is essential for diagnosing performance issues, identifying abuse, and optimizing PromQL queries. However, enabling query logging currently logs every single executed query, including fast metadata fetches and dashboard refreshes that complete in milliseconds. 

This creates several severe drawbacks:
1. **High Disk I/O Overhead:** Logging hundreds or thousands of fast queries per second puts unnecessary write pressure on the storage system.
2. **Rapid Disk Consumption:** Query log files grow gigabytes in size within hours, leading to disk capacity issues.
3. **Difficult Troubleshooting:** Finding slow queries in a massive log file requires complex log parsing/filtering tools (e.g., using `jq` on `evalTotalTime` field).

By introducing `query_log_min_duration`, users can target only the slow, resource-heavy queries (e.g., queries taking >5s) directly at the source. This makes query logging safe to run continuously in production, reducing resource usage and simplifying query performance auditing.

title: Proposal: Always log failed/errored queries regardless of `query_log_min_duration`
body:
Follow up to #18920 

## Description

With the introduction of the `query_log_min_duration` setting under global configuration (`#18920` / `#18921`), Prometheus allows filtering query logs to avoid high disk I/O and log volume by logging only queries that take longer than a specified execution threshold.

However, in its current design, if `query_log_min_duration` is set (for example, to `5s`) and a query fails quickly (for instance, within `15ms` due to hitting the `max_samples` limit, query timeout, or cancellation), it will **not** be logged in the query log because its execution duration is below the threshold. 

This creates a visibility gap where critical query failures and errors go unlogged, making it difficult for cluster administrators to audit and troubleshoot failing client queries.

## Proposed Change

We should modify the query log condition in `promql/engine.go` so that queries that return an error are **always logged** if query logging is enabled, regardless of whether they crossed the `query_log_min_duration` threshold.

Specifically, in `promql/engine.go`:

```go
// Current implementation
execDuration := q.stats.GetTimer(stats.ExecTotalTime).TotalDuration()
if execDuration >= ng.queryLogMinDuration {
    // log query
}
```

Should be changed to:

```go
// Proposed implementation
execDuration := q.stats.GetTimer(stats.ExecTotalTime).TotalDuration()
if err != nil || execDuration >= ng.queryLogMinDuration {
    // log query
}
```

This ensures that:
1. Normal, successful queries are still filtered by `query_log_min_duration` to save I/O and space.
2. Any failing query (`err != nil`) is captured in the query logs for immediate visibility and debugging.

## Verification Plan

### Automated Tests
* Add a test case in `promql/engine_test.go` (similar to `TestQueryLogger_minDuration`) that executes a query that fails quickly (e.g. triggers an error) under a high `query_log_min_duration` threshold, and verify that the error log is successfully written.

title: Transitioning from MD5 to SHA-256 for internal hashing and sharding
body:
# Use Case
Prometheus currently employs crypto/md5 for several internal functional hashing tasks. While these use cases are non-cryptographic, the widespread use of MD5 introduces potential architectural risks and limitations as the project evolves.

# Purposes
- Relabeling (HashMod): Used for target sharding and distribution logic in model/relabel/relabel.go.
- Notifier (configHash): Used to detect changes in Alertmanager configurations in notifier/alertmanagerset.go.
- Remote Storage (toHash): Used for identifying unique remote read/write configurations in storage/remote/storage.go.

# Motivation
- Robustness against collision-based exploits: As target discovery and sharding become more dynamic, MD5’s vulnerability to intentional collision construction presents a theoretical risk of Algorithmic Complexity DoS. Replacing it with SHA-256 ensures robust distribution uniformity and protects against potential hot-spotting attacks.

- Runtime compatibility & Future-proofing: With the Go ecosystem shifting towards strictly enforced secure-by-default runtime environments (e.g., restricted GODEBUG modes), maintaining reliance on legacy hashing algorithms in core logic risks inducing unexpected runtime panics in hardened deployments.

- Modernizing hashing defaults: Aligning with modern hashing standards reduces technical debt and prepares Prometheus for long-term integration into infrastructure where legacy algorithms are being deprecated at the library or OS level.
 
# Proposed Solution
We propose a transition strategy to replace MD5 with SHA-256 while maintaining backward compatibility where necessary:

- Internal Hashing (Low Risk): Replace MD5 with SHA-256 for notifier config hashing and remote storage config identification. Since these hashes are primarily used for in-memory diffing and are not part of a long-term data contract, the impact is minimal.
- Relabeling HashMod (High Risk): Changing the hash for hashmod would break existing sharding (re-distributing all targets). To solve this, we could:
  - Introduce a new relabel action: hashmod_sha256.
  - Add an optional hash_algorithm field to the relabel config, defaulting to md5 for legacy support but allowing users to opt-in to sha256.

title: cmd/prometheus: TestVersionUpgrade_fetchLTSPrefix fails because the LTS regex doesn't handle multiple versions in docs-config.ts
body:
### What did you do?

Ran the version-upgrade tests in `cmd/prometheus` (the "Go tests for Prometheus upgrades and downgrades" CI job), on current `main`:

```
go test ./cmd/prometheus/ -run 'TestVersionUpgrade' -test.version-upgrade=true -count=1
```


### What did you expect to see?

`TestVersionUpgrade_fetchLTSPrefix` and `TestVersionUpgrade_UpgradeDowngradeLatestLTS` pass — `fetchLTSPrefix` parses the current LTS `major.minor` out of the docs config.


### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

Both tests fail deterministically (not a flake), so the "Go tests for Prometheus upgrades and downgrades" job is red on every PR:

--- FAIL: TestVersionUpgrade_UpgradeDowngradeLatestLTS (0.18s)
    main_upgrade_test.go:316: Error: Should NOT be empty, but was []
--- FAIL: TestVersionUpgrade_fetchLTSPrefix (0.00s)
    main_upgrade_test.go:396 (trace: main_upgrade_test.go:60): Error: Should NOT be empty, but was []
FAIL  github.com/prometheus/prometheus/cmd/prometheus

Root cause: fetchLTSPrefix extracts the LTS version with a regex that assumes a single-element array:

  const prometheusDocsLTSConfigURL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/prometheus/docs/main/docs-config.ts"
  regexp.MustCompile(`ltsVersions:\s*{\s*prometheus:\s*\["(\d+\.\d+)"]`)

prometheus/docs now lists two LTS versions:

  ltsVersions: {
    prometheus: ["3.5", "3.13"],
  },

So "3.5" is followed by `, "3.13"]` instead of `]`, the regex matches nothing, and require.NotEmpty fails. The test also hard-asserts require.Equal(t, "3.5", fetchLTSPrefix(t)), which is now ambiguous with two supported LTS lines.

Proposed fix: relax the regex to capture the first entry regardless of extra versions (e.g. match `\["(\d+\.\d+)"`), and decide whether to assert the oldest (3.5) or latest (3.13) LTS — the test names reference "latest LTS", so this needs a maintainer call. Happy to send a PR.

Platform-independent (network-fetch + regex bug; reproduces on any OS). Repro env: Darwin 25.5.0 arm64

remote_write azuread workload_identity hardcodes token file path, ignoring AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE
body:
**What did you do?**

Configured remote write with Azure AD workload-identity auth on AKS:

```yaml
remote_write:
  - url: https://<workspace>.<region>.prometheus.monitor.azure.com/dataCollectionRules/...
    azuread:
      cloud: AzurePublic
      workload_identity:
        client_id: <uuid>
        tenant_id: <uuid>
```

The Prometheus pod uses the [`azure-workload-identity`](https://github.com/Azure/azure-workload-identity) mutating webhook (pod label `azure.workload.identity/use: "true"`). After upgrading the webhook to **v1.6.0**, remote write stopped authenticating.

**What did you expect to see?**

Remote write authenticating successfully with workload identity, as it did with the webhook on `<= v1.5.x`.

**What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?**

```
Failed to get access token: WorkloadIdentityCredential: open /var/run/secrets/azure/tokens/azure-identity-token: no such file or directory
```

**Root cause**

`azure-workload-identity` v1.6.0 ([release notes](https://github.com/Azure/azure-workload-identity/releases/tag/v1.6.0)) moved the projected service-account token mount path from `/var/run/secrets/azure/tokens/azure-identity-token` to `/var/run/secrets/azure/wi/token/azure-identity-token`, and updated the `AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE` env var to point at the new path. The release notes explicitly state:

> Never hardcode the token file path. Always read `AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE`.

Prometheus' `workload_identity` remote-write auth hardcodes the path instead of reading that env var. In [`storage/remote/azuread/azuread.go`](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/v3.12.0/storage/remote/azuread/azuread.go):

- `DefaultWorkloadIdentityTokenPath` is pinned to the old path `/var/run/secrets/azure/tokens/azure-identity-token`.
- In `Validate()`, when `token_file_path` is unset, `TokenFilePath` defaults to that constant.
- `newWorkloadIdentityTokenCredential()` then passes the now-always-populated `TokenFilePath` into `azidentity.WorkloadIdentityCredentialOptions`.

Because azidentity only falls back to `AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE` when `TokenFilePath == ""` ([`sdk/azidentity/workload_identity.go`](https://github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-go/blob/main/sdk/azidentity/workload_identity.go)):

```go
file := options.TokenFilePath
if file == "" {
    if file, ok = os.LookupEnv(azureFederatedTokenFile); !ok {
        return nil, errors.New("no token file specified. Check pod configuration or set TokenFilePath in the options")
    }
}
```

the env var the webhook now maintains is never consulted, and Prometheus opens the stale path → the error above.

This is precisely the anti-pattern the webhook release warns against, so any future webhook-managed path change will break Prometheus again. Note the `sdk` auth method is unaffected because `NewDefaultAzureCredential` reads `AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE` itself. The `workload_identity` block was added in #16788.

**Proposed fix**

When `token_file_path` is not configured, prefer `AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE` and only fall back to `DefaultWorkloadIdentityTokenPath` if the env var is empty (or leave `TokenFilePath` unset so azidentity resolves it). Sketch:

```go
if c.WorkloadIdentity.TokenFilePath == "" {
    if p := os.Getenv("AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE"); p != "" {
        c.WorkloadIdentity.TokenFilePath = p
    } else {
        c.WorkloadIdentity.TokenFilePath = DefaultWorkloadIdentityTokenPath
    }
}
```

**Workaround**

Explicitly set the new path in config:

```yaml
azuread:
  workload_identity:
    token_file_path: /var/run/secrets/azure/wi/token/azure-identity-token
```

**System information**

AKS / Azure Monitor managed Prometheus remote write; azure-workload-identity webhook v1.6.0.

**Prometheus version**

```
prometheus, version 3.12.0
```

**Prometheus configuration file**

See the `remote_write.azuread.workload_identity` block above.

```
Failed to get access token: WorkloadIdentityCredential: open /var/run/secrets/azure/tokens/azure-identit

title: tsdb: silent self-deadlock in mmapHeadChunks during panic or I/O failure
body:
### What did you do?

We investigated a recurring issue where the Prometheus TSDB could experience a silent, unrecoverable self-deadlock during chunk memory mapping (`mmapHeadChunks`), specifically when a panic or catastrophic I/O failure occurs (e.g., when `handleChunkWriteError` triggers a panic in tests, or a disk goes fully offline).

We have already implemented and verified a fix locally by extracting the nested loops into `mmapHeadChunksInStripe` and `mmapSeriesChunks` to leverage `defer` for safe lock release.


### What did you expect to see?

If `mmapChunks()` encounters a write error and panics, the process should crash or recover cleanly, releasing all acquired mutexes (`h.series.locks[i]` and `series.Lock()`) so that deferred cleanup tasks (like `t.Cleanup()` calling `Head.Close()`) can execute without deadlocking the entire test runner or TSDB closer.


### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

A permanent self-deadlock. 

In `tsdb/head.go` within the `mmapHeadChunks` loop, two locks are acquired sequentially:
1. `h.series.locks[i].RLock()`
2. `series.Lock()`

Currently, these locks are released using explicit `RUnlock()` and `Unlock()` calls at the bottom of the loop body rather than being protected by `defer`. If `series.mmapChunks` panics, the loop exits immediately, skipping the unlock instructions. This leaks both the stripe lock and the series lock. 

Subsequently, when cleanup routines (or any concurrent operations) attempt to safely close the TSDB Head by calling `mmapHeadChunks()` again, they block forever waiting for those identical locks, resulting in CI timeouts (particularly visible on 386 architectures) or process hangs.


### System information

Linux (WSL2 / Ubuntu) x86_64

### Prometheus version

```text
prometheus, version HEAD (branch: main)
```

```yaml

```

title: tsdb: Close() errors silently discarded in Querier and blockChunkQuerierForRange cleanup
body:
I noticed a couple of cleanup paths in `tsdb/db.go` where errors returned from `Close()` are currently ignored.

This happens in `Querier()` and `blockChunkQuerierForRange()`:

```go
for _, q := range blockQueriers {
    _ = q.Close()
}
```

These cleanup defers run while handling an error path from the surrounding function. If one of the queriers also fails during `Close()`, that information is currently discarded, so the caller only sees the original error.

One possible improvement would be to preserve both errors using `errors.Join()` so the cleanup failure is not lost, for example:

```go
if closeErr := q.Close(); closeErr != nil {
    err = errors.Join(err, fmt.Errorf("close querier during cleanup: %w", closeErr))
}
```

This would keep the original failure while still surfacing any cleanup issues that happen while closing the queriers.

title: Deltas: Confirm support for ST-per-sample in OTLP endpoint
`promtool: --enable-feature=promql-binop-fill-modifiers` is not recognized, causing `fill()` rule validation to always fail
body:
### Description

`promtool` does not recognise the `promql-binop-fill-modifiers` feature flag in its
`--enable-feature` switch statement.  As a result, users who write recording rules or
alerts with `fill()` / `fill_left()` / `fill_right()` binary-operator modifiers and then
try to validate those rules with `promtool check rules --enable-feature=promql-binop-fill-modifiers`
receive a misleading "WARNING: Unknown feature …" message and the parse fails with
_"binop fill modifiers are experimental and not enabled"_.

---

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a recording rule file `fill_rule.yml`:

```yaml
groups:
  - name: example
    rules:
      - record: job:requests_per_status
        expr: |
          rate(successful_requests[5m]) + fill(0) rate(failed_requests[5m])
```

2. Run promtool with the feature flag:

```
promtool check rules --enable-feature=promql-binop-fill-modifiers fill_rule.yml
```

**Expected:** validation passes (same as when Prometheus itself starts with the flag).

**Actual output:**
```
  WARNING: Unknown feature passed to --enable-feature: promql-binop-fill-modifiers
  FAILED:
    fill_rule.yml: 1 error(s):
      ...expr: [1:34] binop fill modifiers are experimental and not enabled
```

### What did you expect to see?

## Suggested Fix

Add `"promql-binop-fill-modifiers"` to the feature switch in
[`cmd/promtool/main.go`](file:///C:/Users/Vishal/Code_File/Repo%20Folder/prometheus/cmd/promtool/main.go#L353-L369):

```diff
        case "promql-extended-range-selectors":
            promtoolParserOpts.EnableExtendedRangeSelectors = true
+       case "promql-binop-fill-modifiers":
+           promtoolParserOpts.EnableBinopFillModifiers = true
        case "":
            continue
```

A matching test should be added to
`cmd/promtool/unittest_test.go` (or a dedicated test) that:
1. Creates a rules file with a `fill()` expression.
2. Calls `CheckRules` / `RulesUnitTest` with `--enable-feature=promql-binop-fill-modifiers`.
3. Asserts no error is returned.

---

## Affected Files

| File | Line(s) | Change |
|------|---------|--------|
| [`cmd/promtool/main.go`](file:///C:/Users/Vishal/Code_File/Repo%20Folder/prometheus/cmd/promtool/main.go#L353-L369) | 353–369 | Add `case "promql-binop-fill-modifiers"` |
| `cmd/promtool/*_test.go` | — | Add regression test |


### Expected behaviour

`promtool check rules --enable-feature=promql-binop-fill-modifiers` should parse
and validate `fill()` expressions the same way that the Prometheus server does when
started with the same flag.



### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

## Impact

* Users cannot validate fill-modifier rules/alerts with `promtool` before deploying.
* CI pipelines that run `promtool check rules` as a pre-flight check will always
  reject queries that are valid on the live server.
* The flag is otherwise completely ignored — no warning is emitted in other promtool
  subcommands that also construct a parser (e.g. `promtool query instant`).

### System information

go 1.25.0

### Prometheus version

```text
Prometheus 3.12
```

### Prometheus configuration file

```yaml
groups:
  - name: example
    rules:
      - record: job:requests_available
        expr: |
          rate(successful_requests[5m]) + fill(0) rate(failed_requests[5m])
```

title: textparse: ProtobufParser.Next() recurses on empty/skipped metric families, risking stack overflow (DoS)
body:
### Context

The Protocol Buffer parser (`ProtobufParser`) in `model/textparse/protobufparse.go`
processes metric families using recursive calls to `p.Next()` in multiple places.
When encountering empty metric families, ignoring native histograms, or switching
between native and classic histogram representations, the parser recurses rather
than looping. This allows the call stack to grow linearly with the number of
skipped entries.
PR #19143 ("fix(parsing): Parse metrics without recursion") recently fixed the
identical issue in `openmetricsparse.go` and `promparse.go` by converting those
`return p.Next()` calls into `continue` inside a top-level `for` loop. The
`ProtobufParser` was **not** included in that fix and remains vulnerable.
A malicious or misconfigured scrape target serving `application/vnd.google.protobuf`
can trigger a stack overflow crash in the Prometheus server by returning a payload
containing a large number of empty metric families.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Build a binary that runs the following (or stand up a target that returns the
   corresponding protobuf payload):

```go
package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/binary"
    "fmt"
    "runtime/debug"

    "github.com/gogo/protobuf/proto"
    "github.com/prometheus/prometheus/model/textparse"
    dto "github.com/prometheus/prometheus/prompb/io/prometheus/client"
)

func main() {
    // Restrict stack to 1 MB to surface the overflow quickly.
    debug.SetMaxStack(1024 * 1024)

    mf := &dto.MetricFamily{
        Name: "empty_metric",
        Help: "no samples",
        Type: dto.MetricType_GAUGE,
        // No Metric entries -- intentionally empty.
    }
    protoBuf, _ := proto.Marshal(mf)

    const numEmpty = 20_000
    varintBuf := make([]byte, binary.MaxVarintLen32)
    buf := &bytes.Buffer{}
    for i := 0; i < numEmpty; i++ {
        n := binary.PutUvarint(varintBuf, uint64(len(protoBuf)))
        buf.Write(varintBuf[:n])
        buf.Write(protoBuf)
    }

    parser := textparse.NewProtobufParser(
        buf.Bytes(), false, false, false, false, nil,
    )
    fmt.Printf("Calling Next() on %d empty metric families\n", numEmpty)
    entry, err := parser.Next()
    fmt.Printf("entry=%v err=%v\n", entry, err)
}
```

2. Run the binary.

### Expected Result

The parser iterates over empty/skipped metric families without growing the call
stack and returns `(EntryInvalid, io.EOF)` when the payload is exhausted.


### Repo Configuration

Minimal Prometheus scrape configuration targeting an endpoint that returns
`Content-Type: application/vnd.google.protobuf` with many empty metric families:

```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'test'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['malicious-or-misconfigured-target:8080']
    scrape_protocols:
      - PrometheusProto
```

---

### Log Output

```
Created parser with 20000 empty metric families. Starting Next()...
Alloc before Next: 12566 KB
runtime: goroutine stack exceeds 1048576-byte limit
fatal error: stack overflow
```

### Impact

- **Availability (DoS):** Any scraped target (external service, compromised
  exporter, or a misconfigured one emitting only type/help metadata with no
  data) can crash the entire Prometheus server process.
- **Severity:** Medium-High. No authentication is required; any target reachable
  by the scraper can exploit this.

```release-notes
[BUGFIX] textparse: Fix stack overflow in ProtobufParser.Next() when parsing
payloads with many empty or skipped metric families.
```

title: tsdb/wlog: fix shadowed metadata slice decoding in Checkpoint
body:
### What did you do?

During TSDB WAL checkpointing, the `Checkpoint` function in `tsdb/wlog/checkpoint.go` reads records from the WAL segments. For `Metadata` records:
1. The `metadata` slice is decoded at line 361.
2. The outer `metadata` variable is shadowed due to the use of `:=` inside the `case record.Metadata:` block:
   ```go
   case record.Metadata:
       metadata, err := dec.Metadata(rec, metadata)
   ```

All other case blocks use normal assignment `=` (e.g. `series, err = dec.Series(rec, series)`) to update the preallocated outer variable and reuse its capacity.



### What did you expect to see?

The outer variable `metadata` should be reused across loop iterations using assignment `=` rather than short variable declaration `:=`, avoiding a new slice allocation per metadata record.
Also, the `stats.DroppedMetadata` statistic should accurately track the number of dropped metadata records.



### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

A fresh slice allocation is made for every metadata record processed during checkpointing. In addition, the `stats.DroppedMetadata` count is computed incorrectly because the inner shadowed variable's length is subtracted from `repl` (which increments on unique references, not total records).

This happens whenever Prometheus runs a WAL checkpoint (compactions or manual TSDB cleanups) when metadata records are present in the WAL.

title: discovery/aws: panic on nil Provisioned or OpenMonitoring fields during MSK discovery
body:
## Description
A runtime panic (nil pointer dereference) occurs in MSK service discovery (`discovery/aws/msk.go`) when discovering MSK clusters where `Provisioned` or `OpenMonitoring` is `nil`. 

In AWS MSK, Open Monitoring is disabled by default, and Serverless clusters do not use provisioned broker settings. When Prometheus queries these clusters, the AWS SDK returns `nil` for the corresponding nested pointer fields (like `cluster.Provisioned` or `cluster.Provisioned.OpenMonitoring`). Prometheus directly dereferences these pointers without checking for `nil`, causing the Prometheus process to panic and crash.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Configure AWS MSK Service Discovery in `prometheus.yml`:
   ```yaml
   scrape_configs:
     - job_name: 'msk-discovery'
       msk_sd_configs:
         - region: 'us-west-2'
           clusters:
             - 'arn:aws:kafka:us-west-2:123456789012:cluster/my-cluster/abc-123'
   ```
2. Ensure the MSK cluster (either Serverless, or Provisioned but with Open Monitoring disabled/not configured) is returned by AWS API `DescribeClusterV2`.
3. Start Prometheus. Service discovery begins.
4. Prometheus crashes immediately with a nil pointer panic.

## Expected Result
Prometheus should discover the cluster successfully, gracefully omitting or leaving blank any metadata labels related to JMX/Node exporters or broker configuration when those features are not configured or available.

## Actual Result
Prometheus crashes during the service discovery refresh loop:
```
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[signal 0xc0000005 code=0x0 addr=0x50 pc=0x7ff65fb40b91]

goroutine 55 [running]:
github.com/prometheus/prometheus/discovery/aws.(*MSKDiscovery).refresh.func1(0xc000fc54a0, 0xc0002bc0c0)
	C:/Users/Vishal/Code_File/Repo Folder/prometheus/discovery/aws/msk.go:434 +0x551
...
```

## Version
Prometheus: Main/HEAD (v3.0.0-beta or similar development branch)
go version: go1.26.2

## Environment Information
- OS: Windows / Linux / macOS (all platforms affected)
- Compiler (if applicable): go1.26.2

## Repo Configuration
```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'msk'
    msk_sd_configs:
      - region: 'us-east-1'
```

## Log Output
```
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[signal 0xc0000005 code=0x0 addr=0x50 pc=0x7ff65fb40b91]

goroutine 55 [running]:
github.com/prometheus/prometheus/discovery/aws.(*MSKDiscovery).refresh.func1({0x0, 0x18e677ff5640, 0x18e677ff5630, ...}, ...)
	C:/Users/Vishal/Code_File/Repo Folder/prometheus/discovery/aws/msk.go:434 +0x551
created by github.com/prometheus/prometheus/discovery/aws.(*MSKDiscovery).refresh in goroutine 53
	C:/Users/Vishal/Code_File/Repo Folder/prometheus/discovery/aws/msk.go:422 +0x225
```

title: Native histograms: explore new chunk format
body:
### Proposal

This is a cover issue for gathering issues/ideas regarding native histograms chunks format.

**Only for experienced contributors/maintainers, NOT a good first issue.**

Issues:
- We need to use `gauge` [flavor](https://prometheus.io/docs/specs/native_histograms/#flavors) to store delta temporality exponential OTel histograms currently. This results in a weird split brain where the flavor says the histogram is a gauge, but actually it's a counter. PromQL needs special handling of start timestamps to figure out the truth.
- If the buckets in a delta metric / gauge histogram change rapidly, the resulting chunks need [recoding](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/c3e85b8884baf7afca91527e25885dccbe716e5b/tsdb/chunkenc/histogram.go#L672) often, which is slower compared to add only chunks.
- Learning from XOR2 work not applied - although we don't know if they could be.
- ?

Requirements:
- Take into account XOR2
- Format should be append only
- Can tell a gauge and delta temporality counter apart easily
- Ideally handles counter resets per sample
- Ideally doesn't have separate gauge/counter code paths (it must have the hint)

title: bug(notifier): `targetUpdateLoop` spins on closed target-set channel
body:
## What did you do?

The `notifier.Manager.targetUpdateLoop` method uses `break` instead of `return` when the `tsets` channel is closed. This creates a **tight CPU spin loop** because `break` only exits the inner `select`, not the enclosing `for` loop.

This is the exact same bug that was just fixed in the scrape manager in PR #19149 (`fix(scrape): stop on closed target set channel`), but the notifier manager has the identical unfixed code pattern.

### Root Cause

In [`notifier/manager.go` lines 218–236](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/297523f69/notifier/manager.go#L218-L236):

```go
func (n *Manager) targetUpdateLoop(tsets <-chan map[string][]*targetgroup.Group) {
	for {
		select {
		case <-n.stopRequested:
			return
		default:
			select {
			case <-n.stopRequested:
				return
			case ts, ok := <-tsets:
				if !ok {
					break // BUG: only breaks out of inner select, not the for loop
				}
				n.reload(ts)
			}
		}
	}
}
```

When `tsets` is closed (e.g., because the discovery manager shuts down first):
1. The inner `select` receives the zero value from the closed channel
2. `ok` is `false`, so `break` executes
3. `break` exits only the inner `select`, **not** the `for` loop
4. The outer loop immediately re-enters, checks `n.stopRequested` (not closed yet), falls through to `default`
5. The inner `select` immediately receives from the closed channel again
6. This repeats in a tight loop, consuming **100% of one CPU core**

The spin continues until `n.stopRequested` is eventually closed by `Stop()`. Depending on shutdown ordering, this could persist for a non-trivial duration.

### Comparison with the scrape manager fix (PR #19149)

The scrape manager had the exact same bug, which was fixed by changing `break` to `return nil`:

```diff
-				break
+				return nil
```

## What did you expect to see?

When the `tsets` channel is closed, `targetUpdateLoop` should exit gracefully (return), consistent with how the scrape manager now handles this case after PR #19149.

## What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

When the discovery manager's `SyncCh()` channel is closed before `notifierManager.Stop()` is called, the `targetUpdateLoop` goroutine enters a tight CPU spin loop, consuming 100% of one CPU core until `Stop()` is eventually called.

This can happen during shutdown because the `oklog/run` group does not guarantee ordering — the discovery manager may shut down (closing its `SyncCh()`) before the notifier manager's `Stop()` is invoked.

## Environment

### System information

All platforms (Go runtime behavior, not OS-specific).

### Prometheus version

```
prometheus, version 3.13.0 (branch: main, revision: 297523f69)
```

### Prometheus configuration file

```yaml
# Any configuration that includes alerting with service discovery
alerting:
  alertmanagers:
    - static_configs:
        - targets:
            - 'localhost:9093'
```

### Alertmanager version

N/A — this is a Prometheus-internal issue.

### Alertmanager configuration file

N/A

### Logs

No specific log output — the bug is a silent tight loop with no logging.
Can be observed via CPU profiling (`pprof`) showing the `targetUpdateLoop` goroutine consuming 100% of a CPU core during shutdown.

---

## Additional Context

- **Affected file**: [`notifier/manager.go`](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/297523f69/notifier/manager.go#L228-L230) (line 230)
- **Root cause**: `break` in a `select` inside a `for` loop only breaks the `select`, not the loop — a well-known Go footgun
- **Evidence**: Exact same code pattern as the scrape manager bug fixed in PR #19149
- **Impact**: Silent 100% CPU usage on one core during shutdown when the discovery manager's channel closes before the notifier is stopped
- **Possible fix**: Change `break` to `return` on [line 230 of `notifier/manager.go`](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/297523f69/notifier/manager.go#L230)

```release-notes
[BUGFIX] Notifier: Stop `targetUpdateLoop` spinning on cl

title: promql: round() produces NaN for to_nearest=0 and wrong results for negative to_nearest
body:
## Bug Report

The `round()` PromQL function has two bugs in how it handles the `to_nearest` scalar argument:

### 1. `round(v, 0)` returns NaN for all samples

When `to_nearest` is `0`, the computation `1.0 / toNearest` produces `+Inf`, and the final result becomes `NaN` for every sample in the input vector.

**Reproduction:**
```
round(some_metric, 0)
```
**Expected:** original values returned unchanged (rounding to the nearest multiple of 0 is undefined; returning the input is least surprising).
**Actual:** `NaN` for all samples.

### 2. `round(v, -2)` returns wrong results

When `to_nearest` is negative, `toNearestInverse` becomes negative, which flips the direction of `math.Floor`. For example, `round(5, -2)` returns `4` instead of `6`.

The set of multiples of `-2` is identical to the set of multiples of `2`, so the sign of `to_nearest` should not affect the result.

**Reproduction:**
```
round(some_metric, -2)
```
**Expected:** same result as `round(some_metric, 2)`.
**Actual:** incorrect values due to flipped floor direction.

### Root Cause

In `promql/functions.go`, `funcRound`:
```go
toNearestInverse := 1.0 / toNearest
return math.Floor(f*toNearestInverse+0.5) / toNearestInverse
```

No validation is performed on `toNearest`. A negative value inverts the floor operation, and zero causes division by zero leading to NaN.

### Environment

- Prometheus version: main branch (commit f075de91d)

title: Native histograms: improve trim function implementation
body:
For @zenador primarily, but anyone can contribute, just coordinate with them.

This is an optimization / refactoring task. Should not change the semantics of the native histograms trim functions (`</`, `>/`) - unless a genuine bug is found.

Goals:
- do not change tests, only add new ones that match old behavior (unless bug)
- optimize the implementation (remove extra allocations if there's some)
- simplify the code, improve readability
- establish code reuse with histogram_fraction implementation if possible
- cross check in tests with histogram_fraction (might be already there)

For the last point:
`h </ 0.5`  is almost exactly that same as `histogram_fraction(-Inf, 0.5, h) * histogram_count(h)`. The histogram_fraction returns NaN if `h` is zero, whereas the trim returns the empty histogram, which is more useful for defining alerts.

title: promql/parser: Incorrect error position for duration division by zero
body:
## Description
When evaluating a PromQL duration expression that results in a division or modulo by zero (e.g., `foo[5s/0d]`), the parser correctly returns a `division by zero` or `modulo by zero` error. However, it additionally emits a `duration must be greater than 0` error at the wrong position (`0:0`), rather than at the actual position of the duration expression. 

This incorrect position is noted internally in `promql/parser/parse_test.go` with a `// FIXME: this position looks wrong.` comment for multiple test cases.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Attempt to parse a PromQL query containing a duration division by zero, for example: `foo[5s/0d]` or `foo[step()/0d]`.
2. Observe the parse errors returned by the parser.

## Expected Result
The parser should report a single `division by zero` (or `modulo by zero`) error at the appropriate token location (e.g., `6:7`). If the parser also triggers the `duration must be greater than 0` validation error as a fallback, it should report it at the position of the evaluated duration expression.

## Actual Result
The parser reports the following:
1. `division by zero` at position `6:7` (Correct)
2. `duration must be greater than 0` at position `0:0` (Incorrect)

## Version
main branch (commit `c524bc30e`)

## Environment Information
- OS: N/A (Parser behavior, OS agnostic)
- Compiler (if applicable): N/A

## Repo Configuration
Standard Prometheus configuration. No specific configuration is required, as this is a PromQL parsing issue.

## Log Output
```go
errors: ParseErrors{
	ParseErr{
		PositionRange: posrange.PositionRange{Start: 6, End: 7},
		Err:           errors.New(`division by zero`),
		Query:         `foo[5s/0d]`,
	},
	ParseErr{
		PositionRange: posrange.PositionRange{Start: 0, End: 0}, // FIXME: this position looks wrong.
		Err:           errors.New(`duration must be greater than 0`),
		Query:         `foo[5s/0d]`,
	},
},

```

title: remote-write: send scraped metadata when metadata watcher starts
body:
### Proposal

When `metadata_config.send` is enabled for remote write v1,
`MetadataWatcher` sends scraped metadata only after the first
`metadata_config.send_interval` tick.

This can leave remote-write receivers with samples but no metric metadata for
one full interval after Prometheus startup, even though the scrape manager may
already have that metadata.

`MetadataWatcher` should perform one collection when it starts, then continue
using the configured interval for later sends.

### Use case

Remote-write receivers use metadata to show metric type, help, and unit for
incoming series. Sending the first metadata batch at watcher startup makes that
metadata available as soon as Prometheus has it, instead of delaying it until the
first periodic tick.

title: notifier: targetUpdateLoop spins at 100% CPU when target-set channel is closed
body:
### What did you do?


Run Prometheus with Alertmanager configured. Close the service discovery target-set channel passed to `notifier.Manager.Run` while `stopRequested` has not been signalled (e.g. during a shutdown sequence where the discovery manager stops before the notifier).

Minimal reproduction:

```go
tsets := make(chan map[string][]*targetgroup.Group)
// ... start manager ...
close(tsets) // triggers the spin
```

### What did you expect to see?

`targetUpdateLoop` detects the closed channel (`ok == false`) and exits cleanly, the same way it does when `stopRequested` is signalled.
- - - 

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?


The goroutine spins indefinitely at 100% CPU. No error is logged. The process does not crash but becomes unresponsive and pegs a CPU core.

Root cause in `notifier/manager.go`: when `tsets` is closed, `ok = false` and `break` is executed. But `break` exits the inner `select` only, not the outer `for` loop. The loop re-enters the `default` branch immediately and reads from the closed channel again, forever.

```go
func (n *Manager) targetUpdateLoop(tsets <-chan map[string][]*targetgroup.Group) {
	for {
		select {
		case <-n.stopRequested:
			return
		default:
			select {
			case <-n.stopRequested:
				return
			case ts, ok := <-tsets:
				if !ok {
					break  // exits inner select only, NOT the for loop
				}
				n.reload(ts)
			}
		}
	}
}
```

Replacing `break` with `return` fixes the spin.
- - -

### System information

 Linux 6.8.0-124-generic x86_64

### Prometheus version

```text
prometheus, version 3.13.0 (branch: HEAD, revision: f1cad001b)
  go version: go1.24.x
  platform:   linux/amd64
```

### Prometheus configuration file

```yaml

  scrape_interval: 15s

alerting:
  alertmanagers:
    - static_configs:

```

### Alertmanager version

title: discovery/moby: docker_sd and dockerswarm_sd can hang forever on unix:// and npipe:// hosts (no request timeout)
body:
### What did you do?

Configured `docker_sd_config` (or `dockerswarm_sd_config`) against a local Docker daemon over a unix socket — the most common deployment shape:

```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: docker
    docker_sd_configs:
      - host: unix:///var/run/docker.sock
        refresh_interval: 60s
```

Then let it run against a Docker daemon that at some point accepts the connection on the socket but stops responding to the API request (a wedged/overloaded `dockerd`, a stalled storage driver, a paused daemon).

This is code-inspection-driven rather than a deliberate reproduction — see *Under which circumstances* below for the reproduction path and for the field reports.

### What did you expect to see?

A request that stalls should be bounded, so that a stuck refresh eventually returns an error, is logged and counted in `prometheus_sd_refresh_failures_total`, and the next tick retries. Discovery should self-heal once the daemon recovers.

That is exactly what happens today when `host` is `http://` or `https://` — that path gets `http.Client{Timeout: refresh_interval}`.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

Discovery freezes **permanently**, silently, until the process is restarted. The target set stays pinned at the last successful snapshot, so removed containers are never reaped and newly created containers are never discovered. Nothing is logged, because a hang is not an error.

Two independent gaps combine:

**1. The request timeout is only wired up for TCP schemes.** `discovery/moby/docker.go:161-176` (and the identical block in `discovery/moby/dockerswarm.go:155`) at `2cf323988`:

```go
// There are other protocols than HTTP supported by the Docker daemon, like
// unix, which are not supported by the HTTP client. Passing HTTP client
// options to the Docker client makes those non-HTTP requests fail.
if hostURL.Scheme == "http" || hostURL.Scheme == "https" {
	rt, err := config.NewRoundTripperFromConfig(conf.HTTPClientConfig, "docker_sd")
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	clientOpts = append(clientOpts,
		client.WithHTTPClient(&http.Client{
			Transport: rt,
			Timeout:   time.Duration(conf.RefreshInterval),
		}),
		...
	)
}
```

For `unix://` and `npipe://` the whole block is skipped, so the client falls back to moby's `defaultHTTPClient` (`github.com/moby/moby/client@v0.4.1/client.go:270`), which sets only `MaxIdleConns` and `IdleConnTimeout` — **no `http.Client.Timeout`**. The unix transport from `docker/go-connections` (`sockets/sockets.go:52`, `configureUnixTransport`) installs a dialer with a 10s timeout, but that is a **dial** timeout only. Once the socket is accepted, a response that never arrives is waited on indefinitely.

The comment above the conditional is correct about `WithHTTPClient`/`WithScheme` breaking non-HTTP transports — but the *timeout* was never the part that breaks. It got skipped along with everything else.

**2. There is no per-refresh deadline either.** `discovery/refresh/refresh.go:69,88` calls `d.refresh(ctx)` synchronously with the long-lived Discoverer context and no bound of its own:

```go
case <-ticker.C:
	tgs, err := d.refresh(ctx)
```

So one blocked `ContainerList`/`NetworkList` blocks the loop itself. The ticker keeps firing into a select that never comes back around. (No SD in `discovery/` currently bounds its refresh — the only `context.WithTimeout` uses in the tree are the AWS config-validation probes. Every other SD relies on its HTTP client timeout, which is exactly what the unix Docker path lacks.)

**Diagnostic signature.** When this happens, `prometheus_sd_refresh_duration_seconds_count{mechanism="docker"}` stops incrementing entirely, while `prometheus_sd_refresh_failures_total` stays flat. That distinguishes a hang from the (deliberate) behaviour where a persistently *erroring* refresh also freezes the target set — that path logs `Unable to refresh target groups` and does increment both series.

**Reproduction.** Point `host` at a unix socke

title: tsdb: memSeries state is not restored for m-mapped chunks on restart
body:
### What did you do?

1. Started a Prometheus TSDB instance.
2. Appended samples to a series until a head chunk was m-mapped to disk (or forced an m-map via `truncateMemory`).
3. Appended a stale NaN marker to the series (or a native histogram sample, making it a native histogram series), and ensured this sample was also m-mapped to disk.
4. Restarted the Prometheus TSDB.
5. Observed the values of the metrics `prometheus_tsdb_head_series_stale`, `prometheus_tsdb_head_native_histogram_series`, and `prometheus_tsdb_head_native_histogram_buckets`.

Additionally, the same bug can be reproduced programmatically with this Go test added to `tsdb/head_test.go`:

```go
func TestHead_NumStaleSeries_RestartWithMmap(t *testing.T) {
	opts := DefaultHeadOptions()
	opts.ChunkRange = 1000
	opts.ChunkDirRoot = t.TempDir()

	wal, err := wlog.NewSize(nil, nil, filepath.Join(opts.ChunkDirRoot, "wal"), 32768, compression.None)
	require.NoError(t, err)

	head, err := NewHead(nil, nil, wal, nil, opts, nil)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.NoError(t, head.Init(0))
	defer func() { require.NoError(t, head.Close()) }()

	app := head.Appender(context.Background())
	series1 := labels.FromStrings("a", "1")
	_, err = app.Append(0, series1, 100, 1.0)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.NoError(t, app.Commit())

	// Append a stale marker
	app = head.Appender(context.Background())
	_, err = app.Append(0, series1, 200, math.Float64frombits(value.StaleNaN))
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.NoError(t, app.Commit())

	require.Equal(t, uint64(1), head.NumStaleSeries())

	// Force mmap by truncating
	require.NoError(t, head.truncateMemory(300))

	require.Equal(t, uint64(1), head.NumStaleSeries())

	// Restart
	require.NoError(t, head.Close())

	wal, err = wlog.NewSize(nil, nil, filepath.Join(opts.ChunkDirRoot, "wal"), 32768, compression.None)
	require.NoError(t, err)

	head, err = NewHead(nil, nil, wal, nil, opts, nil)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.NoError(t, head.Init(0))

	// Fails! Expected 1, got 0.
	require.Equal(t, uint64(1), head.NumStaleSeries(), "NumStaleSeries should be 1 after restart when stale sample is in mmap chunk")
}
```

### What did you expect to see?

I expected the TSDB to accurately track its internal series state across restarts.
Specifically, `prometheus_tsdb_head_series_stale` should reflect the correct number of stale series, and `prometheus_tsdb_head_native_histogram_series` / `prometheus_tsdb_head_native_histogram_buckets` should reflect the correct histogram counts, regardless of whether the latest sample was stored in a WAL-backed head chunk or an m-mapped head chunk.

Furthermore, I expected `isStaleSeries()` to correctly evaluate to `true` for these series so that garbage collection (e.g. `truncateStaleSeries`) properly cleans them up.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

After the restart, the TSDB completely "forgets" the `lastValue`, `lastHistogramValue`, and `lastFloatHistogramValue` of any series whose latest sample is inside an m-mapped chunk. 

- `head.NumStaleSeries()` drops to `0`.
- `head.NumNativeHistogramSeries()` drops to `0`.
- The series is no longer considered "stale" by GC, potentially leaking series references or keeping them alive longer than intended.
- If a new float or histogram sample is appended to the series after restart, the metrics delta calculation in `updateNativeHistogramMetricsOnAppend` will be incorrect because `sampleState()` wrongly evaluates the series as a float series (`isHistogram=false`).

**Root Cause Analysis:**
During startup, `loadMmappedChunks()` correctly rebuilds the `mmappedChunk` list for each series, but it explicitly does not decode the chunks to populate the series' `lastValue` or `lastHistogramValue`.
Subsequently, WAL replay skips replaying samples that fall within the time bounds of the already m-mapped chunks (`ms.append` and `ms.appendHistogram` are bypassed). 
Because these append functions are bypassed, the `lastValue` and `lastHistogramValue` fields

title: Deltas: add PromQL function to disable processing of start times
body:
We anticipate that some exporters will generate bad start times, and users may need a way to ignore those start times on a per-query basis.  While the preferred solution to bad data is fixing the bad data, this could appear as breakage for users if queries used to work and suddenly don't when they enable start time processing. We want to give them an option short of having to leave start time processing disabled globally, so a new function seems to be a good approach.

Such a function could be called something like `ignore_start_times()` or `drop_st()` and would essentially return the contained series as-is, but with all start times removed.  (This will require design: do we want them to be NaN, or zero, or empty slice of STs?)

Please do not volunteer for this issue, it is for internal tracking and will be assigned.

title: docs: clamp_max() and clamp_min() don't document their NaN behaviour
body:
`clamp()` documents what happens when one of the bounds is `NaN`:

> * Float samples are clamped to `NaN` if `min` or `max` is `NaN`

`clamp_max()` and `clamp_min()` don't say anything similar, but they go through the same `clamp()` helper in `promql/functions.go`, so they behave the same way:

```
clamp_max(some_metric, NaN)  # every float sample comes back NaN
clamp_min(some_metric, NaN)  # same
```

This is easy to hit by accident when the bound comes from a scalar expression that can evaluate to `NaN` rather than a literal. The result is silent: no warning, no annotation, just `NaN` propagating into whatever aggregation comes next.

There's no test coverage pinning it either. `functions.test` has cases for `clamp(test_clamp, 0, NaN)` and `clamp(test_clamp, NaN, 0)`, but nothing for the two single-bound variants.

I'll open a PR adding the note to both functions and the two missing test cases.

title: CI: Fix flaky `TestStartupInterrupt` and `FuzzParseOpenMetric` timeouts on contended runners
body:
## 1. `TestStartupInterrupt`

**Location:** `cmd/prometheus/main_unix_test.go`

### Failure

```
Should be true
prometheus didn't start in the specified timeout
```

### Root Cause

The test launches a real `prometheus` binary as a subprocess and polls:

```
http://localhost:<port>/graph
```

every **500 ms** for **10 attempts** (5 seconds total) before failing.

The test also uses `t.Parallel()`, so during `go test -race ./...` it competes with other tests for CPU time.

In the failing CI run, the environment reported:

```
GOMAXPROCS=4: CPU quota undefined
```

meaning the runner's cgroup CPU limit was not detected, increasing scheduling contention on shared runners.

A fixed **5-second** startup budget for:

- spawning the process,
- initializing TSDB,
- replaying WAL (if applicable), and
- binding the HTTP listener

can occasionally be insufficient under `-race` on a heavily loaded CI runner, resulting in a timeout despite Prometheus functioning correctly.

### Suggested Fix

Increase the startup polling budget to provide more headroom on contended CI runners, for example by:

- increasing the number of polling attempts (e.g. from 10 to 20–30), or
- increasing the overall timeout.

---

## 2. `FuzzParseOpenMetric`

**Location:** `util/fuzzing/fuzz_test.go`

### Failure

```
context deadline exceeded
```

### Root Cause

The failure is a timeout rather than a discovered crashing input.

Verification performed:

- Running the fuzz target standalone locally completed successfully.
- No crash reproducer exists under `testdata/fuzz/`, which Go would automatically generate if a failing input had been found.

During the failing CI run:

- `FuzzParseOpenMetric` and `FuzzParseMetricText` both executed for approximately four minutes.
- Both continued discovering new coverage until the end of execution.
- One target completed just before the deadline and passed.
- The other exceeded the deadline slightly and was terminated with `context deadline exceeded`.

This pattern is consistent with the overall test timeout being configured too close to the fuzzing duration (for example, `-timeout=4m` together with `-fuzztime=4m`), leaving little or no time for corpus write-out and cleanup after fuzzing completes.

### Suggested Fix

Configure the overall test timeout to provide headroom beyond the fuzzing duration, for example:

```bash
-fuzztime=4m
-timeout=5m
```

(or a larger timeout if appropriate).

---

title: Bug: Remote Write metadata intervals can panic Prometheus
body:
### What did you do?

Configured Remote Write 1 with metadata sending enabled and a zero metadata
send interval:

```yaml
remote_write:
  - url: http://localhost:9090/api/v1/write
    metadata_config:
      send: true
      send_interval: 0s
```

Before the fix, this configuration was accepted by config validation and could
be used with `promtool check config` or Prometheus startup.

Anyway, i'll make PR for this.

### What did you expect to see?

The configuration should be rejected with a clear validation error, for
example:

```text
remote write metadata send_interval must be positive
```

An invalid interval should not reach the metadata watcher or crash the
Prometheus process.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

Before the fix, `RemoteWriteConfig.UnmarshalYAML` did not validate
`metadata_config.send_interval` for Remote Write 1 when metadata sending was
enabled. `QueueManager.Start` then started `MetadataWatcher`, whose loop
created a ticker directly from the configured duration:

```go
time.NewTicker(time.Duration(mw.interval))
```

With `send_interval: 0s`, Go panicked with:

```text
panic: non-positive interval for NewTicker
```

The failure is reachable during Prometheus startup or configuration reload
when the invalid Remote Write configuration is activated.

Relevant pre-fix locations:

- `config/config.go`: `RemoteWriteConfig.UnmarshalYAML` accepted the zero interval.
- `storage/remote/queue_manager.go`: starts the metadata watcher when metadata sending is enabled.
- `storage/remote/metadata_watcher.go`: passes the configured interval to `time.NewTicker`.

Negative duration strings such as `-1s` are rejected earlier by duration
parsing. The missing explicit validation is the zero interval accepted by the
configuration loader.

### System information

_No response_

### Prometheus version

```text
Version v3.13.X
```

title: OTLP receiver: a metric with zero data points rolls back and 500s the entire write request (regression since the AppenderV2 refactor)
body:
## What did you do?

Sent OTLP metrics to `/api/v1/otlp/v1/metrics` where some payloads contain instruments with **zero data points** (instruments created but not recorded in that interval — e.g. eagerly-registered counters, or observable instruments whose callback records nothing).

## What did you expect to see?

The empty metric skipped and the rest of the request ingested, as on 3.5.0. The translator's own message describes the condition as a per-metric skip:

```go
errs = errors.Join(errs, fmt.Errorf("empty data points. %s is dropped", metric.Name()))
```

https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/v3.13.2/storage/remote/otlptranslator/prometheusremotewrite/metrics_to_prw.go#L256

## What did you see instead?

`HTTP 500`, and **every sample in the request discarded** — including healthy metrics from unrelated services that happened to share the batch.

```
level=ERROR source=write_otlp_handler.go:184 msg="Error appending remote write" component=web \
  err="empty data points. breaker.callback_failures is dropped
       empty data points. breaker.fallbacks is dropped
       empty data points. breaker.transitions is dropped
       empty data points. breaker.event.timestamp is dropped"
```

In production this took out ~25% of our OTLP ingest continuously (~1,330 of ~5,300 requests per 5 minutes; zero 500s on 3.5.0). Metrics with nothing wrong with them vanished because they shared a request with an empty instrument: one gauge went from 54 series to 0, a counter from 304 series to 0, another from ~730 series to 15. Senders also retry the 500, so a payload that can never succeed is resent indefinitely.

## Where the behaviour changed

The translator error is **identical in both versions**. What changed is how the exporter treats it.

**3.5.0 — logged as a warning and discarded, successfully translated series still written:**

```go
annots, err := converter.FromMetrics(ctx, md, otlptranslator.Settings{...})
if err != nil {
    rw.logger.Warn("Error translating OTLP metrics to Prometheus write request", "err", err)
}
...
err = rw.write(ctx, &prompb.WriteRequest{...})   // err reassigned; translation error dropped
return err
```

https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/v3.5.0/storage/remote/write_handler.go#L592-L612

**3.13.2 and `main` — the same error propagates and rolls the appender back:**

```go
annots, err := converter.FromMetrics(ctx, md, otlptranslator.Settings{...})

defer func() {
    if err != nil {
        _ = app.Rollback()
        return
    }
    err = app.Commit()
}()
...
return err
```

https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/v3.13.2/storage/remote/write_otlp_handler.go#L118-L145
https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/storage/remote/write_otlp_handler.go#L125-L152

The handler then maps anything that is not out-of-order to 500:

https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/v3.13.2/storage/remote/write_otlp_handler.go#L177-L188

So a condition that is documented in its own message as "dropped" is now request-fatal *and* causes rollback of everything already appended. This looks like unintended fallout of switching the remote receivers to AppenderV2 (#17675) rather than a deliberate strictness change — `FromMetrics` returns a `errors.Join` of per-metric skip reasons mixed with genuine append failures, and the new code cannot distinguish them.

## Suggested fix

Distinguish per-metric skip conditions from real append errors. Either:

1. **Report empty-data-point metrics as annotations** rather than joining them into `errs` (they are already surfaced via `annots`, and `main` now even has `annotations.go` in that package), or
2. **Commit what was appended** and return 200 (or a partial-success response) when the only errors are skip-class, reserving rollback + 5xx for genuine storage failures.

Option 1 restores 3.5.0 semantics with no protocol change.

## Environment

- Prometheus **3.13.2** (also present on `main`), `--web.enable-otlp-receiver`
- Senders: Grafana Alloy forwarding OTLP f

title: Promtool recording rule block generation should support 24hr blocks
body:
### Proposal

While prometheus compacted tsdb blocks use sizes like 6, 18, and 54hr, other tsdb systems (like Mimir) use 24hr daily blocks. In recording rule block generation mode, promtool does not let the user create 24hr blocks because it wants to match prometheus' own tsdb block sizes, but for best compatbility with other tsdb systems we should at least make it possible to specify 24h blocks, and possibly arbitrarily-sized blocks (perhaps requiring division/multiples of 24hr?).  We can notify the user or require a break-glass flag to select non-standard sizes, but it should be an available option.

### What did you do?

the DescribeInstances API response has a nil `Placement` field (similar to
