title: scrape: memory doubles for bodies over 59MB
body:
### What did you do?

Scraped a target returning ~60MB of text, gzipped.

### What did you expect to see?

Memory proportional to one copy of the body.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

Roughly double. The body sits on the heap twice for the whole parse.

Buffers come from a pool topping out at 59049000 bytes. Past that `Get` returns a slice sized exactly to the body, so `cap == len` and something has to reallocate:

- `ReadFrom` grows by `MinRead` before every `Read`, so the last one copies the buffer.
- `NewPromParser` appends a newline, same thing, and that copy lives as long as the parser.

Only `Content-Length` responses return the last bytes together with `io.EOF` and skip that final grow, so with gzip it is the read side that copies.

Reserving `MinRead` avoids both. One byte does not; the threshold is `MinRead`, not `cap > len`.

#19394 has the fix.

### System information

linux/amd64

### Prometheus version

On `main` as of `4bf303df8`, and in v3.

title: tsdb: avoid retaining unbounded OOO record buffers in bytesPool
body:
### What did you do?

Ran a TSDB Head with substantial out-of-order ingestion.

### What did you expect to see?

Temporary WBL-encoded OOO records should become collectible after `Commit()`.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

Heap profiles can attribute a large amount of retained memory to
`(*appenderCommitContext).collectOOORecords`.

`collectOOORecords` obtains record buffers through `Head.getBytesBuffer()`.
At the end of `Commit`, each is returned using:

title: discovery/ionos: panic on servers with null optional fields
body:
### What did you do?

Read through discovery/ionos/server.go while looking at the AWS SD nil-guard fixes (#19184, #19374) to see if other SD implementations have the same issue.

### What did you expect to see?

Optional fields being omitted from the label set when absent, matching the guard pattern already used elsewhere in the same file (e.g. `server.Properties.BootCdrom`) and in other SDs.

### What did you see instead?

`refresh()` builds part of the label set from a struct literal that dereferences several pointer fields with no nil check:

```go
labels := model.LabelSet{
    model.AddressLabel:          model.LabelValue(addr),
    serverAvailabilityZoneLabel: model.LabelValue(*server.Properties.AvailabilityZone),
    serverCPUFamilyLabel:        model.LabelValue(*server.Properties.CpuFamily),
    serverServersIDLabel:        model.LabelValue(*servers.Id),
    serverIDLabel:               model.LabelValue(*server.Id),
    serverIPLabel:               model.LabelValue(join(ips, metaLabelSeparator)),
    serverLifecycleLabel:        model.LabelValue(*server.Metadata.State),
    serverNameLabel:             model.LabelValue(*server.Properties.Name),
    serverStateLabel:            model.LabelValue(*server.Properties.VmState),
    serverTypeLabel:             model.LabelValue(*server.Properties.Type),
}
```

All of `Id`, `AvailabilityZone`, `CpuFamily`, `Name`, `VmState`, `Type` (on `ServerProperties`), plus `Id` on `Server`/`Servers`, and `Metadata`/`State` (on `DatacenterElementMetadata`), are declared as pointers with `omitempty` in the IONOS SDK (github.com/ionos-cloud/sdk-go/v6), so the API can legitimately omit any of them. If it does, this panics. There's no `recover()` in discovery/, so it takes down the whole process, same as the EC2 case in #19374.

### System information

Code inspection against `main`.

title: otlptranslator: valid OTLP histogram stored with le="+Inf" below its own _count
body:
### What did you do?

On `main` at `44d6a0e0b`, translated a classic `HistogramDataPoint` whose explicit bounds end at `+Inf`, then read back
its series:

```go
pt.SetCount(42)
pt.SetSum(100)
pt.BucketCounts().FromRaw([]uint64{5, 10, 20, 7})
pt.ExplicitBounds().FromRaw([]float64{1, 2, math.Inf(1)})
```

**Correction (2026-08-17):** this data point satisfies the arithmetic only on paper. `bucket_counts` is one longer than
`explicit_bounds`, the bounds are strictly increasing, and `count` equals their sum (`5 + 10 + 20 + 7 = 42`) — but with
`+Inf` as the last explicit bound the trailing bucket spans `(+Inf, +infinity)`, which cannot hold the 7 observations it
is given, so `count = 42` is not attainable. The reachable shape is below.

### What did you expect to see?

`le="+Inf"` equal to `_count`, as the cumulative convention requires.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

`le="+Inf"` is written **twice** for the same series and timestamp, and nothing reports it. The two writes are equal
whenever `count` equals the sum of the bucket counts **below** the infinite bound, which the reachable shape satisfies —
so the defect there is the duplicate alone. They disagree, `_count` `42` against `le="+Inf"` `35`, when the counts below
the bound do not add up to `count`, as in the example above, where the `7` sits in a bucket this path never reads.

**The same input is rejected on the other path.** With `convert_histograms_to_nhcb: true` the identical data point
becomes

```
{count:42, sum:100, [-Inf,1]:5, (1,2]:10, (2,+Inf]:20, (+Inf,+Inf]:7}
```

and `checkHistogramCustomBounds`, reached from `Histogram.Validate`, refuses it:

```
custom buckets: last +Inf bound must not be explicitly defined: histogram custom bounds must be finite
```

That rule is in `model/histogram/generic.go`, and `tsdb/head_append.go` turns it into a rejected sample by calling
`h.Validate()`. It also looks deliberate rather than incidental: #17320 revisited that function to accept `-Inf` and
kept `+Inf` rejected. So the invariant is already stated here, an explicit `+Inf` bound must not be defined, and the
classic path is the one that does not hold to it — while being the default, since `convert_histograms_to_nhcb` is absent
from `DefaultOTLPConfig`.

**Where the second `le="+Inf"` comes from.** The loop over explicit bounds writes one `_bucket` series per bound,
formatting the bound into `le`, so the `+Inf` bound emits `le="+Inf"` carrying the running sum at that point, `35`. Then
`le="+Inf"` is synthesized again from `pt.Count()` after the loop. Both reach `Append` with identical labels and
timestamp. Both are accepted and the commit keeps the first: two appends of `35` then `42` at the same timestamp in one
batch return no error and store `35`, while the same second append issued after a commit is refused as a duplicate
sample for that timestamp. The fourth bucket count, `7`, is the overflow bucket, which this path never reads.

**Tests.** #19425 pins three shapes in `TestPrometheusConverter_AddHistogramDataPoints` — the reachable one and two
that are invalid in different ways — and all three fail without the guard.

**How often this happens — measured, and my first guess was wrong.** I wrote that an SDK has no reason to emit such a
bound. The Go SDK accepts one: `AggregationExplicitBucketHistogram.err()` in
`go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/metric` validates only that the boundaries are monotonic, so
`Boundaries{1, 2, math.Inf(1)}` is accepted with no error, and recording through it emits

```
explicit_bounds = [1 2 +Inf]
bucket_counts   = [5 2 3 0]   (the trailing bucket is necessarily empty)
count           = 10
```

so the input is reachable from a plain misconfiguration, though I still have not counted producers in the wild. It is
worth fixing because nothing reports it: the bucket series stays monotonic, no error is returned, and the guard is one
condition.

#19425 carries the change, and reports the bound as a translation warning rather th

title: promtool: no tool to find inconsistent classic histograms in a TSDB
body:
### Proposal

Quantiles, alerts and recording rules can be computed from classic histograms whose stored buckets
contradict each other — and nothing lists which series are affected, or since when.

**How the data gets there.** No ingest path cross-checks the float series of a classic histogram:
scrape, remote write and the OTLP receiver append what was sent. Buckets whose cumulative counts
decrease, or a `le="+Inf"` bucket disagreeing with `_count`, are stored as-is. Native histograms are
rejected at append (`model/histogram/histogram.go:474`, `ErrHistogramCountMismatch`); classic ones have
no equivalent check anywhere.

**What it costs while it sits there.** `histogram_quantile` repairs non-monotonic input on the fly
(`util/annotations/annotations.go:163`) and keeps returning plausible numbers, so SLOs and alerts built
on an affected histogram are computed from silently patched data. The only signal is a per-query info
annotation, phrased as a property of the query — the data stays broken for every next query. That
annotation had to be taught to at least name the affected metric (#15411); finding all affected series
in a TSDB still has no tool.

**The fix.** `promtool tsdb check-histograms [db path]`
scans a TSDB range (`--min-time`/`--max-time`) and reports, per histogram: non-monotonic cumulative
buckets; `le="+Inf"` disagreeing with `_count`; `le` labels that do not parse as a float (`le="NaN"` is
storable today); duplicate `le` spellings carrying different values at the same timestamp (`le="1"` vs
`le="1.0"` on disjoint timestamps — the v3 migration shape — is recognized as clean); histograms with no
`+Inf` bucket at all. Exits non-zero when anything is found, so it
can run from cron or CI. Placed under `promtool tsdb` because it takes a database path like `dump` and
`analyze` (`promtool check` takes config files and server URLs), and marked `[Experimental]` like
`dump-openmetrics`.

**Limits.** Native histograms are out of scope — already validated at append. And I have not measured
how often such data occurs in the wild — this tool is how an operator answers that for their own TSDB.

Found and verified on `main` at `44d6a0e`; file and line references are against that commit.

cc @dgl — promtool is your path, and this proposes a new subcommand in it.

title: promtool tsdb create-blocks-from rules panics on a rule file with multiple YAML documents
body:
### What did you do?

Ran `promtool tsdb create-blocks-from rules` over a rule file that contains a second YAML document. The file is otherwise valid, and the rule loader only means to warn that it will process the first document.

`rules.yml`:

```yaml
groups:
  - name: example
    rules:
      - record: job:http_requests:rate1m
        expr: sum by (job)(rate(http_requests_total[1m]))
---
groups: []
```

```console
$ promtool tsdb create-blocks-from rules \
    --start=2026-08-01T00:00:00Z --end=2026-08-02T00:00:00Z \
    --output-dir=./out rules.yml
```

No running Prometheus is needed to hit this. The rule files are loaded before the first range query is issued, so the process dies before it ever contacts `--url`.

### What did you expect to see?

The warning that only the first document is processed, followed by the backfill running against the rules from that document. That is what `promtool check rules` does with the very same file:

```console
$ promtool check rules rules.yml
Checking rules.yml
time=2026-08-16T17:03:40.271+08:00 level=WARN source=rulefmt.go:369 msg="Multiple document yaml rules files are not supported, only the first document is processed"
  SUCCESS: 1 rules found

$ echo $?
0
```

So the two commands disagree about the same file: one warns and succeeds, the other crashes.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

A nil pointer dereference (frames in the middle elided):

```text
time=2026-08-16T17:03:40.303+08:00 level=INFO source=rules.go:62 msg="new rule importer" component=backfiller start="01 Aug 26 00:00 UTC" end="02 Aug 26 00:00 UTC"
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x1 addr=0x0 pc=0x905758]

goroutine 1 [running]:
log/slog.(*Logger).Handler(...)
	/usr/local/go/src/log/slog/logger.go:121
log/slog.(*Logger).log(0x0, ...)
	/usr/local/go/src/log/slog/logger.go:244 +0x98
log/slog.(*Logger).Warn(...)
	/usr/local/go/src/log/slog/logger.go:219
github.com/prometheus/prometheus/model/rulefmt.Parse(...)
	model/rulefmt/rulefmt.go:369 +0x373
github.com/prometheus/prometheus/model/rulefmt.ParseFile(...)
	model/rulefmt/rulefmt.go:396 +0x88
github.com/prometheus/prometheus/rules.FileLoader.Load(...)
	rules/manager.go:341
github.com/prometheus/prometheus/rules.(*Manager).LoadGroups(...)
	rules/manager.go:357 +0x12b
main.(*ruleImporter).loadGroups(...)
	cmd/promtool/rules.go:75
```

Note the receiver in the `log` frame is `0x0`: the logger the group loader holds is nil.

It comes from `NewManager`. `ManagerOptions.Logger` is optional and gets a no-op logger when it is left unset:

```go
if o.Logger == nil {
	o.Logger = promslog.NewNopLogger()
}
```

but that runs *after* the default group loader has already been built out of the same field:

```go
if o.GroupLoader == nil {
	o.GroupLoader = FileLoader{parser: o.Parser, logger: o.Logger}
}
```

`FileLoader` captures the logger by value, so it keeps the nil forever, while `Manager.opts.Logger` ends up perfectly valid. That is why this went unnoticed: the manager looks like it has a logger, only its loader does not.

Nothing dereferenced it until #18114 added the multi-document warning to `rulefmt.Parse`, which has no nil check:

```go
err = decoder.Decode(&secondDoc)
if !errors.Is(err, io.EOF) {
	logger.Warn("Multiple document yaml rules files are not supported, only the first document is processed")
}
```

`promtool tsdb create-blocks-from rules` walks into it because its importer builds the manager without a logger, in `newRuleImporter`:

```go
ruleManager: rules.NewManager(&rules.ManagerOptions{
	NameValidationScheme: config.nameValidationScheme,
}),
```

The backfill command is just the one caller that ships in this repo. Anything else that constructs a rule manager and leaves `ManagerOptions.Logger` unset is exposed in the same way, including projects that embed the rule manager as a library, so I would not treat this as promtool-specific.

The Prometheus server

title: scrape: go test -shuffle aborts the test run with "select on synctest channel from outside bubble"
body:
Root cause is upstream in Go's `net`, which I reported as golang/go#80903. It needs a change here regardless: the upstream fix covers two of the three channels involved, and the third is the one this hits on the default resolver path.

### What did you do?

Ran the `scrape` package's own tests with Go's test shuffling enabled, on a clean checkout of `main` at `7a73c9ae6`:

```
go test -count=1 -shuffle=42 ./scrape/
```

### What did you expect to see?

The same result as the default order, which passes.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

The run aborts. No test is reported as failing — the process is gone first:

```
fatal error: select on synctest channel from outside bubble

goroutine 2196 [running]:
net.cgoLookupIP ← net.(*Resolver).lookupIP ← internal/singleflight.(*Group).doCall
  created by internal/singleflight.(*Group).DoChan in goroutine 1823
FAIL	github.com/prometheus/prometheus/scrape	1.745s
```

`-shuffle` appears in no workflow, so the default order is the only one CI runs, which is why this passes upstream on
every commit.

Nine tests in this package reach `osutil.GetFQDN`, and the fatal needs the `synctest` one —
`TestScrapeOffsetDistribution`, through `setOffsetSeed` — to be the **first** lookup in the process; once an outside
caller has reached the resolver, the in-bubble one is harmless. Measured two ways: each of the other eight can abort
when paired with it, and on one such pair ten seeds split cleanly by which test ran first. It is not the `singleflight`
group the stack trace suggests: the object is a package-level channel in `net`, created lazily under a `sync.Once`, so
whoever calls first decides which bubble it belongs to for the rest of the process. The full write-up is in
golang/go#80903.

`manager.go:390-393` already describes the hazard, and `setupSynctestManager` avoids it with a fake server, a `net.Pipe`
per dial and `skipJitterOffsetting`. `TestScrapeOffsetDistribution` is the one `synctest` site that doesn't go through
the helper, and the lookup isn't in the scraping path a fake network covers: it arrives from `ApplyConfig` →
`setOffsetSeed`.

Setting the existing flag on that test isn't a way out on its own:

```
--- FAIL: TestScrapeOffsetDistribution
    scrape_test.go:8033: "1" is not greater than "2"
    Expected targets to be scraped at staggered offsets rather than simultaneously at scrape index 0
```

The flag does two things at once: it skips the seed calculation, and at `scrape.go:1313` it zeroes each scrape loop's
offset — which is what that test asserts. The three tests using the helper depend on the second effect; this one needs
the first and cannot have the second.

Fixing it here does not depend on the upstream fix landing: the third channel, `net.threadLimit`, derives its capacity
from `rlim.Cur`, so it cannot simply be created eagerly, and with the other two changed the default resolver path on
this platform still aborts.

Related: `#17941`, though the mechanism there is different.

### System information

```
darwin/arm64, go1.26.1
```

### Prometheus version

```
Reproduced from source at 7a73c9ae6, not from a release binary.
```

### Prometheus configuration file

```
n/a — this is a test-suite failure, no configuration involved.
```

title: deadlock on `stripeSeries` due to lock ordering
body:
### What did you do?

From Mimir we call `CompactSelectedSeries` from another goroutine under some circumstances.

### What did you expect to see?

No deadlock / wedged prometheus/ingester instances.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

Deadlock due to AB - BA lock ordering, AFAICT, this can only happen when calling `CompactSelectedSeries` (maybe more) methods from another goroutine. The issues is that
- `gcSeries.func1` locks series mutex first (series.Lock()), then tries the stripe RWMutex write lock
- `mmapHeadChunksInStripe` locks the stripe RWMutex read lock first, then tries series mutex via mmapSeriesChunks (head.go:2245), if this happens for the same series, we DL.

```

sync.(*Mutex).Lock(...)
(*Head).mmapSeriesChunks(0x3f1657808808, 0x3f17e60d09c0)
(*Head).mmapHeadChunksInStripe(0x3f1657808808, ...)
(*Head).mmapHeadChunks(0x3f1657808808) 
(*DB).run(...)

Goroutine 9563 :
(*RWMutex).Lock(...)
(*stripeSeries).gcSeries.func1(0x2709, ..., 0x3f17e60d09c0, ...)
(*stripeSeries).iterForDeletion(0x3f16570c2200, ...)
(*stripeSeries).gcSeries(0x3f16570c2200, ...)
(*Head).gcSeries(0x3f1657808808, ...)
(*Head).truncateSeries
```

title: web/api/v1: Search API panics when Querier is nil during TSDB reload

### What did you do?

 the experimental search API (`--web.enable-feature=memory-snapshot-on-shutdown` is not needed, just `--web.search` / search APIs enabled on `main`) and queried the new search endpoints while Prometheus was reloading.

Steps:
1. Build Prometheus from `main` (tested on commit `a1b2c3d` ~ 2026-09-01) with search endpoints enabled
2. Start with a standard config (TSDB, single node, no special storage settings)
3. In one terminal, loop reloads:

while true; do kill -HUP $(pidof prometheus); sleep 2; done
```

title: remote-write: a series with a duplicate label name is answered 204 and silently dropped
body:
## What happens

A remote-write `WriteRequest` containing a series with the same label name twice
is answered `204 No Content`. Prometheus logs the problem, increments a counter,
and stores nothing. The sender is told the write succeeded.

Remote-write 1.0 has no partial-success field, so the status code is the only
signal a sender has, and here it says the opposite of what happened.

## Reproduction

Prometheus 3.14.0 started with the receiver enabled:

```
docker run -d -p 9090:9090 prom/prometheus:v3.14.0 \
  --config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml --web.enable-remote-write-receiver
```

The body below is a snappy-compressed `WriteRequest` holding one series,
`dup_demo{zone="a", zone="b"}`, with a single sample. (Its timestamp is fixed,
so if it falls outside the ingest window, regenerate rather than reusing it.)

```
echo 'QIgKPgoUCghfX25hbWVfXxIIZHVwX2RlbW8KCQoEem9uZRIBYRkLSGISEAkAAAAAAADwPxCMtI+XiDQ=' | base64 -d > dup.pb.snappy

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:9090/api/v1/write \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/x-protobuf' \
  -H 'Content-Encoding: snappy' \
  -H 'X-Prometheus-Remote-Write-Version: 0.1.0' \
  --data-binary @dup.pb.snappy
```

Observed:

```
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content

$ curl -sG localhost:9090/api/v1/series --data-urlencode 'match[]=dup_demo'
{"status":"success","data":[]}

$ curl -s localhost:9090/metrics | grep invalid_labels
prometheus_api_remote_write_invalid_labels_samples_total 1
```

and in the log:

```
level=WARN source=write_handler.go:181 msg="Invalid labels for series."
  labels="{__name__=\"dup_demo\", zone=\"a\", zone=\"b\"}" duplicated_label=zone
```

## Is this intended?

I ask because it looks deliberate rather than accidental, and because #14716
already moved the *TSDB append* duplicate-label path from 5xx to 4xx. This is a
different path — validation in `write_handler.go`, which counts the sample and
continues — so a request whose every series is invalid still gets a 204.

I can see the argument for it: failing the whole request over one bad series
would cost every good series batched alongside it, and a sender that retries a
5xx forever is worse than one that loses a sample. If that is the reasoning, is
the intended answer for a 1.0 sender simply that it cannot know, and that the
remote-write 2.0 written-samples response headers are where this gets fixed?

If so I'd suggest saying it in the remote-write receiver documentation, since
"2xx means stored" is the natural reading and it is not true here.

## How this was found

Sending deliberately unusual but conformant payloads to several stores and
comparing what comes back. On the same request:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Prometheus 3.14.0 | 204, stores nothing |
| Grafana Mimir 3.2.0 | 400, "received a series with duplicate label name, label: 'zone'" |
| VictoriaMetrics 1.151.0 | 204, keeps `zone="b"` |
| GreptimeDB 1.2.0 | 204, keeps `zone="b"` |

Mimir refuses; two stores take the later label; Prometheus keeps neither. Only
the Mimir answer is distinguishable by a sender.

title: Question: should SearchLabelValues return the first N alphabetical values when ordered ascending?
body:
Hi there!

I noticed that SearchLabelValues returns different values for a limited ascending search depending on whether the filter is nil or accepts everything. I wanted to check whether this is intended.

If I add `z_metric`, `m_metric`, then `a_metric` to Head and ask for two values in ascending order, I get:

- With a nil filter: `m_metric`, `z_metric`
- With a filter that accepts everything with score 1: `a_metric`, `m_metric`

I expected those calls to return the same values. It looks like the nil-filter path applies the limit before sorting, while the filter path checks the full set first.

I did search the issues but didn't see this specifically. However, I did see that #12795 says ordering isn't guaranteed for limited results in the legacy API. Does that also apply to the search interface added in #18497? In other words, does ascending order mean “give me the first N alphabetical values”, or “pick N values, then sort them”?

I've tried a small local patch that sorts before limiting for Head and keeps the early limit for format-v2 blocks, where the values are already ordered. There's a test showing the difference too. Some informal benchmarks show a substantial increase in time and allocations for Head when there are lots of values, so there's a trade-off here. Happy to share the patch, test and detailed numbers if useful.

Before taking that further, is this a bug, or have I misunderstood the intended behaviour?

Cheers,

-Lea.

PS: I used AI tools to help with the investigation and this draft, but I've reviewed everything - just disclosing this.

title: tsdb: no metric for how many series stale series compaction actually evicts
body:
### Proposal

I was reading through the stale series compaction code and I think there's a gap in what it reports.

Right now there are six metrics for stale and selected series compaction:

- `prometheus_tsdb_stale_series_compactions_triggered_total`
- `prometheus_tsdb_stale_series_compactions_failed_total`
- `prometheus_tsdb_stale_series_compaction_duration_seconds`
- and the same three for selected series compaction

All of them tell you the compaction ran. None of them tell you whether it actually freed anything.

That matters because eviction is deliberately conservative. `truncateStaleSeries` skips a series if it picked up out of order data, got a new sample, or its fingerprint changed while the block was being written. So a run can go through 50k candidates and evict zero of them, and from the outside it looks identical to a run that evicted all of them. Triggered counter goes up, failed counter stays flat, duration gets recorded, done.

The log line doesn't really help either:

```go
db.logger.Info("Ending stale series compaction", "num_series", len(staleSeriesRefs.sortedByRef), "duration", elapsed)
```

`num_series` there is the candidate count, not the number that got evicted. So a run that freed nothing still logs `num_series=50000`, which reads like it worked.

The slightly odd part is the number already exists. `truncateSeries` returns `len(deleted)` and both callers throw it away:

```go
func (h *Head) truncateStaleSeries(...) error {
	_, err := h.truncateSeries(seriesRefs, maxt, func(s *memSeries) bool {
```

Same thing in `truncateSelectedSeries`.

I checked whether `prometheus_tsdb_head_series_removed_total` covers it and it doesn't. That one gets incremented from four different places (WAL replay, normal head gc, this path, and `deleteSeriesByID`), so you can't pull stale compaction out of it.

Why I think it's worth adding: `stale_series_compaction_threshold` is opt in and still experimental, so the people running it are exactly the people who need to know if it's helping. In #18379 someone turned it on, hit problems, and was debugging off a memory graph because there wasn't anything better to look at.

I hit a smaller version of this myself while writing a test against this code. I spent a while assuming eviction was happening when it actually wasn't, and only worked it out by reading `head.metrics.seriesRemoved` directly. An operator can't do that.

What I'd suggest:

- counters for candidates and evicted per compaction type, so something like `prometheus_tsdb_stale_series_compaction_series_candidates_total` and `prometheus_tsdb_stale_series_compaction_series_evicted_total`, plus the selected series versions
- add `num_evicted` to both log lines, and leave `num_series` alone so nothing parsing logs breaks

Both numbers are useful since evicted over candidates is the thing you'd actually alert on, and you can't work one out from the other with what's there today. If four new metrics feels like too many, just the evicted ones would still fix the main problem.

The change itself is small. The count already gets computed, it just needs returning instead of dropping, and the callers can capture it in the closure they already pass so `headSeriesEvictor` doesn't need to change.

title: tsdb: OOO blocks contain dead symbols
body:
### What did you do?

An out-of-order (OOO) block can accumulate symbols, that aren't referenced by any entry in the block's postings offset table.

That is, TSDB is configured with non-zero `OutOfOrderTimeWindow`. When it cuts its OOO head, the `OOOCompactionHeadIndexReader.Symbols()` produces a string iterator, that walks over symbols from the entire head, without applying the OOO-series (or any time-range) filtering. This results in OOO block, that contains dead symbols.

These symbols later survive `LeveledCompactor.Compact()`, because the `DefaultBlockPopulator.PopulateBlock()` merges the complete symbol iterators from all input indices and writes their union into the output index (ref [tsdb/compact.go][1]).

[1]: https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/a08aa73ce120bd1e098d61247167fae89d941fa5/tsdb/compact.go#L957-L962

### What did you expect to see?

Either production of OOO block should filter out symbols, that aren't referenced by postings offset table. Or, the compaction should clear those out.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

In grafafan/mimir, we observed OOO blocks, that over many rounds of non-split compaction cycles can accumulate gigabytes of such dead symbols.

title: tsdb/agent: a failed WAL write returns a dirty buffer to the pool and corrupts the WAL
body:
### What did you do?

Ran agent mode with the WAL on a filesystem that filled up, then freed space. I first hit this in Grafana Alloy, which carries a copy of the same appender code, and reproduced it on Prometheus main at 46ef3704189798f58af5dd4ac7d2f87ac8880f30 with the test below.

`(*appenderBase).log()` takes a buffer from `bufPool` and returns it in a deferred `Put`, but only resets it after a successful `wal.Log()`. All 7 error returns hand the pool a buffer that still holds the encoded record:

https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/46ef3704189798f58af5dd4ac7d2f87ac8880f30/tsdb/agent/db.go#L1226-L1236

`record.Encoder` appends to the buffer it's given, and `bufPool` is one `sync.Pool` on `DB`, so the next commit writes its record after the failed one and `wal.Log()` checksums the concatenation as one valid record. `logSeries()` has the same shape (L1344-L1354).

Fix, since the closure captures `buf` by reference:

```go
defer func() {
	a.bufPool.Put(buf[:0]) //nolint:staticcheck
}()
```

Same change in `logSeries()`.

### What did you expect to see?

A failed write loses that batch, and the next commit writes a clean record.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

The test fills a 1 MiB tmpfs, commits until N commits fail with ENOSPC, frees the space, commits twice more, decodes every WAL record, then reopens the DB. Linux arm64, run in Docker.

| series, failed commits | main | main + fix above |
|---|---|---|
| 50, 5 | 5 of 10 records fail with `decode error after 152 samples: invalid size`; replay repairs at offset 5711 and deletes 6 records, including 2 commits that returned nil | 0 undecodable, 0 lost |
| 200, 3 | one record decodes to 602 samples, 69 of them fabricated; replay logs `found sample referencing non-existing series`; 2 acknowledged commits lost | 0 fabricated, 0 lost |

Same result with `-test.cpu 1` and `8`. Spliced records are byte-exact prefixes of each other, which is also what I found in the WAL of two affected Alloy hosts.

Two related things the same test shows, which this fix doesn't cover:

* At 1000 and 2000 series both builds lose acknowledged commits to `unexpected first record, dropping buffer`. That's the TODO in `wlog.log()` at L764, and I've added detail on #13027.
* A failed `Commit()` puts the appender back in the pool without `clearData()`, so the next commit logs the failed samples again (1200 duplicate samples in the patched 200-series run).

title: promtool tsdb create-blocks-from rules: loop terminates prematurely if first block has no evaluation points
body:
### What did you do?

Ran `promtool tsdb create-blocks-from rules` to backfill recording rules over a historical time range where `--start` falls near the end of a TSDB block boundary:

```bash
promtool tsdb create-blocks-from rules \
  --start="2026-09-16T11:50:00Z" \
  --end="2026-09-16T16:00:00Z" \
  --url="http://localhost:9090" \
  recording_rules.yml
```

The rule group in `recording_rules.yml` has an evaluation interval of `15m`:
```yaml
groups:
  - name: test_group
    interval: 15m
    rules:
      - record: job:test_rate:15m
        expr: rate(test_metric[15m])
```

### What did you expect to see?

`promtool` should backfill all evaluation points between `11:50:00` and `16:00:00`. Since the first aligned 2-hour TSDB block `[10:00:00, 12:00:00)` contains no evaluation points (the first 15m evaluation point falls at `12:00:00`), `promtool` should skip that initial block and proceed to generate blocks for `[12:00:00, 14:00:00)` and `[14:00:00, 16:00:00)`.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

`promtool` exited with status `0` without generating any blocks.

Looking at `cmd/promtool/rules.go:114-117`:
```go
end := time.Unix(min(endOfBlock/int64(time.Second/time.Millisecond), end.Unix()), 0).UTC()
if end.Before(startWithAlignment) {
    break
}
```

1. Local variable `end` shadows the function parameter `end time.Time` (the overall backfill end time).
2. In the first block `[10:00:00, 11:59:59]`, `currStart` is `11:50:00` and `startWithAlignment` is `12:00:00`.
3. `end` is computed as `min(endOfBlock, userEnd)`, which evaluates to `11:59:59`.
4. `11:59:59.Before(12:00:00)` evaluates to `true`.
5. Because `break` is executed instead of `continue`, the entire `startOfBlock` loop terminates immediately, skipping all remaining blocks (`[12:00:00, 14:00:00)`, `[14:00:00, 16:00:00)`).
6. The function returns `nil` and `promtool` exits `0`, resulting in silent data omission.

The empty leading block should be skipped with `continue`, and `break` should only occur if `startWithAlignment` is after the overall requested end time:
```go
blockEnd := time.Unix(min(endOfBlock/int64(time.Second/time.Millisecond), end.Unix()), 0).UTC()
if end.Before(startWithAlignment) {
    break
}
if blockEnd.Before(startWithAlignment) {
    continue
}
```

### Environment

- System information: Linux / Windows (OS independent)
- Prometheus / promtool version: main (introduced in commit `bd217c58a7356bdc74f74b5a5645bfa85265942e`, affects all releases since v2.31.0)

title: Scrape timeout defaults and validation ignore per-target __scrape_interval__ from SD/relabeling
body:
### What did you do?

### Context

I am moving scrape jobs to service discovery (`http_sd_configs`) where the SD endpoint provides the scrape interval per target via the `__scrape_interval__` label, so intervals are managed centrally instead of in each job. Some exporters compute metrics dynamically at scrape time and need several minutes to respond, so they use a long interval (5m) and a long timeout (4m).

I first reported this against vmagent (VictoriaMetrics/VictoriaMetrics#11597). While investigating, the VictoriaMetrics maintainer compared behavior with Prometheus and found that Prometheus has the same underlying issue: the scrape timeout is resolved and validated at job level, before per-target `__scrape_interval__` is known.

### Case A: explicit job-level timeout, interval provided by SD

```yaml
global:
  scrape_interval: 1m
  scrape_timeout: 1m

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: example
    scrape_timeout: 4m
    # no scrape_interval: provided per target by SD
    http_sd_configs:
      - url: http://sd.example/targets
```

SD response:

```json
[
  {
    "targets": ["target.example:9100"],
    "labels": { "__scrape_interval__": "5m" }
  }
]
```

### Case B: timeout inherited from global, job interval overridden by SD

```yaml
global:
  scrape_interval: 1m
  scrape_timeout: 1m

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: example
    scrape_interval: 40s
    http_sd_configs:
      - url: http://sd.example/targets
```

Same SD response as above (`__scrape_interval__: 5m`).

### What did you expect to see?

The timeout should be resolved and checked against the **final per-target** scrape interval, after SD labels and relabeling are applied:

- Case A: the target is accepted with `__scrape_interval__="5m"` and `__scrape_timeout__="4m"`, since 4m < 5m.
- Case B: `__scrape_interval__="5m"` and `__scrape_timeout__="1m"`. The only timeout setting is the global 1m, which is valid against the 5m per-target interval.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

- Case A: Prometheus refuses to load the configuration:
  `scrape timeout greater than scrape interval for scrape config with job name "example"`
  The job's `scrape_timeout` is compared with the global interval (1m) inherited by the job, even though every target from SD has a 5m interval.

- Case B: the target gets `__scrape_interval__="5m"` and `__scrape_timeout__="40s"`. The default timeout is capped to the job-level interval (40s) at config load time, and this capped value is then used for targets whose SD-provided interval is 5m.

### Root cause

1. `ScrapeConfig.Validate` fills in the job interval from global, then rejects an explicit timeout that exceeds it, or caps the inherited timeout to it (`min(global timeout, job interval)`):
   https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/50461b669f0be3a9f0b31a94f72cde8e98f2779f/config/config.go#L919-L934
2. `PopulateLabels` sets `__scrape_timeout__` from this job-level value as a default target label:
   https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/50461b669f0be3a9f0b31a94f72cde8e98f2779f/scrape/target.go#L620-L625
3. After relabeling, the per-target interval and timeout are checked against each other, but the timeout is not re-derived from the final interval:
   https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/50461b669f0be3a9f0b31a94f72cde8e98f2779f/scrape/target.go#L666-L686

### Possible approach

Keep the per-target validation in `PopulateLabels` (step 3) as the source of truth, and resolve the default timeout per target from the final `__scrape_interval__` instead of at config load. The load-time check could remain for jobs where the interval cannot be overridden, or be turned into a warning.

Workaround: set `__scrape_timeout__` explicitly in the SD response or via `relabel_configs`.

```yaml

title: TSDB: a WAL checkpoint can drop a series record that the out-of-order WAL (WBL) still needs
body:
### What did you do?

Prometheus writes out-of-order samples to a separate write-behind log, the WBL.
Each WBL record points to a series through a series reference. 
This sequence makes the WAL lose the record that resolves one of those references:

1. Start Prometheus with an out-of-order time window above zero.
2. Write samples for a series.
3. Let head compaction write the series into a block. The head drops the series.
4. Write a new in-order sample for the same series. The head creates the series
   again under a new series reference.
5. Write an out-of-order sample for the same series. Prometheus logs it to the WBL
   under the new reference.
6. Restart Prometheus. WAL replay finds two series records with the same labels. It
   puts them onto one in-memory series and records the mapping in `multiRef`.
   Prometheus keeps that mapping only in memory.
7. Let an in-order head compaction run. It writes a WAL checkpoint.
8. Stop Prometheus before out-of-order compaction writes the WBL into a block.
9. Start Prometheus again.

### What did you expect to see?

The out-of-order sample from step `5` is still in the database after step `9`.
Prometheus acknowledged that sample to the writer.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

The sample is gone.

The checkpoint in step `7` removes the series record for the new reference. The head
no longer holds that reference, and its WAL expiry is below the `mint` of the
checkpoint. The WBL still addresses the samples through that reference, so WBL
replay cannot resolve it. Prometheus counts the reference in
`prometheus_tsdb_wbl_replay_unknown_refs_total{type="series"}` and drops the samples.

The `walExpiries` map cannot prevent this. It keeps a record until a given
timestamp. An out-of-order sample has a timestamp below the in-order data that the
checkpoint truncates, so the record looks expired while it is still needed.
The window between the checkpoint and out-of-order compaction is short, but both run
inside the same `DB.Compact` call, in that order. A restart in that window loses the
samples.

I reproduced this on `main` at commit 3da2514. 
A test for the sequence above returns two samples instead of three.

### System information

Darwin 27.0.0 arm64

### Prometheus version

```text
prometheus, version  (branch: , revision: 3da2514eff5ce503de2e8f355cae8ca58a2a35ed)
  build user:       
  build date:       
  go version:       go1.27.1
  platform:         darwin/arm64
  tags:             unknown
```

#### 5. Reject empty quoted label names in `parseLVals`

title: TSDB: WAL replay can overwrite mapped chunk state when series references are merged
body:
### What did you do?

With OOO ingestion enabled:

1. Compact a series out of the head, then recreate it with the same labels under a new reference. Keep both series definitions in the WAL.
2. Restart. WAL replay merges the references onto one live series.
3. Append enough OOO samples to write a mapped chunk under that live reference.
4. Restart again, without checkpointing or compacting the OOO data first.

This is the scenario in #19756 with the checkpoint step omitted. It reproduces on `main` at `dc54060dbe3fea84d0bfb75a40fec28e1b44632f`, without #19737.

### What did you expect to see?

All acknowledged samples remain queryable after restart.

### What did you see instead?

Only 3 of 35 samples remain queryable, across all seven tested sample types.

WAL replay recognizes that both references describe the same series, but `resetSeriesWithMMappedChunks` replaces that series' mapped chunk lists with the chunks belonging to each reference in turn. A later definition can therefore overwrite still-needed chunks loaded for an earlier reference, even with an empty list. WBL replay subsequently clears the in-memory copies at mmap markers, assuming those chunks are still attached.

The same reset also affects in-order chunks: with a healthy WAL, I reproduced duplicate chunk files that trigger out-of-sequence mmap recovery on the next restart; with WAL corruption, samples in healthy mapped chunks also became unqueryable.

### Possible direction

Preserve still-needed mapped chunk state when another reference resolves to the same live series, while retaining the intended cleanup of already-compacted history. Processing multiple definitions is supported; unconditionally replacing their shared state is the problem.

Tested locally with Go 1.26.7, darwin/arm64. Related to #19737 and #19756, but distinct from the missing-definition problem in #19744.

title: Web TLS loses HTTP/2 with Go 1.27.1: exporter-toolkit reload callback returns empty ALPN protocols
body:
### What did you do?

Compared the same HTTPS server using `github.com/prometheus/exporter-toolkit/web.Serve`, built with **Go 1.26.8** and **Go 1.27.1**, with TLS and `http_server_config.http2: true`.

The standalone reproduction below uses **unmodified upstream exporter-toolkit v0.19.0**, which is also the dependency in [Prometheus main at `605ea20826de`](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/605ea20826de3b4a9eb0dc1752246bc58c79d00f/go.mod#L71). [The Prometheus web server calls this toolkit serving path](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/605ea20826de3b4a9eb0dc1752246bc58c79d00f/web/web.go#L780-L783).

The client binary is built once with Go 1.26.8 and reused for both server builds. It verifies the generated loopback certificate, enables `ForceAttemptHTTP2`, performs a warm-up request, then sends ten concurrent requests whose handlers each wait 500 ms. Connection counts are distinct server-observed TCP peer addresses across those ten requests.

### What did you expect to see?

Both server builds negotiate `h2` and multiplex the requests over one connection when HTTP/2 is enabled.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

| Server compiler | `http2` setting | Response protocol | Negotiated ALPN | Connections used by 10 concurrent requests |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Go 1.26.8 | `true` | HTTP/2.0 | `h2` | 1 |
| Go 1.27.1 | `true` | HTTP/1.1 | empty | 10 |
| Go 1.26.8 | `false` | HTTP/1.1 | empty | 10 |
| Go 1.27.1 | `false` | HTTP/1.1 | empty | 10 |

All requests succeed in this small test. With HTTP/2 enabled, toolkit still logs `TLS is enabled.` with `http2=true`, but the Go 1.27.1 server does not negotiate HTTP/2. Certificate rotation is not required to trigger this: the callback runs on new TLS connections.

The fallback increases TCP connection demand for concurrent requests. In a busy Prometheus deployment, that can put pressure on `--web.max-connections` and delay new accepts.

### Source-level explanation

[exporter-toolkit v0.19.0, `web/tls_config.go:434–446`](https://github.com/prometheus/exporter-toolkit/blob/v0.19.0/web/tls_config.go#L434-L446) installs a callback that returns a freshly loaded TLS configuration and copies:

```go
config.NextProtos = server.TLSConfig.NextProtos
```

In [Go 1.26.8](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.26.8/src/net/http/h2_bundle.go#L4277-L4281), HTTP/2 setup populates `NextProtos` on the original `http.Server.TLSConfig`, so this copy preserves `h2`.

In [Go 1.27.1](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.27.1/src/net/http/server.go#L3584-L3629), `ServeTLS` supplies the effective protocol list to an internal cloned TLS configuration, while the original `server.TLSConfig.NextProtos` remains empty in this setup. The toolkit callback therefore copies an empty list into its replacement configuration. [`crypto/tls` uses the returned configuration for the handshake](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.27.1/src/crypto/tls/handshake_server.go#L166-L175), losing the clone's ALPN advertisements.

The new HTTP/2 initialization is visible in [`net/http/http2.go`](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.27.1/src/net/http/http2.go#L52-L84) and [`net/http/internal/http2/server.go`](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.27.1/src/net/http/internal/http2/server.go#L151-L182): it registers HTTP/2 support but no longer appends the protocol names to the original TLS configuration.

TLS-config cloning predates Go 1.27. The change is that the original configuration no longer receives the ALPN protocol list that the toolkit callback copies.

Related: [Go issue #79642](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/79642) documents the loss of the same ALPN side effect in the explicit `x/net/http2.ConfigureServer` wrapper. The reproduction here uses the standard library's `ServeTLS` initialization path.

[exporter-toolkit PR #72](https://github.com/prometheus/exporter-toolkit/pull/72) introduced this copy to address an earlier HTTP/2 negotiation problem.

title: storage/remote: ensure metadata instrumentation make sense for PRW2
body:
## Context

Part of https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/16944

The four metadata metrics in [`queue_manager.go`](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L134) were designed in #6815 for the **PRW1 `metadata_config.send` side channel**, where metadata is:

* sent in **separate requests** containing *only* `MetricMetadata` entries,
* **per metric family** (not per series),
* emitted **once per `send_interval`** (default 1m).

```
prometheus_remote_storage_metadata_total
prometheus_remote_storage_metadata_failed_total
prometheus_remote_storage_metadata_retried_total
prometheus_remote_storage_metadata_bytes_total
```

In **PRW2** metadata is a field of every `writev2.TimeSeries`, always encoded, attached per series, in the *same* request as samples. The old model does not map onto the new one, and today's code reflects that confusion.

This issue is to decide what these metrics should mean (or whether they should exist) for PRW2 **before we call PRW2 stable** — metric names and semantics are user-facing API, so changing them after GA is a breaking change.

<details>
<summary>
Problems observed in current `main`
</summary>

### 1. Three of the four metrics are permanently `0` under PRW2

| Metric | v1 | v2 | 
| --- | --- | --- | 
| `metadata_total` | ✅ [L638](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L638) | ✅ [L2303](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L2303) (`recordBatchAttempt`) | 
| `metadata_failed_total` | ✅ [L588](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L588) | ❌ never — `updateMetrics` doesn't even take `metadataCount` | 
| `metadata_retried_total` | ✅ [L632](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L632) | ❌ never — `recordRetry` omits metadata | 
| `metadata_bytes_total` | ✅ [L639](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L639) | ❌ never | 

A flat-zero counter is worse than an absent one: it reads as "metadata is perfectly healthy".

Note `metadata_failed_total` is arguably *not computable* in PRW2: the [`Written-*` response headers](https://prometheus.io/docs/specs/prw/remote_write_spec_2_0/#required-written-response-headers) only report samples, histograms and exemplars, so there is no receiver-reported metadata stat to diff against, the way [`updateMetrics`](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L1717) does for the other types.

### 2. `metadata_total` silently changes meaning by ~3 orders of magnitude

* v1 rate ≈ `metric_families / send_interval` (e.g. ~500/60s).
* v2 rate ≈ **samples rate**, because every batched series that carries metadata is counted, on every send attempt.

Same metric name, same queue, wildly different magnitude. Any dashboard/alert/report comparing `metadata_total` to `samples_total`, or trending it across a v1 → v2 migration, breaks silently.

### 3. `bytes_total` HELP text is wrong under PRW2

> "The total number of bytes of **data (not metadata)** sent by the queue after compression."

Under PRW2, help/unit strings live in the symbols table of the very same request, so metadata bytes *are* counted in `bytes_total` — while `metadata_bytes_total` stays 0.

### 4. The counting rule in `populateV2TimeSeries` is incoherent

In [`populateV2TimeSeries`](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L1975):

* `type-and-unit-labels` branch: type **and** unit are always written into the request, but `nPendingMetadata++` only happens **if help exists** → undercount.
* `default` branch: a `Metadata{Type: UNKNOWN}` message *is* still encoded and sent → counted as nothing.
* So the counter is neither "series carrying metadata" nor "series with complete metadata".

Also, `nUnexpectedMetadata` (a `tMetadata` record reaching the v2 path, which should be imposs

title: Proposal: Metadata manipulation — let users fix a metric's type, unit and help
body:
### TL;DR Prometheus lets operators rewrite **labels** freely (`metric_relabel_configs`, `write_relabel_configs`), but gives them **no supported way to rewrite metadata** — `TYPE`, `UNIT`, `HELP`. Metadata is whatever the target or sender said it was, forever. That was tolerable while metadata was decorative. We are slowly in the world where it no longer is: with [PROM-39](https://github.com/prometheus/proposals/blob/main/proposals/2024-09-25_metadata-labels.md) / `--enable-feature=type-and-unit-labels`, type and unit are part of series identity, selectable in PromQL, [drive `rate()` counter-ness annotations](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/10f69629039e0215d056eb4948f0bd0fd22f5c89/promql/engine.go#L2445-L2462), and are necessary for downstream systems e.g. OpenTelemetry and Google. **Wrong metadata could be now assumed as actively harmful, and users cannot fix it in Prometheus.** This issue is primarily a **collection of use cases** to see if we have some consensus to add such mechanism to Prometheus (or other use cases I am missing). Proper proposal should be done, but I wanted to gather feedback first. ## Use cases ### 1. Specifying a missing or wrong type, unit or help ##### Example: The exporter miss `# TYPE` (or says `untyped`) A large share of exposition in the wild is untyped: textfile collector output, `statsd_exporter`, JMX exporter, home-grown `/metrics` handlers, legacy vendor agents. ``` # HELP myapp_requests_total Total requests. myapp_requests_total{route="/api"} 4213 ``` The operator knows well this is a counter. They cannot patch the exporter (third party, vendored, or 200 teams own it). With type-aware PromQL UX they now get warned — or silently degraded — forever on metrics they don't own. > **Wants:** "for this job, anything matching `myapp_.*_total` is a counter." ##### Example: No `# UNIT` (impossible in Prometheus text format anyway) The name encodes milliseconds. The operator wants `__unit__="milliseconds"` so unit-aware UI formatting and future unit-aware functions work. The inverse also happens: an exporter declares a misleading unit that the operator wants to strip. ``` # TYPE http_request_latency_ms gauge http_request_latency_ms 12.5 ``` > **Wants:** derive `__unit__` from a name suffix, or set/clear it outright. ##### Example: RW/OTLP parity metadata fixed on RW or OTLP receive OTel users have the Collector `transform` processor: ```yaml transform: metric_statements: - set(metric.unit, "s") where metric.name == "foo" - set(metric.description, "") ``` Pushing OTLP **directly** to Prometheus loses this entirely: `OTLPConfig` exposes nine fixed knobs and no transform hook. Users end up deploying a whole Collector purely to fix a unit string. > **Wants:** the same metadata fixes available on the OTLP and RW receive path. ### 2. Do certain relabelling based on type, unit ##### Example: Rename all __type__==counter without _total suffix to have _total suffix. > **Wants:** perform relabel action based on metadata Today this **silently drops the metadata** — the family match is done against the post-relabel name. If we let users rename, we should let them restate the metadata that goes with the new name. > **Wants:** rename and metadata stay consistent, or can be re-declared in the same block. ### 3. Dropping huge `HELP` strings Real-world exporters ship multi-kilobyte `HELP` text: whole paragraphs, embedded JSON, even stack traces. That costs head memory, WAL bytes, and Remote Write 2.0 bandwidth — repeated per series. There is no knob for this today short of all-or-nothing `metadata_config.send: false` (RW1 only), which also throws away type and unit. > **Wants:** "drop HELP for this job" / "truncate HELP to N bytes" / "drop HELP only for these metrics."

Current state — two unsynchronized metadata channels (click to expand)

 There are **two parallel metadata channels**, and one of them is *already user-mutable,

title: kubernetes_sd role: endpointslice: pod metadata (__meta_kubernetes_pod_phase) not refreshed on pod updates
body:
### What did you do?

We scrape Services through kubernetes_sd_configs with role: endpointslice and, as usual, drop targets whose pod is not running:

```
relabel_configs:
  - action: drop
    source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_phase]
    regex: (Failed|Pending|Succeeded)
```

Some Services select the pods of a CronJob. When a Job pod completes, the pod goes to phase Succeeded but stays in the Service's EndpointSlice, with all conditions set to false:

```
endpoints:
- addresses:
  - 10.233.133.240
  conditions:
    ready: false
    serving: false
    terminating: false
  targetRef:
    kind: Pod
    name: my-cronjob-29838420-8jj49
```



### What did you expect to see?

The target should be dropped once the pod is Succeeded, because __meta_kubernetes_pod_phase reflects the current pod phase.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

The target stays active, and is reported down (dial tcp 10.233.133.240:8081: connect: no route to host), for hours. It stays that way until the EndpointSlice changes again, usually on the next CronJob run. /api/v1/targets shows stale pod metadata:

```
"__meta_kubernetes_endpointslice_endpoint_conditions_ready": "false",
"__meta_kubernetes_endpointslice_endpoint_conditions_serving"
"__meta_kubernetes_pod_phase": "Running",
"__meta_kubernetes_pod_ready": "false"
```

kubectl get pod reports status.phase: Succeeded for that same pod at the same moment. As a result, the phase-based drop never fires and alerts such as
`up == 0` keep firing on pods that no longer exist.

Likely cause: in discovery/kubernetes/endpointslice.go, NewEndpointSlice registers event handlers on the EndpointSlice, Service, and (optionally) Node and Namespace informers, but none on the Pod informer. Pod metadata is only resolved (resolvePodRef → podStore) when an EndpointSlice or Service event is processed. The EndpointSlice update (endpoint turning not-ready) is typically processed while the pod store still holds the pod as Running. The later pod update to Succeeded does not re-enqueue the slice, so the target stays frozen with stale labels.

The same problem was reported and fixed for role: endpoints in #11305 / #13337. endpoints.go now re-enqueues endpoints on pod phase changes:

```
// the Pod's phase may change without triggering an update on
// https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/11305.
if curPod.Status.Phase != oldPod.Status.Phase {
    e.enqueuePod(namespacedName(curPod.Namespace, curPod.Name
}
```

That fix was never ported to endpointslice.go. This is still the case on main / v3.15.0. It is a problem because endpointslice is now the recommended role, since the Endpoints API is deprecated in Kubernetes.

Suggested fix: port the pod UpdateFunc handler from endpoints.go to endpointslice.go: on a pod phase change, re-enqueue the EndpointSlices referencing
that pod, for example through an index on targetRef.

Current workaround: we drop not-ready endpoints of Job-owned pods, using only labels that cannot be stale. controller_kind never changes for a pod, and endpoint conditions come from the slice itself:

```
- action: drop
  source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_controller_kind, __meta_kubernetes_endpointslice_endpoint_conditions_ready]
  regex: Job;false
```

Steps to reproduce

```
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: repro
spec:
  schedule: "*/10 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        metadata:
          labels: {app: repro}
        spec:
          restartPolicy: Never
          containers:
          - name: repro
            image: busybox
            command: ["sh", "-c", "httpd -f -p 8081 & sleep 120"]
            ports: [{containerPort: 8081, name: metrics}]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: repro
spec:
  selector: {app: repro}
  ports: [{name: metrics, port: 8081}]
```

Scrape it with role: endpointslice and the phase drop above. Once the Job pod completes, the target remains in /api/v1/targets with __meta_kubernetes_pod_phase="Run

title: tsdb: head querier no longer safe for concurrent use since v3.12.0 (wrong samples, not-found errors, panics)
body:
### What did you do? I used one `storage.Querier` (or `storage.ChunkQuerier`) over the TSDB head from several goroutines at once, in two ways: - concurrent `Select` calls; - concurrent iteration of the series returned by one range-query `Select` (`hints.Step > 0`). thanos-io/promql-engine works this way by design: it has shared one querier across goroutines since 2022. That's how I found this. Its tests fail under `go test -race` when built against Prometheus v3.15.0, and per the analysis below, any release from v3.12.0 on would fail them too. It reproduces in plain Prometheus. The regression test in #19841 does exactly this: - a head with several in-memory head chunks per series, with and without out-of-order data; - one querier from `db.Querier` or `db.ChunkQuerier`; - `Select` plus full iteration from several goroutines, each compared with a sequential baseline. To reproduce, apply `TestHeadQuerierConcurrentUse` from #19841 to `main` and run `go test -race -run TestHeadQuerierConcurrentUse ./tsdb/`. It fails on every run, with and without `-race`. ### What did you expect to see? The same samples as the sequential baseline, and no data races, as on v3.11.x and earlier. Until v3.12.0 the head index and chunk readers only had constant fields. The #18302 review noted that `headIndexReader` "only had constant fields so far, making it de-facto thread safe". #18302 then documented the readers as not safe for concurrent use, on the assumption that nobody used them that way. The public `storage.Querier` API does not forbid concurrent use, and the persisted-block readers still keep no per-call state. ### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances? - **With `go test -race`:** data races in `headIndexReader.Series` (`head_read.go:210` at 270db2915), `appendSeriesChunks`, `collectHeadChunks`, `headChunkReader.getOrCollectHeadChunks`, `memSeries.chunk` and `EnableChunkCache`. - **Without `-race`:** - samples of other series (see Logs); - `cannot populate chunk …: not found` errors; - nil-pointer panics in `appendSeriesChunks`. In an ad-hoc stress test on `main` (100 series with 4–12 head chunks each, 8 goroutines; not part of the PR), 1053 of 1600 concurrent instant `Select`s over the head failed: 143 returned wrong samples, 510 returned errors and 400 panicked. - **Affected versions:** v3.12.0 through v3.15.0 and `main`, including the 3.13 LTS (v3.13.3). v3.11.3 is not affected. - **Not affected:** - persisted blocks; - the Prometheus server itself, because its engine uses each querier from a single goroutine. No test used one querier from several goroutines either, which is why CI didn't catch this. Library users that share a head querier across goroutines are affected. **Root cause.** #18302 (v3.12.0) added mutable state to the head readers: - **A scratch buffer on `headIndexReader`** that `Series` collects head chunks into. It races for every concurrent `Select` of series with two or more head chunks, instant queries included. - **A single-entry head-chunk cache** for range queries. In v3.12 and v3.13 only `HeadAndOOOChunkReader` implemented `EnableChunkCache`, so the cache was only used for queries overlapping out-of-order data. #19136 (v3.14.0) added it to `headChunkReader`, so all head range queries now use it. A querier has one index reader and one chunk reader, and all of its series sets and iterators share them. So concurrent use races on that state. A fix is in #19841. ### System information Darwin 25.5.0 arm64 ### Prometheus version ```text v3.12.0 – v3.15.0, and main at 270db2915 ``` ### Prometheus configuration file ```yaml _No response_ (library use; no configuration involved) ``` ### Alertmanager version _No response_ ### Alertmanager configuration file _No response_ ### Logs
First race report with go test -race on unfixed main, an error and a wrong sample without -race ```text WARNING: DATA RACE Read at 0

title: Future-dated exemplars can collapse remote write shards and advance WAL truncation
body:
### What did you do?

- Scraped a target on a node whose clock temporarily moved into the future for about 10 minutes.
- Used Alloy `v1.19.0-rc.3`, with Prometheus `v0.313.2`.


### What did you expect to see?

- Scraping and remote write should continue normally after the source clock recovers; future timestamps should be handled without disabling the instance or losing unrelated data.


### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

- Remote write shards dropped from ~40 to 1; throughput fell ~97%, and we started losing data.
- `prometheus_remote_storage_shards_desired` became ~−10 million (negative); `prometheus_remote_storage_shards` fell to 1.
- `prometheus_remote_storage_queue_highest_timestamp_seconds` and `prometheus_remote_storage_queue_highest_sent_timestamp_seconds` jumped ~79 days ahead, while `prometheus_remote_storage_highest_timestamp_in_seconds` stayed normal.
- The queue did not recover when the source clock returned to normal.

**Possible causes**

- An exemplar with explicit timestamp in the future advances outgoing timestamp tracking, but the [received tracker](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/v0.313.2/storage/remote/write.go#L322-L380) ignores exemplar timestamps.
- [Shard sizing](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/v0.313.2/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L1156-L1227) uses `highestRecv - highestSent` to estimate backlog. The negative difference could drive desired shards below zero, then the minimum-shard clamp reduces sending capacity to one shard. That would explain the negative `prometheus_remote_storage_shards_desired` and the shard collapse.
- [Agent WAL truncation](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/v0.313.2/tsdb/agent/db.go#L689-L722) uses `LowestSentTimestamp() - MinWALTime` without an upper bound against wall-clock time. A future cutoff can discard normal samples and segments still needed by readers. We saw logs with `mint` almost 79 days in the future, which would be expected in this scenario.

**Possible fixes**

- Include exemplar timestamps in received tracking for both Appender APIs. [AppendExemplar](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/v0.313.2/storage/remote/write.go#L331) would need to update the `highestTimestamp`. Not clear if this was a deliberate omission or an oversight?
- Clamp negative backlog estimates to zero before calculating shards. This would be more local solution to the shards calculation issue.
- Bound the WAL cutoff against wall-clock time to not allow it to move to the future.
- Account for reader progress before deleting segments in WAL?
- Protect against future timestamps at the point of receiving them more reliably? clamp them to the current time?


### System information

_No response_

### Prometheus version

- Prometheus Go module `v0.313.2`.
- Originally observed in Alloy `v1.19.0-rc.3`.

### Prometheus configuration file

Alloy was configured with:

- RWv2, `send_exemplars = true`.
- Queue: `capacity = 7500`, `max_samples_per_send = 5000`, `retry_on_http_429 = true`.
- Shards: `min_shards = 1` (default), `max_shards = 100`.
- Other queue defaults: `batch_send_deadline = "5s"`, `min_backoff = "30ms"`, `max_backoff = "5s"`, `sample_age_limit = "0s"`.
- WAL: `truncate_frequency = "15m"`

### Logs

- `mint=1797523130000` is **2026-12-17 15:58:50 UTC**, about 79 days after the log timestamp.
  - `ts=2026-09-29T10:47:52.956144234Z level=info msg="Creating checkpoint" component_path=/ component_id=[redacted] subcomponent=wal from_segment=408 to_segment=418 mint=1797523130000`
- `mint=1797523126000` is **2026-12-17 15:58:46 UTC**, about 79 days after the log timestamp.
  - `ts=2026-09-29T10:52:34.013945354Z level=info msg="Creating checkpoint" component_path=/ component_id=[redacted] subcomponent=wal from_segment=469 to_segment=479 mint=1797523126000`
- The same reader later failed to open segment **473**, within the checkpoint range **469–479** above.
  - `ts=2026-09-29T11:01:33.473856588Z level=error msg="error tail

title: textparse: OpenMetrics 2.0 puts classic histogram exemplars on `_count`, protobuf and OpenMetrics 1.0 put them on the matching `_bucket`
body:
When the OpenMetrics 2.0 parser expands a classic histogram composite value into flat series, every exemplar on the line is returned with the first series, `_count` (or `_gcount`). `TestOpenMetrics2ParseExemplarOnCompositeLine` pins this.

The same histogram scraped as protobuf, or as OpenMetrics 1.0 (one exemplar per bucket line), stores each exemplar on the `_bucket` series whose bucket it falls in. The OpenMetrics 2.0 spec describes exemplars the same way ("An exemplar without Labels falls within the "0.1" bucket...", and recommends one exemplar per classic bucket).

So switching a target from OpenMetrics 1.0 or protobuf to OpenMetrics 2.0 moves its exemplars from `foo_bucket{le=...}` to `foo_count`. Exemplar queries that select the bucket series, such as those behind `histogram_quantile` panels, stop finding them.

Would you accept attaching each exemplar to the `_bucket` series with the smallest `le` >= the exemplar value (falling back to `+Inf`), as the other formats do? Happy to send the PR.

Related to #19745.

title: mixin: remote-write failure alert mixes outcomes with send attempts
body:
### What did you do?

I rendered the complete `PrometheusRemoteStorageFailures` rule from [the current mixin](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/c45b13bbdd96b47a5441000fb454dce42894349d/documentation/prometheus-mixin/alerts.libsonnet#L186-L207) at `c45b13bbdd96b47a5441000fb454dce42894349d` and ran synthetic 1m counter traces through `promtool 3.15.0 test rules` (fixtures below). The source [increments `samples_total` on each Store attempt](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/c45b13bbdd96b47a5441000fb454dce42894349d/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L1797-L1843); [the queue test confirms this](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/c45b13bbdd96b47a5441000fb454dce42894349d/storage/remote/queue_manager_test.go#L191-L193).

### What did you expect to see?

When all 100 sent samples fail terminally, report 100% failed, not 50%. For a steady completed-retry trace with 400 attempts, 300 retries and 2 terminal failures per minute (100 distinct first sends), the 2% terminal-failure fraction should remain above the 1% threshold for 15m.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

`promtool test rules observed.test.yml` passes: the annotation says 50.0% in the all-failed case, while the retry trace emits no alert at 30m. `promtool test rules intent.test.yml` fails exactly those two expectations (100.0% versus 50.0%; expected alert versus none). This arises with the legacy `samples_total` fallback: the rule divides `failed` by `failed + samples_total`, counting terminal failures twice and treating retry attempts as more samples. It still needs to support both legacy metric aliases.

A simple `samples_total - samples_retried_total` denominator is not a proven fix: canceled backoff can count a retry with no subsequent attempt; hard shutdown can count failures with no send; accepted subsets may have incomplete/overlapping v1 response stats; and attempts/retries can land on opposite sides of a 5m rate window. `promtool test rules edge.test.yml` passes expression controls for cancellation/window arithmetic. Could we agree on the intended alert population (attempts, terminal outcomes, or distinct samples) before changing the rule or instrumentation? I found this while studying alert rules across projects; results are published only in aggregate.

### Environment

Synthetic promtool fixture only; macOS darwin/arm64, `promtool 3.15.0`. No live remote-write incident or deployment asserted. Prometheus source pin: `c45b13bbdd96b47a5441000fb454dce42894349d`.


AI tools assisted with the analysis and synthetic tests.

Save each block under the indicated filename and run `promtool test rules observed.test.yml intent.test.yml edge.test.yml`. The two intent failures are expected on the current rule.

<details>
<summary>rule.yml</summary>

```yaml
# Rendered from documentation/prometheus-mixin/config.libsonnet + alerts.libsonnet
# at c45b13bbdd96b47a5441000fb454dce42894349d; only this alert retained.
"groups":
- "name": "prometheus"
  "rules":
  - "alert": "PrometheusRemoteStorageFailures"
    "annotations":
      "description": "Prometheus {{$labels.instance}} failed to send {{ printf \"%.1f\" $value }}% of the samples to {{ $labels.remote_name}}:{{ $labels.url }}"
      "summary": "Prometheus fails to send samples to remote storage."
    "expr": |
      (
        (rate(prometheus_remote_storage_failed_samples_total{job="prometheus"}[5m]) or rate(prometheus_remote_storage_samples_failed_total{job="prometheus"}[5m]))
      /
        (
          (rate(prometheus_remote_storage_failed_samples_total{job="prometheus"}[5m]) or rate(prometheus_remote_storage_samples_failed_total{job="prometheus"}[5m]))
        +
          (rate(prometheus_remote_storage_succeeded_samples_total{job="prometheus"}[5m]) or rate(prometheus_remote_storage_samples_total{job="prometheus"}[5m]))
        )
      )
      * 100
      > 1
    "for": "15m"
    "labels":
      "severity": "critical"

```

title: template: stripDomain truncates IPv6 zone identifiers containing dots
body:
### What did you do?

At main `5ba0e8648a4314e7d12adc6dbeb34b9d76cafab2`, I expanded `{{ . | stripDomain }}` through the public `template.NewTemplateExpander` text and HTML entry points, using IPv6 addresses with interface zones containing dots.

| Input | Actual output |
|---|---|
| `fe80::1%eth0.100` | `fe80::1%eth0` |
| `[fe80::1%eth0.100]:9090` | `[fe80::1%eth0]:9090` |
| `::ffff:192.0.2.1%eth0.100` | `::ffff:192` |

### What did you expect to see?

Each IP address should be returned unchanged, including its zone and port, consistently with the IP-preservation branch introduced in #10475.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

`net.ParseIP` rejects addresses containing zones. The function then treats the address as a hostname and truncates it at the first dot. A dotted interface name loses its suffix; a scoped IPv4-mapped IPv6 address can also lose part of the address.

I have a scoped local draft using `netip.ParseAddr` for the IP check while leaving hostname splitting, port handling, and `stripPort` unchanged. The original production source fails six of 22 public text/HTML regression cases; the draft passes the full template package with race detection, targeted vet, formatting, and the configured package-level golangci-lint. Existing hostname and ordinary IP controls remain passing.

I would like to work on this fix if the scope is acceptable. Is preserving zoned IPv6 inputs the intended behavior? #18787 concerns scrape URL escaping rather than this template function.

- Source revision: `5ba0e8648a4314e7d12adc6dbeb34b9d76cafab2`, Go 1.26.7.

title: promql: BucketFraction panics for nil or empty buckets
body:
### What did you do?

Called `promql.BucketFraction(0, 1, nil)`. A non-nil empty `promql.Buckets{}` produces the same panic. This follows the [maintainer request on merged #19927](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/19927#issuecomment-6015925239) to cover BucketFraction as well.

Place this test in `promql/bucket_fraction_empty_test.go`:

```go
package promql_test

import (
    "testing"

    "github.com/prometheus/prometheus/promql"
)

func TestBucketFractionEmpty(t *testing.T) {
    promql.BucketFraction(0, 1, nil) // promql.Buckets{} also panics.
}
```

Run `GOMAXPROCS=2 go test -p 1 -count=1 ./promql -run '^TestBucketFractionEmpty$' -v`.

### What did you expect to see?

Return `NaN` for an empty histogram, consistent with the native counterpart's [zero-observation behavior](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/39c878f024238783f54631e3a5998e835d04db86/promql/quantile.go#L384) and BucketFraction's existing result for a `+Inf` bucket with count zero.

This is the proposed empty-input behavior: BucketFraction's current one-line comment does not explicitly define it or require a nonempty slice.

### What did you see instead?

`panic: runtime error: index out of range [-1]`

The [last-bucket access](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/39c878f024238783f54631e3a5998e835d04db86/promql/quantile.go#L544) indexes `buckets[len(buckets)-1]` before checking the length. A broader deterministic probe reproduces the panic for nil/non-nil empty slices and finite, infinite, NaN or reversed bounds. Neighboring nonempty and native zero-count controls pass.

The [current PromQL caller](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/39c878f024238783f54631e3a5998e835d04db86/promql/functions.go#L2306) skips empty lists before calling this helper. The demonstrated scope is the helper; no query or server crash has been reproduced.

#19927 repaired the adjacent BucketQuantile helper. The first-bucket/interpolation reports #17367, #18474 and #19657 concern different inputs and mechanisms.

### Environment

Linux 6.12.63 x86_64; Go 1.26.7 (`linux/amd64`). Source reproduction against `promql/quantile.go` byte-identical to upstream main `39c878f024238783f54631e3a5998e835d04db86`, checked 2026-10-06. No server configuration is required.

Reproduction and source analysis prepared with AI assistance by OpenAI Codex.
