title: template: humanize prints 1000k instead of 1M for values that round up to the next prefix
body:
### What did you do?

Used `humanize` and `humanize1024` in alert templates on values that sit just below a unit boundary. For example, an alert description like this:

```yaml
annotations:
  description: "Memory used: {{ $value | humanize1024 }}B, requests: {{ $value | humanize }}"
```

Some inputs and what the functions return on current main:

| Template | Input | Output | Expected |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `humanize` | 999.95 | `1000` | `1k` |
| `humanize` | 999999 | `1000k` | `1M` |
| `humanize` | -999999 | `-1000k` | `-1M` |
| `humanize` | 0.99996 | `1000m` | `1` |
| `humanize` | 0.0009999996 | `1000u` | `1m` |
| `humanize1024` | 1023.99 | `1024` | `1ki` |
| `humanize1024` | 1048575 | `1024ki` | `1Mi` |

### What did you expect to see?

The same output as for a value one unit higher: `1k`, `1M`, `1`, `1m`, `1ki`, `1Mi`. A prefix should never be shown with a number of 1000 or more (1024 or more for `humanize1024`), because that number is exactly what the next prefix is for.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

`humanize` picks the unit prefix by comparing the raw value against 1000 and then prints it with `%.4g`, which rounds to 4 significant digits. When the value is below 1000 but rounds up to 1000, the prefix has already been chosen, so the rounded number is printed with the smaller prefix: 999999 becomes 999.999 with `k`, and `%.4g` prints that as `1000k`.

The same happens in the branch for values below 1 (0.99996 scales to 999.96 with `m` and prints as `1000m`) and in `humanize1024` with 1024 as the step.

This shows up in alert notifications for values like 1048575 bytes or 999.97 requests, which are common near round limits.

### System information

Linux and macOS (the code is platform independent)

### Prometheus version

```text
v3.15.0, and current main at 2213c3c19
```

### Prometheus configuration file

```yaml
Not relevant. Any alerting rule whose annotations use humanize or humanize1024 reproduces it.
```

### Alertmanager version

```text
Not relevant
```

### Alertmanager configuration file

```yaml
Not relevant
```

### Logs

```text
None. The functions return a wrong string, not an error.
```

I have a fix with tests ready and will open a PR for it: choose the prefix from the value as it will be printed (rounded to 4 significant digits), and in the below-1 branch step back up one prefix when rounding reaches 1000.

title: tsdb: duplicate pending metadata amplifies WAL writes when metadata-wal-records is enabled
body:
### What did you do?

Enabled `--enable-feature=metadata-wal-records` and used AppenderV1 to append many samples of one series in a single transaction, each with the same metadata and a large help text.

At the reported revision, `headAppender.UpdateMetadata` compares incoming metadata only with the series' committed metadata, using Go struct equality. When it differs, repeated calls can queue identical metadata for the same series before commit.

AppenderV2 receives metadata through `Append(..., AOptions{Metadata: ...})`. With metadata WAL recording enabled, it processes non-empty metadata after successful, non-stale sample appends and compares it with committed metadata using semantic equality. Despite these differences, it also lacks a check for identical pending entries.

At commit, the WAL encoder encodes the metadata entries in each append batch, including each entry's type, unit and full help text.

Ingestion-path context at the reported revision (`main` at fd4847802):

- **Remote Write 2.0:** The receiver uses AppenderV1 and calls `UpdateMetadata` once per series entry. Repeated entries for the same series can reference one shared help symbol while queuing multiple copies for WAL encoding.
- **Scrapes:** The V1 scrape path updates metadata for new series or changed family metadata; the V2 path passes available family metadata with eligible samples when metadata WAL recording is enabled. Separate metadata records for distinct series are expected and remain outside same-series deduplication.

AppenderV1 reproduction on `main` at fd4847802: one series, 64 float samples, each with `UpdateMetadata` and the same 1 MiB help string, followed by one `Commit`. This is a throwaway test in package `tsdb`:

```go
func TestReproMetadataWALAmplification(t *testing.T) {
	const n, helpSize = 64, 1 << 20
	opts := DefaultOptions()
	opts.EnableMetadataWALRecords = true
	dir := t.TempDir()
	db, err := Open(dir, nil, nil, opts, nil)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	t.Cleanup(func() { require.NoError(t, db.Close()) })

	help := strings.Repeat("h", helpSize)
	lset := labels.FromStrings("__name__", "m")
	app := db.Appender(t.Context())
	for i := range n {
		ref, err := app.Append(0, lset, int64(i), 1)
		require.NoError(t, err)
		_, err = app.UpdateMetadata(ref, lset, metadata.Metadata{Type: "gauge", Help: help})
		require.NoError(t, err)
	}
	require.NoError(t, app.Commit()) // Measure WAL growth and allocations around this.
}
```

### What did you expect to see?

Avoid redundant identical pending metadata for the same series within an append batch, while preserving changes such as A -> B -> A, including a return to the committed value. Later sample-type batches may still need their own metadata entries.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

The original AppenderV1 reproduction reported WAL growth of 67,124,988 bytes and about 356 MB allocated during `Commit`: 64 copies of one shared 1 MiB help string. Those allocation measurements apply to V1.

The independent [AppenderV2 regression](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/87e0d45ead06944118d6e59778b3bf0c126623b1/tsdb/metadata_test.go#L67) in #20001 also records 64 metadata entries before the fix and one afterward for 64 float samples sharing a 1 MiB help string within one append batch.

Possible fix:

- Check the series' latest pending metadata before appending another identical entry in the same batch, preserving metadata transitions and entries in later sample-type batches.

Metadata string-size limits would provide additional protection against oversized metadata. They remain separate follow-up work.

### Prometheus version

```text
main at fd4847802
```

title: rules: store and deduce metric metadata (type, help, unit) for recording rules
body:
Related to [prometheus#11969](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/11969), [prometheus#17864](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/17864), [prometheus#19555](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/19555), and [prometheus#19563](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/19563).

### Motivation

Recording rules currently write samples to storage without metric metadata (`type`, `help`, `unit`). Because of this, recorded series are missing from `/api/v1/metadata`, carry empty metadata in WAL records and Remote Write 2.0, and lack `__type__` / `__unit__` when `type-and-unit-labels` is enabled.

Storing metadata for recording rules solves several problems:

- Humans and AI agents rely on `/api/v1/metadata` (and UIs like Grafana's metrics explorer) to discover metrics, understand what a pre-computed rule represents, and autocomplete PromQL queries.
- Strongly typed backends receiving data via Remote Write 2.0 or OTLP (such as Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus) require a valid metric type for every series and have to fall back or reject untyped recorded metrics.
- Type-aware query engines, linters, and type-based aggregations need to know whether a recorded series is a float gauge, a counter, or a native histogram.

### Sketch of solution

Working on a formal proposal, but the rough idea is as follow:

Rule manager migrated to `AppenderV2` already. Through [`headAppenderV2.Append`](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/6e69e843b38d22ded60a13e0163f6326136f59fa/tsdb/head_append_v2.go#L226), this populates WAL metadata records, Remote Write 2.0 metadata, `type-and-unit-labels`, and the native TSDB metadata store ([prometheus#19563](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/19563)).

#### Expand manual config in `rulefmt`

Extend recording rule definitions in [`model/rulefmt`](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/10f69629039e0215d056eb4948f0bd0fd22f5c89/model/rulefmt/rulefmt.go#L186-L196) so users can optionally specify `help`, `type`, and `unit` (as explored in [prometheus#17864](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/17864) and [prometheus#19555](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/19555)):

```yaml
groups:
  - name: example
    rules:
      - record: job:http_requests:rate5m
        expr: sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
        help: "Per-job HTTP request rate over 5 minutes."
        type: gauge
        unit: requests_per_second
```

Any explicitly configured field overrides the automatically deduced value (see below), and `promtool check rules` validates that `type` is a known OpenMetrics / Prometheus metric type.

#### Automatic metadata deduction (feature flag / config option)

Add a feature flag and configuration setting to automatically populate type for recording rules without requiring users to annotate every existing rule file.

- For float samples (`s.H == nil`), defaulting to `gauge` could be a sufficient heuristic. Almost all float recording rules (`rate()`, `increase()`, `histogram_quantile()`, `avg()`, arithmetic) produce values that can go up and down. Even aggregating counters without `rate()`, like `sum by (job) (http_requests_total)`, is not a monotonic counter in practice because series churn when targets restart or disappear causes the sum to decrease without a counter reset.
- For native histogram samples (`s.H != nil`), `gaugehistogram` is likely a sufficient choice. We can inspect `s.H.CounterResetHint` ([`model/histogram/histogram.go#L26-L33`](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/10f69629039e0215d056eb4948f0bd0fd22f5c89/model/histogram/histogram.go#L26-L33)) on the evaluated sample: PromQL functions like `rate()`, `irate()`, `increase()`, `delta()`, and histogram subtraction already set `CounterResetHint = histogram.GaugeType` ([`promql/functions.go#L441`](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/10f69629039e0215d056eb4948f0bd0fd22f5c89/promql/functions.go#L441)). If `CounterResetHint == histogram.GaugeType

title: Runtime retention reload does not update TSDB compaction ranges
body:
### What did you do?

1. Start Prometheus with following `storage` YAML:
```yaml
storage:
  tsdb:
    retention:
      time: 2y
```
2. Do not configure `--storage.tsdb.retention.time` or `--storage.tsdb.max-block-duration` command-line arguments.
3. Without restarting the Prometheus process, change `retention.time` to `190d` and reload the configuration.



### What did you expect to see?

The reload should update all behavior related to the retention period. With `190d` retention, the default maximum block duration is 10%, or `19d` (`456h`). The `486h` compaction tier should therefore be excluded and the largest eligible tier should be `162h`.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

After the successful reload:

- `prometheus_tsdb_retention_limit_seconds / 86400` correctly returns `190`
- Status > Command-line flags still shows `--storage.tsdb.retention.time = 2y`, even though that flag was never explicitly supplied.

Compaction continues using the ranges calculated from the retention configured at start up.  It compacted three `162h` source blocks into a `486h` (`20d6h`) block after the successful reload:

```text

```

```console
$ promtool check rules --enable-feature=promql-experimental-functions rules.yml
Checking rules.yml
  SUCCESS: 1 rules found

$ promtool test rules --enable-feature=promql-experimental-functions unit.yml
$ promtool --enable-feature=promql-experimental-functions test rules unit.yml
```

### What did you expect to see?

The unit test to run and pass. A rule file that `check rules` accepts with a feature flag should be testable by `test rules` with the same flag.


### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

Both flag positions fail identically:

```
  FAILED:
    rule: s, time: 0s, err: 1:1: parse error: function "mad_over_time" is not enabled
```

The flag is honoured for loading and ignored for evaluation.

`cmd/promtool/main.go` turns the flag into `parser.Options{EnableExperimentalFunctions: true}` and builds a parser from it. That parser is stored on the test group (`cmd/promtool/unittest.go:224`) and passed to `rules.ManagerOptions.Parser` (`unittest.go:258`), so `LoadGroups` parses the expression fine.

Evaluation uses a different engine. `testGroup.test()` builds `promqltest.NewLazyLoader(...)`, and `LazyLoader.clear()` (`promql/promqltest/test.go:1981`) constructs `promql.EngineOpts` without a `Parser`. `LazyLoaderOpts` (`test.go:1927`) has no field to pass one. `promql.NewEngine` then defaults it:

```go
if opts.Parser == nil {
    opts.Parser = parser.NewParser(parser.Options{})
}
```

`parser.Options{}` has `EnableExperimentalFunctions` false, so the recording rule's expression is re-parsed at evaluation time by a parser that rejects it. `time: 0s` and a rule name rather than a file is the tell.

The sibling constructor in the same package does pass one (`NewTestEngine` uses `TestParserOpts`), which is why Prometheus' own PromQL tests can use these functions.

This looks like the unfinished half of #16412 ("Allow PromTool to check rules with experimental promql functions"), closed by #16443. That PR wired the `check` path; the `test` path was missed. From that issue: "The intention is exactly as you suggest, that promtool takes feature flags which make sense for rules and tests, but unfortunately the code didn't match that intention."

Impact: rules using `mad_over_time`, `double_exponential_smoothing`, `info`, `ts_of_*` or `sort_by_label` can be validated but not unit tested, so the official test harness is unavailable for exactly the rules whose value is their arithmetic.


### System information

Darwin 25.5.0 arm64

promtool, version 3.15.0

Also reproduced with a build of `main` at c052a79dc7fd0f2df2219ffe336f510b0d149b72.
```

title: file_sd: invalid SD file is re-read in a tight loop when logs are written to the same directory
body:
I found this while looking into grafana/alloy#7298, where `discovery.file` re-reads an invalid file in a tight loop. Alloy uses the Prometheus file SD code for that component, so I tried the same thing on Prometheus itself and got the same loop.

### What did you do?

Ran Prometheus with a `file_sd_configs` file and wrote its logs to a file in the same directory, then made the SD file invalid JSON.

```sh
docker run -d --name prom -u root \
  -v "$PWD/prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml:ro" \
  --entrypoint sh prom/prometheus:latest -c '
    mkdir -p /sd && echo "[{\"targets\":[\"127.0.0.1:9090\"]}]" > /sd/targets.json
    exec /bin/prometheus --config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml --storage.tsdb.path=/tmp/data >> /sd/prometheus.log 2>&1'

sleep 5
docker exec prom sh -c 'echo "[{\"targets\":[\"127.0.0.1:9090\"]" > /sd/targets.json'
sleep 15
docker exec prom grep -c "Error reading file" /sd/prometheus.log
```

### What did you expect to see?

One `Error reading file` line, then nothing until the file changes again or the refresh interval runs.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

641,837 `Error reading file` lines in 15 seconds, and Prometheus used about one full CPU core (114%) until the file was fixed.

File SD watches the directory of each configured file, and every event in that directory triggers a refresh ([file.go#L258-L273](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/c052a79dc7fd0f2df2219ffe336f510b0d149b72/discovery/file/file.go#L258-L273)). The refresh logs an error for the invalid file, writing that log line is a new event in the same directory, and that event triggers the next refresh.

Any other file that is written often in that directory also causes a re-read on every write, even when the SD file is valid.

I could reproduce the loop in Alloy the same way, by writing its logs next to the SD file. I haven't confirmed yet that this is also the setup of the reporter of grafana/alloy#7298.

Related: #13929 explains why the directory is watched instead of the file.

### System information

Linux 6.12.5-linuxkit aarch64 (Docker Desktop)

### Prometheus version

```text
prometheus, version 3.15.0 (branch: HEAD, revision: 5241a27fe3c6983549fccc32f6e65917408c63cd)
  build date:       20260925-07:36:49
  go version:       go1.27.1
```

### Prometheus configuration file

```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: t
    file_sd_configs:
      - files: [/sd/targets.json]
```

### Logs

```text
time=2026-10-17T09:00:03.072Z level=ERROR source=file.go:341 msg="Error reading file" component="discovery manager scrape" discovery=file config=t path=/sd/targets.json err="unexpected end of JSON input"
time=2026-10-17T09:00:03.073Z level=ERROR source=file.go:341 msg="Error reading file" component="discovery manager scrape" discovery=file config=t path=/sd/targets.json err="unexpected end of JSON input"
(about 40,000 lines per second)
```

I have a fix with tests ready and will open a PR for it.

title: PrometheusNotificationQueueRunningFull can never fire: queue_length has an `alertmanager` label that queue_capacity lacks
body:
## What happened

`PrometheusNotificationQueueRunningFull` in `documentation/prometheus-mixin/alerts.libsonnet` can never fire on a current Prometheus. Its expression compares two series that no longer carry the same labels:

```
predict_linear(prometheus_notifications_queue_length{...}[5m], 60 * 30)
>
min_over_time(prometheus_notifications_queue_capacity{...}[5m])
```

`prometheus_notifications_queue_length` has an `alertmanager` label (one series per Alertmanager URL). `prometheus_notifications_queue_capacity` does not. A binary operator pairs series on their full label set, so the two sides never match and the result is always empty. The rule loads, reports `health="ok"` and `state="inactive"`, and stays that way even with a full queue, so nothing looks wrong.

## Evidence

Prometheus v3.15.0, one Prometheus with one Alertmanager target:

```
prometheus_notifications_queue_length{alertmanager="http://10.244.1.91:9093/api/v2/alerts", instance=..., job=...}   -> 1 series
prometheus_notifications_queue_capacity{instance=..., job=...}                                                      -> 1 series
```

The left side has an extra `alertmanager` label, so 0 pairs match. Observed on the kube-prometheus-stack 88.6.2 copy of the rule, which is generated from this mixin.

## Expected

The alert fires when the notification queue is predicted to fill within 30 minutes.

## Suggested fix

Drop the `alertmanager` label from the left side so both sides have the same labels:

```
(
  max without (alertmanager) (
    predict_linear(prometheus_notifications_queue_length{%(prometheusSelector)s}[5m], 60 * 30)
  )
>
  min_over_time(prometheus_notifications_queue_capacity{%(prometheusSelector)s}[5m])
)
```

`max` takes the fullest queue, which is the one to alert on. `ignoring(alertmanager)` alone is not enough: with more than one Alertmanager it turns the mismatch into many-to-one matching and errors. I run this corrected copy in production; the same fix was made downstream in thaum-xyz/ankhmorpork#1274.

I can send a PR if that is welcome.

title: TSDB: late out-of-order samples lost after restart on a low-volume server
body:
### What did you do?

Set `out_of_order_time_window: 6h` with one scraped series, sent 40 samples 2.5h late, restarted, then sent a second late batch after the next head compaction. The test below does this through the `tsdb` package, calling `ForceHeadMMap` and `Compact` every minute like the DB run loop does. I get the same result from the prometheus binary with both batches sent over remote write and a SIGTERM restart.

```go
package tsdb_test

import (
	"context"
	"math"
	"testing"
	"time"

	"github.com/stretchr/testify/require"

	"github.com/prometheus/prometheus/model/labels"
	"github.com/prometheus/prometheus/tsdb"
	"github.com/prometheus/prometheus/tsdb/chunkenc"
)

func TestOOOSamplesLostAfterRestart(t *testing.T) {
	dir := t.TempDir()
	opts := tsdb.DefaultOptions()
	opts.OutOfOrderTimeWindow = (6 * time.Hour).Milliseconds()
	open := func() *tsdb.DB {
		db, err := tsdb.Open(dir, nil, nil, opts, nil)
		require.NoError(t, err)
		db.DisableCompactions()
		return db
	}
	add := func(db *tsdb.DB, name string, ts ...time.Duration) {
		app := db.Appender(context.Background())
		for _, x := range ts {
			_, err := app.Append(0, labels.FromStrings("__name__", name), x.Milliseconds(), 1)
			require.NoError(t, err)
		}
		require.NoError(t, app.Commit())
	}
	// One scrape per minute, then what the DB run loop does every minute.
	run := func(db *tsdb.DB, from, to time.Duration) {
		for ts := from; ts < to; ts += time.Minute {
			add(db, "scraped", ts)
			db.ForceHeadMMap()
			require.NoError(t, db.Compact(context.Background()))
		}
	}
	// 40 late samples, 2.5h old.
	late := func(db *tsdb.DB, now time.Duration) {
		var ts []time.Duration
		for i := range 40 {
			ts = append(ts, now-150*time.Minute+time.Duration(i)*15*time.Second)
		}
		add(db, "late", ts...)
	}
	count := func(db *tsdb.DB) int {
		q, err := db.Querier(math.MinInt64, math.MaxInt64)
		require.NoError(t, err)
		defer q.Close()
		ss := q.Select(context.Background(), false, nil, labels.MustNewMatcher(labels.MatchEqual, "__name__", "late"))
		n := 0
		for ss.Next() {
			it := ss.At().Iterator(nil)
			for it.Next() != chunkenc.ValNone {
				n++
			}
		}
		return n
	}

	db := open()
	run(db, 0, 3*time.Hour)
	late(db, 3*time.Hour)
	run(db, 3*time.Hour, 4*time.Hour+20*time.Minute)
	require.NoError(t, db.Close())

	db = open()
	run(db, 4*time.Hour+20*time.Minute, 5*time.Hour+5*time.Minute)
	late(db, 5*time.Hour+5*time.Minute)
	t.Log("after second late batch:", count(db))
	run(db, 5*time.Hour+5*time.Minute, 10*time.Hour)
	require.NoError(t, db.Close())

	db = open()
	defer db.Close()
	t.Log("after compactions and restart:", count(db))
	require.Equal(t, 80, count(db))
}
```

### What did you expect to see?

All 80 late samples returned by queries.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

48 of 80 right after the second batch, and still 48 after later compactions and a restart. Without the first restart all 80 are returned.

After `ChunkDiskMapper.Truncate` resets the file sequence ([head_chunks.go#L999](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/v3.15.0/tsdb/chunks/head_chunks.go#L999)), the new out-of-order chunk gets ref 1:8, which is below `lastGarbageCollectedMmapRef` (2:8).

### System information

linux/arm64, go1.26.9

### Prometheus version

```text
v3.15.0 and main (c052a79)
```

### Prometheus configuration file

```yaml
storage:
  tsdb:
    out_of_order_time_window: 6h
```

### Alertmanager version

_No response_

### Alertmanager configuration file

_No response_

### Logs

_No response_

title: tsdb: start timestamps are written to XOR2 chunks when st-storage is disabled
body:
### What did you do?

I ran the TSDB head with XOR2 float chunks and `EnableSTAsZeroSample` (`created-timestamp-zero-ingestion`), but without `EnableSTStorage` (`st-storage`). XOR2 can be enabled on its own, with `storage.tsdb.chunk_encoding.floats: xor2` or `--enable-feature=xor2-encoding`. I appended 100 samples of a counter through `AppenderV2`, each with the counter's start timestamp, and one sample per commit, like a scrape. Then I restarted the head from its WAL.

### What did you expect to see?

No start timestamps stored, since `st-storage` is off. The `HeadOptions.EnableSTStorage` doc comment says it "determines whether databases (WAL/WBL, tsdb, agent) should set a Start Time value per sample".

### What did you see instead?

The start timestamps are stored in the head chunk anyway. On commit, the head passes each sample's `ST` to `memSeries.append`, which passes it to the chunk appender whether or not `storeST` is set. XOR2 stores it. The WAL follows `EnableSTStorage` and doesn't record it, so the start timestamps are gone after WAL replay:

| | Chunk bytes | Start timestamps in the chunk |
|---|---|---|
| Before restart | 439 | 0 ×1 (the zero sample), 1000000 ×100 |
| After WAL replay | 142 | 0 ×101 |

So the same data is encoded differently depending on whether it was replayed. Chunks m-mapped before a restart keep their start timestamps, and data rebuilt from the WAL doesn't. The difference carries over into compacted blocks. The chunk is this big because of the zero sample's start timestamp, which is #20067.

Should the head pass `st = 0` to the chunk appenders when `storeST` is false? That covers `append`, `appendHistogram`, `appendFloatHistogram`, and `insert` for out-of-order samples. I've only checked floats, but ST-capable histogram chunks (`histograms-st-encoding`) presumably behave the same.

This matters more once XOR2 becomes the default (#19080). Every `created-timestamp-zero-ingestion` user would then write start timestamps into chunks without enabling `st-storage`. I found this while reviewing Grafana Mimir's switch to `AppenderV2`, where the first chunk of a new series grew by about 2.7×.

Reproduction, in package `tsdb` on `main` (79cee8108):

```go
func dumpHeadChunk(t *testing.T, h *Head, lbls labels.Labels) {
	s := h.series.getByHash(lbls.Hash(), lbls)
	s.Lock()
	defer s.Unlock()
	c := s.headChunks.chunk
	sts := map[int64]int{}
	it := c.Iterator(nil)
	for it.Next() == chunkenc.ValFloat {
		sts[it.AtST()]++
	}
	t.Logf("chunk bytes=%d, start timestamps=%v", len(c.Bytes()), sts)
}

func TestSTInXOR2ChunksWithoutSTStorage(t *testing.T) {
	lbls := labels.FromStrings("__name__", "c_total")
	const st = int64(1_000_000)
	newHead := func(dir string) *Head {
		opts := DefaultHeadOptions()
		opts.ChunkDirRoot = dir
		opts.FloatChunkEncoding.Store(uint32(chunkenc.EncXOR2))
		opts.EnableSTAsZeroSample = true // EnableSTStorage stays false.
		w, err := wlog.New(nil, nil, filepath.Join(dir, "wal"), compression.None)
		require.NoError(t, err)
		h, err := NewHead(nil, nil, w, nil, opts, nil)
		require.NoError(t, err)
		require.NoError(t, h.Init(0))
		return h
	}

	dir := t.TempDir()
	h := newHead(dir)
	for i := int64(1); i <= 100; i++ {
		app := h.AppenderV2(t.Context())
		_, err := app.Append(0, lbls, st, st+i*60_000, float64(i), nil, nil, storage.AOptions{})
		require.NoError(t, err)
		require.NoError(t, app.Commit())
	}
	dumpHeadChunk(t, h, lbls) // chunk bytes=439, start timestamps=map[0:1 1000000:100]
	require.NoError(t, h.Close())

	h = newHead(dir) // Replays the WAL.
	defer h.Close()
	dumpHeadChunk(t, h, lbls) // chunk bytes=142, start timestamps=map[0:101]
}
```

### Prometheus version

`main` at 79cee8108.

title: tsdb: zero sample from EnableSTAsZeroSample has start timestamp 0, tripling XOR2 chunk size
body:
### What did you do?

I ran the TSDB head with XOR2 float chunks, `EnableSTStorage` (`st-storage`) and `EnableSTAsZeroSample` (`created-timestamp-zero-ingestion`). I appended 100 samples of a new counter through `AppenderV2`, each carrying the counter's start timestamp, one sample per commit.

### What did you expect to see?

A chunk about the size of one without start timestamps, since the start timestamp is the same for every sample of the series.

### What did you see instead?

The chunk is about three times bigger. `bestEffortAppendSTZeroSample` appends the zero sample with a start timestamp of 0 (`a.appendFloat(s, 0, st, 0, true)`, and the same for histograms), while every following sample carries the series' start timestamp. When the start timestamp changes within an XOR2 chunk, every sample after it is encoded with a start-timestamp delta. Here that change comes right after the first sample:

| Zero sample's start timestamp | Chunk bytes | Start timestamps in the chunk |
|---|---|---|
| 0 (current) | 439 | 0 ×1, 1000000 ×100 |
| The series' start timestamp | 143 | 1000000 ×101 |
| For reference: no start timestamps | 142 | 0 ×101 |

The numbers are the same after WAL replay. Without `st-storage` you get the same 439 bytes, because of #20066.

Could the zero sample be appended with `st` as its start timestamp as well, as in `a.appendFloat(s, st, st, 0, true)`? It's the counter's value at its start, so a start timestamp equal to its timestamp seems right to me, and the head accepts such a sample. Is there a reason it uses 0?

Reproduction, in package `tsdb` on `main` (79cee8108). The second run appends the zero sample explicitly, with the start timestamp set:

```go
func dumpHeadChunk(t *testing.T, h *Head, lbls labels.Labels) {
	s := h.series.getByHash(lbls.Hash(), lbls)
	s.Lock()
	defer s.Unlock()
	c := s.headChunks.chunk
	sts := map[int64]int{}
	it := c.Iterator(nil)
	for it.Next() == chunkenc.ValFloat {
		sts[it.AtST()]++
	}
	t.Logf("chunk bytes=%d, start timestamps=%v", len(c.Bytes()), sts)
}

func TestSTZeroSampleInflatesXOR2Chunk(t *testing.T) {
	lbls := labels.FromStrings("__name__", "c_total")
	const st = int64(1_000_000)
	for _, zeroIngestion := range []bool{true, false} {
		opts := DefaultHeadOptions()
		opts.ChunkDirRoot = t.TempDir()
		opts.FloatChunkEncoding.Store(uint32(chunkenc.EncXOR2))
		opts.EnableSTStorage.Store(true)
		opts.EnableSTAsZeroSample = zeroIngestion
		h, err := NewHead(nil, nil, nil, nil, opts, nil)
		require.NoError(t, err)
		require.NoError(t, h.Init(0))
		if !zeroIngestion {
			// The zero sample that EnableSTAsZeroSample writes, but with its start timestamp set.
			app := h.AppenderV2(t.Context())
			_, err := app.Append(0, lbls, st, st, 0, nil, nil, storage.AOptions{})
			require.NoError(t, err)
			require.NoError(t, app.Commit())
		}
		for i := int64(1); i <= 100; i++ {
			app := h.AppenderV2(t.Context())
			_, err := app.Append(0, lbls, st, st+i*60_000, float64(i), nil, nil, storage.AOptions{})
			require.NoError(t, err)
			require.NoError(t, app.Commit())
		}
		t.Logf("EnableSTAsZeroSample=%v", zeroIngestion)
		// true:  chunk bytes=439, start timestamps=map[0:1 1000000:100]
		// false: chunk bytes=143, start timestamps=map[1000000:101]
		dumpHeadChunk(t, h, lbls)
		require.NoError(t, h.Close())
	}
}
```

### Prometheus version

`main` at 79cee8108.

title: OTLP receiver: target_info is not emitted when keep_identifying_resource_attributes is true and resource only has identifying attributes
remote_write: send_native_histograms is documented as a no-op (always true) for io.prometheus.write.v2.Request, but the queue manager still drops histograms when it is false
body:
### What did you do?

Configured a `remote_write` entry with `protobuf_message: io.prometheus.write.v2.Request` and left `send_native_histograms` at its default (false), with `scrape_native_histograms: true` and `convert_classic_histograms_to_nhcb: true`, sending to an OpenTelemetry Collector `prometheus_remote_write` receiver. Prometheus 3.13.2 and 3.14.0.

### What did you expect to see?

`docs/configuration/configuration.md` says for `send_native_histograms`: "For the `io.prometheus.write.v2.Request` message, this option is noop (always true)." So the native histograms and the NHCB-converted classic histograms should be sent over the v2 message without setting it.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

No histograms leave Prometheus. `QueueManager.AppendHistograms` and `AppendFloatHistograms` return early when `!t.sendNativeHistograms`, and `populateV2TimeSeries` fills the histogram field only when `sendNativeHistograms` is true (`storage/remote/queue_manager.go` on `release-3.14`, same on `main`). With `send_native_histograms: true` on the same entry the histograms arrive at the receiver.

Either the documentation should say that the option is required for v2 as well, or the v2 code path should force it on as documented. The second matches the documented intent and what users of the OpenTelemetry receiver need: remote write v2 is the only message it accepts, and it drops classic histograms unless they are converted to NHCB and sent as native histograms.

### System information

Linux x86_64, Kubernetes, official quay.io/prometheus/prometheus images

### Prometheus version

```text
prometheus, version 3.13.2 and 3.14.0
```

### Prometheus configuration file

```yaml
global:
  scrape_interval: 30s
  scrape_native_histograms: true
  convert_classic_histograms_to_nhcb: true
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: sample-app
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['sample-app:8080']
remote_write:
  - url: http://otel-collector:9090/api/v1/write
    protobuf_message: io.prometheus.write.v2.Request
    # send_native_histograms not set (default false)
```

title: metadata-wal-records has no effect in 3.10 to 3.15: no Metadata WAL records are written, remote write v2 carries no type, unit or help (backport of #19678)
body:
### What did you do?

Started Prometheus 3.13.2 with `--enable-feature=metadata-wal-records` and one `remote_write` entry using `protobuf_message: io.prometheus.write.v2.Request`, pointing at an OpenTelemetry Collector `prometheus_remote_write` receiver (opentelemetry-collector-contrib 0.158.0). Scraped ordinary targets (node_exporter, kube-state-metrics, a sample application with counters and classic histograms) with the default scrape protocols.

Then repeated the same setup with the official `quay.io/prometheus/prometheus` images of 3.8.1, 3.9.1, 3.10, 3.11, 3.12, 3.14 and a build of `main`, and for each version counted the WAL record types in the data directory (record type byte 6 = Metadata, after decompressing the snappy-compressed records) and checked the metric types that the collector receives (debug exporter).

### What did you expect to see?

Metadata records in the WAL and remote write v2 messages that carry the type, unit and help of every series, so the receiver emits typed counters and histograms. This is what 3.8.1, 3.9.1 and `main` do with the same configuration.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

On 3.10 to 3.14 (and 3.15.0 by inspection of the `release-3.15` branch) the WAL contains no Metadata records at all, and every series reaches the receiver as `METRIC_TYPE_UNSPECIFIED`, which the collector turns into untyped gauges. The flag is accepted and listed as enabled; there is no warning.

Cause: `--enable-feature=metadata-wal-records` set `scrape.AppendMetadata` and `web.AppendMetadata` but never set `tsdb.Options.EnableMetadataWALRecords`. The classic `storage.Appender.UpdateMetadata` path does not check that option, but since #17978 (3.10) the scrape manager prefers `AppenderV2`, which appends metadata records only when `EnableMetadataWALRecords` is set. #19678 (merged 2026-09-10) wires the option and adds a regression test, but it is only on `main`: `cmd/prometheus/main.go` on `release-3.13`, `release-3.14` and `release-3.15` has no `EnableMetadataWALRecords`, and 3.13.4 and 3.15.0 were released without it.

Request: backport #19678 to `release-3.15` and to `release-3.13` (which still receives patch releases), and call the regression out in the changelog: the flag has silently done nothing since 3.10, and metadata over remote write v2 (type, unit, help) is the main reason to enable it. Related: #17075.

title: storage/remote: retry metrics count samples dropped by sample_age_limit
body: ### What did you do? While developing #20107 that adds RW2 sender metrics for samples and histograms sent without metadata, I tested the existing retry metrics when `sample_age_limit` expires a sample during backoff. The first RW2 request contained one sample and returned a recoverable error. The retry backoff was longer than `sample_age_limit`, causing the retry request to be rebuilt without the expired sample. reproduce test code ```go func TestSendV2SamplesWithBackoffMetricsAfterSampleAgeLimit(t *testing.T) { cfg := config.DefaultQueueConfig cfg.MaxShards = 1 cfg.MaxSamplesPerSend = 1 cfg.SampleAgeLimit = model.Duration(100 * time.Millisecond) cfg.MinBackoff = model.Duration(300 * time.Millisecond) cfg.MaxBackoff = model.Duration(300 * time.Millisecond) c := NewTestWriteClient(remoteapi.WriteV2MessageType) c.injectErrors([]error{RecoverableError{errors.New("pretend 500"), 0}, nil}) m := newTestQueueManager(t, cfg, config.DefaultMetadataConfig, defaultFlushDeadline, c, remoteapi.WriteV2MessageType) recs := testwal.GenerateRecords(testwal.RecordsCase{ Series: 1, SamplesPerSeries: 1, TsFn: func(_, _ int) int64 { return timestamp.FromTime(time.Now()) }, }) m.StoreSeries(recs.Series, 0) m.Start() defer m.Stop() require.True(t, m.Append(recs.Samples)) require.Eventually(t, func() bool { c.mtx.Lock() defer c.mtx.Unlock() return c.writesReceived == 1 }, 5*time.Second, 10*time.Millisecond) require.Equal(t, 1.0, client_testutil.ToFloat64(m.metrics.droppedSamplesTotal.WithLabelValues(reasonTooOld))) require.Equal(t, 1.0, client_testutil.ToFloat64(m.metrics.samplesTotal)) } ``` ### What did you expect to see? The metrics should reflect the data actually included in each outgoing attempt: - `prometheus_remote_storage_samples_total`: `1` - `prometheus_remote_storage_samples_dropped_total{reason="too_old"}`: `1` The failed first attempt contained one sample, while the rebuilt retry request contained zero samples. ### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances? ```sh go test ./storage/remote \ -run '^TestSendV2SamplesWithBackoffMetricsAfterSampleAgeLimit$' \ -count=1 -v ``` ``` prometheus git:(main) ✗ go test ./storage/remote \ -run '^TestSendV2SamplesWithBackoffMetricsAfterSampleAgeLimit$' \ -count=1 -v === RUN TestSendV2SamplesWithBackoffMetricsAfterSampleAgeLimit queue_manager_test.go:2416: Error Trace: /Users/shiloh.lee/workspace/prometheus/storage/remote/queue_manager_test.go:2416 Error: Not equal: expected: 1 actual : 2 Test: TestSendV2SamplesWithBackoffMetricsAfterSampleAgeLimit --- FAIL: TestSendV2SamplesWithBackoffMetricsAfterSampleAgeLimit (0.32s) FAIL FAIL github.com/prometheus/prometheus/storage/remote 0.787s FAIL ``` ### System information _No response_ ### Prometheus version ```text ``` ### Prometheus configuration file ```yaml ``` ### Alertmanager version ```text ``` ### Alertmanager configuration file ```yaml ``` ### Logs ```text ```

title: remote_write: restart from savepoint tracking issue
body:
This tracks the work for remote write restarting from a segment-based savepoint, based on the proposal (https://github.com/prometheus/proposals/pull/72). The first piece is the initial feature behind `--enable-feature=remote-write-savepoint` (#18485).

Follow ups:

- [ ] Keep the savepoint when `queue_config` changes by excluding it from the queue hash (proposal goal 3).
- [ ] Prevent unread segments from being truncated in agent mode (#17616)
    - It should be capped by `--storage.agent.retention.max-time`.
    - ^^ is the main thing preventing unbounded WAL grownth in the event we cannot truncation due to WAL lag
- [ ] Document that server mode can't recover a backlog once head truncation has checkpointed it.
- [ ] Require a non-zero `sample_age_limit` when the feature is enabled (proposal goal 4).
- [ ] Make the savepoint persist interval configurable.
- [ ] Decide what to do with queue shutdown ordering noted here, https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/18485#discussion_r4334883031. 
    - Once a queue stops, `Append` returns false and the watcher keeps reading and dropping. 
    - #18485 will work around this by persisting before the stop but there might be a more ideal scenario
- [ ] Decide how external label changes should interact with a resumed savepoint. Right now old samples could get re-sent with the new labels.
- At-least-once delivery
    - [ ] Track the lowest timestamp sent on each savepoint
    - [ ] Only advance the savepoint once every shard has sent a segment

title: CI: tsdb package regularly hits the 10m go test timeout under -race
body:
The "Go tests" job runs `go test -race ./...` (through `make`) with the default 10m timeout. The `tsdb` package uses most of that time, so it sometimes fails when a runner is slow, even when no test hangs.

Recent failures (none of these PRs change `tsdb`):

- #20110, two attempts on the same commit failed, the third passed: [job 1](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/actions/runs/39510583199/job/118930302389), [job 2](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/actions/runs/39510583199/job/119097502784)
- #20099: [job](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/actions/runs/39668395700/job/119459425869)

Each failure has the same signature:

```
panic: test timed out after 10m0s
	running tests:
		TestBlockReloadInterval/one_second_interval (3s)
		TestOOOCompactionWithNormalCompaction_AppendV2/custom_buckets_float_histogram (0s)
		...
FAIL	github.com/prometheus/prometheus/tsdb	600.294s
```

The tests in the "running tests" list are different in each failure, and each of them had run for only 0 to 3 seconds. No goroutine was blocked for minutes. So this is not a hang. The package as a whole goes over the limit.

Time for `tsdb` under `-race` on green `main` runs:

| Date | Duration |
|---|---|
| 2026-07-24 | 547s |
| 2026-08-19 | 447s |
| 2026-09-14 | 529s |
| 2026-10-03 | 427s |
| 2026-10-21 (6 runs) | 407s, 458s, 484s, 545s, 557s, 596s |

A normal run uses 70% to 99% of the 600s limit, so a small slowdown makes it fail.

#18630 reported the same problem and was closed by #18632, which made `TestCancelCompactions` faster. That helped, but the margin is still very small.

Possible fixes:

1. Increase the timeout for the race run, for example `-timeout 20m`. This is a small change, but it can hide future slowdowns. If we do this, we should probably set it in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` and not in `Makefile.common`, because other repos share `Makefile.common`.
2. Make the `tsdb` tests faster. For example, skip some long variants under `-race`, or let more tests run in parallel.
3. Run `tsdb` in its own CI step or job, with its own timeout.
